WEBSTER (JOHN) 1610–1682.
4202. *The Displaying of Supposed Witchcraft.* In which it is argued that there are many sorts of deceivers and impostors, and various people suffering from a passive delusion of melancholy and imagination <note>original: "Fancy"</note>. However, the idea that a physical pact <note>original: "Corporeal League"</note> is made between the Devil and the witch... or that witches are turned into cats or dogs, raise tempests, or the like, is utterly denied and disproved. Within this work is also handled the existence of angels and spirits... with other profound <note>original: "abstruse"</note> matters... small folio. *London, printed by J. M.,* 1677.
With handwritten <note>original: "MS."</note> notes by William Blackford, 1678.
Webster had been a chaplain and surgeon in the Parliamentary army. A popular preacher in London, he retired to the country in 1657 to practice medicine.

# To his Honorable and honored Friends *Thomas Parker* of *Braisholme*, *John Assheton* of the *Lower-Hall*, *William Drake* of *Barnoldswick-coat*, *William Johnson* of the *Grange*, *Henry Marsden* of *Gisburne* Esquires, and his Majesty’s Justices of Peace and *Quorum* <note>original: *Quorum*; a term referring to select justices whose presence was legally required to hold a session of court</note> in the West Riding of *Yorkshire*.

->*Honorable Gentlemen and honored Friends,*<-

I do not dedicate this piece of my labors to you to beg protection for it, as though I feared either its weakness or the malicious criticisms of the ignorant. For I know very well, and have experienced, that it is the usual habit of idle and meddlesome <note>original: "pragmatical"</note> persons to please their own spiteful moods by condemning and scoffing at the hard-earned writings <note>original: "painful lucubrations"</note> of others. I have always judged that nothing ought to be published that, like a *noun substantive* <note>original: "Noun Substantive"; in older grammar, a noun that can stand alone and does not require an adjective to complete its meaning</note>, cannot stand by itself without being supported by any other joined help. Nor is this out of a vain confidence or an excessive opinion of my own abilities, though I know very well that some are as much in love with the creations of their own brains as others are with their own children <note>original: "fruit of their loines"</note>. I have for many years been as wary and vigilant as anyone could be to watch over myself, so that I might both know and maintain a clear distinction between flattering *imagination* <note>original: "Phantasie"</note> and true, sound judgment. But I shall briefly show you the true reasons for my presenting this humble piece for your reading and judgment.

1. The first reason is because you have all been gentlemen well known to me for many years, being my near neighbors. Furthermore, I have been freely admitted to noble and generous conversation with you, and have been trusted and honored by you in your domestic concerns, where through my *medical profession* I might be of service to

<meta>catchword: you,</meta>

you or your families, far beyond my poor merit and desert. *And having been for many years a careful observer of your conduct <note>original: "deportments"</note> in your positions of trust as* magistrates—*for someone who is merely a bystander looking on may perhaps have noticed as much as those who are* players <note>original: "Gamesters"; here referring to those actively involved in the "game" of public affairs</note>—*I was moved to present this piece of my labors to you because of that knowledge and acquaintance* <gloss>I had with you</gloss> *rather than to others whose abilities and integrity I did not understand as well. And I hope I may say, without suspicion of flattery (of which I am sure both yourselves and others who know me will acquit me—for if I am guilty in any way, it is rather in being too blunt and open), that you have been and are true* patriots *to your* country, *and not only* justices of the peace, *but true preservers of it and* peacemakers *among all your* neighbors; *and really, this is one of the chief reasons why I have dedicated this* treatise *to you.*

2. Another reason is that *you have all known me well, along with most of the details of my life—both my follies and weaknesses, as well as my other talents and abilities. Therefore, considering these things, I thought none more fit than yourselves to whom I might offer this laborious work. For you know well that (excepting my* medical practice <note>original: "Physical Practice"</note>, *which age and infirmity will not allow me to attend to very much), I have lived a solitary and sedentary life for many years past, for myself and the Muses <note>original: *mihi & Musis*; a Latin phrase indicating a life dedicated to private study and the arts</note>, having had more conversation with the dead than the living—that is, more with* books *than with* men. *Therefore, I present this to you, as you are better able than most others who do not know me to judge what I am capable of achieving in a subject such as this.*

3. Also, it is well known to you *that I have had a large portion of trouble and persecution in this outward world, in which you did not, like many others, stand far off as though you did not know me. Instead, like people of* justice *and true* greatness of spirit <note>original: "Magnanimity"</note>, *you dared both to look upon and assist wronged innocence, even though it was smeared over with the envious dirt of malicious scandals, and even at that very moment in time when the whole giddy pack of barking dogs and ra-* <note>The text ends mid-word due to damage; the catchword "venous" suggests the word is "ravenous."</note>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's dedication to several Yorkshire Justices of the Peace. He is expressing his deep gratitude for their support during a time when he was under attack from critics or legal adversaries.</meta>

...venomous wolves labored to devour me. But then, even then, <gloss>you</gloss> extended your helping hands and were willing to declare what you knew of my innocence. This was so generous, noble, and Christian a kind of just compassion that I would forever consider myself a wretched person if I did not have it deeply impressed upon my heart <note>original: "breast"</note> and memory—something that no time nor adversity can ever erase. However, being in a condition where I may truly say with the Apostle Saint Peter, *Silver and gold have I none* <note>original Greek: "Αργύριον καὶ χρυσίον οὐχ ὑπάρχει μοι"</note> (which I know you do not expect), the greatest power I have is my weak pen, to testify to my thankfulness for your unparalleled kindness. Therefore, I offer this treatise as a perpetual and monumental memorial to all future generations <note>original: "Posterities"</note> of my gratitude and your goodness.

And further, to whom can a subject of this nature be more suitably and fitly presented than to such magistrates as yourselves? You often have occasion to be burdened and troubled with ignorant, envious, and sometimes malicious <note>original: "knavish"</note> accusations against people suspected of <term>witchcraft</term>, <term>sorcery</term>, <term>charming</term>, and <term>enchantment</term>. In these cases, to acquit the guilty and condemn the innocent is equally an abomination to the Lord. Therefore, much judgment, caution, care, and diligent inspection ought to be used in examining and determining these matters. In this work, I have used as much clarity and plainness as possible to distinguish between those who are <term>impostors</term>, <term>cheaters</term>, and active <term>deceivers</term>, and those who are merely under a passive delusion through an ignorant and superstitious education, a <term>melancholy</term> <note>At the time, "melancholy" was considered a physical imbalance that could cause hallucinations or irrational beliefs.</note> temperament and constitution, or led by the vain belief in ineffective charms, pictures, ceremonies, and the like, which were traditionally taught to them. 

The first sort deserve to be punished for defrauding the people and pretending to bring to pass things that they have neither the skill nor power to perform. But the other sort merit pity and instruction, or a physician's help, rather than any punishment at all. And I make bold to remind you of this one thing especially: that in things of this nature, great heed ought to be taken regarding the conditions, qualities, goals, and intentions of the <term>complainants</term> and <term>informers</term>, who are often...

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page concludes the author's dedication to several Yorkshire Justices of the Peace. Webster is finishing his argument that many witchcraft accusations are based on deception or mental illness rather than reality.</meta>

<page-type>dedication</page-type>
<header>The Epistle Dedicatory.</header>

---

...more worthy of punishment than the persons accused. For many, out of a mere deluded fancy, an envious mind, ignorance, and superstition, attribute natural diseases, ailments, and accidents to *witches* and *witchcraft*, when in truth there is no such matter at all. And sometimes they counterfeit strange fits and diseases, such as the vomiting of unnatural and strange things, which—if narrowly looked into and examined—are nothing but jugglings and deceitful conspiracies <note>original: "confederacies"</note>. Yet, out of malice, revenge, or some other base motives, these people accuse others of being the causes of their suffering.

And though you should find some people confidently confessing that they have made a visible and physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> pact <note>original: "league"</note> with the *Devil*, and that he has carnal intercourse with them, and that he sucks upon some parts of their bodies, and that they are transformed <note>original: "Transubstantiated"</note> into dogs, cats, and the like, or that they fly through the air and raise tempests; yet (I hope) I have sufficiently proved by the Word of God, the true grounds of theology, and sound reason, that there never has been any such witch existing in the nature of things <note>original: "rerum natura"</note>. Therefore, you may know what credit should be given to such fables and impossibilities.

*So, wishing that you may long live in health and happiness to serve His Majesty and your country—which is and shall be my faithful prayer for you—I take my leave, subscribing myself,*

->**Your Worships'**<-

->**most Faithful Friend,**<-

->**and Devoted Servant,**<-

->**John Webster.**<-

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page begins the author's preface to the reader. Webster anticipates criticism for his work, noting that he faced similar mockery after publishing his previous book on metals.</meta>

---

# THE
## PREFACE or INTRODUCTION.

---

Readers,

Knowing for certain that all writings, once published, share a single fate: to stand or fall by the common criticisms, judgments, and opinions of men. Therefore, I have attached no title or label <note>original: "Epithete"</note> to this work, as I foresee that this treatise—like a man at sea who is forced to endure all kinds of weather—must survive the criticisms of all sorts of people, no matter how varied their minds and principles may be. And although people’s preferences and opinions are usually as different as their faces, I will list a few general categories that are broad enough to include most other specific types, in this order:

1. First, what a man has found to be true through experience in similar cases may reasonably lead him to expect the same thing to happen again. For example, after I had published my book *The History of Metals*, I encountered some people who were no more learned than parrots—who could not even write proper English and whose greatest skill was in various forms of vice <note>original: "debauchery"</note>—and other poor pedants <term>pedant: someone who makes a show of knowledge but lacks real understanding</term> who were hardly masters of grammar. Yet this group and others like them were rash and bold enough to criticize my hard work <note>original: "painful endeavours"</note> and to scoff at it as a mere collection of other people's ideas. Therefore, in publishing this work—which deals with a dark and mysterious subject—I will very likely encounter groups of such rash and ignorant people. To them, I will only offer this sharp but appropriate response <note>original: "responsion"</note>. It is common for many who could never craft a shoe to criticize and find fault with the shoemaker. But such "wise" men (who belong in Gotham <note>a village famous in English folklore for the foolishness of its inhabitants</note>) may learn these two proverbs: *None is so bold as blind Bayard* <note>an old proverb referring to a blind horse that charges ahead without seeing danger</note>, and *A fool's bolt is soon shot* <note>a "bolt" was a short, heavy arrow; the proverb means a foolish person acts or speaks too quickly without thinking</note>. Their heads may be better suited for feathers than the laurel wreath <note>an ancient symbol of victory and poetic achievement</note>. When any of them have compiled such a collection as my former book, or published a work like this one, only then will I give them a better answer. Until then: *Lettuce should not be given to these donkeys to eat, as thistles are sufficient for them* <note>original: "Lactucas non esse dandas hisce Asinis comedendas, cum illis sufficiant cardui"</note>.

<summary>Webster opens his preface by acknowledging that all published works face public criticism. He recounts the mockery he faced from "ignorant" critics for his previous book on metals and warns that he expects similar attacks on this new, mysterious subject.</summary>
<keywords>criticism, public opinion, History of Metals, pedantry, proverbs, ignorance, John Webster, Gotham, blind Bayard</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's classification of potential critics. Having already addressed the ignorant in the previous section, he now turns his attention to the arrogant and the envious.</meta>

-> **The Preface,** <-

2. There is another group of people who think they are very wise in their own eyes, but their brains are like inflated bladders filled with the wind of arrogance and self-conceit. These people usually huff, snuff, and puff at everything that does not match their own whimsical opinions <note>original: "Capricious Cockcombs", a term for the heads of conceited people, often comparing them to a jester’s cap.</note>. For the most part, their actual abilities consist only of snippets they have gathered from the theaters, or from conversations held in taverns and coffeehouses. If they can manage a few pitiful bits of mockery and teasing, they think themselves qualified and able to judge anything—even if they have never read or seen it, except for the title page. To these people, I have little to say, as they are merely shallow and empty "vaporosos" <note>original: "Vaporoso’s", likely meaning people full of "vapors" (hot air or vanity) rather than substance.</note> who vanish into smoke and nothingness at the slightest blast of sound reasoning. I only wish for them to seriously consider the saying of the wise man: <margin>Proverbs 26:12</margin> *Do you see a man wise in his own conceit? There is more hope for a fool than for him.* Furthermore, the advice of a learned Father is fitting for such vain and overconfident people: "It is better to fear rightly than to trust wrongly; and it is more useful for a man to recognize himself as weak so that he may become strong, than to wish to appear strong and turn out to be weak." <note>original: "Expedit benè timere, quam malè fidere; & utilius est, ut infirmum se homo cognoscat, ut fortis existat, quàm fortis videri velit, & infirmus emergat."</note>

3. There is another sort of person who is so harshly envious that they can tolerate nothing that is not their own work or does not meet their personal approval. They cannot help but condemn the work of others, no matter how good or beneficial it may be, simply because it might overshadow their own fame or fail to increase their own reputation. Just as various kinds of insects feed on the waste of other animals, these people feed their own moods and please their own whims by slandering and blackening the work of others. Being guilty of irritable gloominess <term>morosity: a state of being sullen, gloomy, or ill-tempered</term>, they cannot look kindly upon anyone else's achievements without frowning, feeling disgust, and passing judgment. We have little to say to such people, but will leave them to the bitterness of their own hearts and the resentment of their own minds. We did not intend our work for them, nor do we value their criticisms, no matter how sharp and bitter they may be. For "no success is so great that it can escape the teeth of malice." <note>original: "nulla fœlicitas tam magna est, ut malignitatis dentes vitare possit."</note> Therefore, it is wise to use discretion and patiently endure that for which human foresight can find no remedy.

4. There are others who have grown stubborn in their minds

<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<summary>In this part of the preface, the author dismisses two types of critics: the arrogant who gain their "wisdom" from gossip and plays, and the envious who instinctively attack any work they did not produce themselves.</summary>
<keywords>criticism, arrogance, envy, self-conceit, Proverbs 26:12, Augustine, malice, taverns, theaters</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's critique of people who are stubbornly set in their ways regarding the supernatural. He transitions from describing those who refuse to learn to those for whom he actually wrote the book.</meta>

<header>or Introduction.</header>

...and intentions concerning spirits, apparitions, witchcraft, sorcery, enchantment, and the like. They have grown stubborn <note>original: "pertinacious"</note> and determined to stick to the opinions they absorbed through an ignorant education. They do not consider that while perseverance in a good cause or a well-grounded opinion is praiseworthy and commendable, stubbornness in a bad or poorly founded belief <note>original: "tenent"</note> is just as harmful. It is every wise person’s duty to strive for the cultivation and improvement of their intellect and never to be ashamed of learning something they did not know before. The minds of men were not only darkened by the fall of Adam, but are also significantly misled by absorbing errors in their younger and more reckless years; they should try with all their strength to free themselves from these errors. 

But anyone who is willfully settled on the sediment and dregs of former opinions—no matter how erroneous—has blocked out all further light from shining into their understanding and has become willfully blind. To such people, we shall only offer the example and practice of the Apostle, who said: <margin>1 Corinthians 13:11</margin> *When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things.* I also advise them not to refuse the counsel of St. Augustine, who said:

> "No age can seem too late to learn what is necessary; for although it is more fitting for the elderly to teach than to learn, it is nonetheless more fitting to learn than to be ignorant." <note>original: "Ad discendum quod opus est, nulla ætas sera videri potest : quia etsi senes magis decet docere quàm discere; magis tamen decet discere, quam ignorare."</note>

And they need not be ashamed to imitate Socrates, who grew old learning something new every day. <insert>by</insert>

5. Just as we did not intend this treatise and introduction for the types of people we listed previously, there are others to whom we freely offer and present it. We will show the grounds and causes that moved us to undertake such a mysterious and dangerous subject. These readers are those who possess a humble, lowly, and fair <note>original: "equal"</note> mind, who usually read books to be informed and to learn truths of which they are ignorant, or to be confirmed in things they already partly knew. It is to these people alone that we offer our labors. Therefore, we shall honestly declare to them the causes and reasons for our undertaking, which are as follows:

1. Although there is a numerous company of authors who...

<sig>a 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: have</meta>

<summary>The author criticizes those who stubbornly cling to childhood errors about the supernatural and urges readers to seek intellectual growth. He clarifies that his book is intended for humble, fair-minded readers who seek truth rather than those who are willfully ignorant.</summary>
<keywords>intellectual growth, stubbornness, St. Augustine, Socrates, 1 Corinthians 13:11, witchcraft, spirits, education, religious errors</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues the author's preface, moving from a general exhortation on learning to a critique of existing literature on the supernatural.</meta>

<header># The Preface,</header>

...have written about magic, witchcraft, sorcery, enchantment,
spirits, and apparitions across various ages, in different countries,
and in various languages. Yet for the most part, they have only bor-
rowed from one another or have transcribed what others had
written before them. Consequently, there has been no real
progress made in truly discovering the theory or basis of these
dark and hidden matters, nor has any precise care been
taken to provide examples of factual matters that have been reliably and suffici-
ently attested. Instead, there are only collections and confused heaps of sto-
ries and accounts shuffled together, where not one in a hundred
of them appeared to be true or even plausible.
Because of this, the understandings of readers have remained
unenlightened, their memories confused, and their brains
stuffed with whimsies and fantasies <note>original: "Chimera’s"</note>. And although there is
nothing more common than disputes about witches and witch-
craft, both in speech and writing, not one person among the great multi-
tudes has plainly told us in what sense or under what
definition they use the words, nor what description is a-
greed upon for either of these, so that their existence or non-
existence, and their power and operations, might be known and deter-
mined. Instead, all the disputes concerning them so far have
been loose, wild, and vague <note>original: "in *vagum*"</note>. Therefore, to remedy
this, as far as such a subject allows and our abilities
permit, we were moved and have attempted to clear those
difficulties. And if we do not flatter and deceive ourselves (which is a common affliction <note>original: "epidemical"</note> to man-
kind), we have in some measure reasonably succeeded,
since we have plainly laid down the definition and meaning of
the words "witches" and "witchcraft," explaining in
what sense we grant that they exist, and in what sense and re-
spect we do not, which we believe is more (as we conceive)
than has yet been achieved by anyone else. And although our ex-
amples of factual matters are neither as precise nor as full as
might be desired—for things of this nature are deep and hidden—
yet they are the best we could select or choose; and this is one
chief reason why I undertook to treat this subject.

Yet finding that recently two persons of great learning and note—who are both (as I am informed) beneficed ministers in the Church, namely *Dr. Casaubon* and *Mr. Glanvil*—have newly embraced such a bad cause and taken the conflict upon themselves; and for that purpose, they have newly polished the old weapons and raked up the old arguments from the Popish sewer <note>original: "Sink"</note> and dunghills, and put them into a new dress so that they might appear with greater luster. Thus, they labor with tooth and nail to maintain the old, rotten assertions: the one in his book called *A Treatise proving Spirits and Witches, etc.*, the other in a treatise called *A Blow at Modern Sadducism, etc.*

Finding these (I say) as two new champions defying all who are of a contrary judgment, I was stirred up to answer their supposedly strong arguments and invincible examples. This I have done (I confess) without fear or any great regard for their titles, positions, or worldly dignities, but only considering the strength or weakness of their arguments, proofs, and reasoning. For in this particular matter with which I must deal, it is not with the men themselves, but with their opinions and the grounds upon which they would lay their foundations. And if I am criticized for dealing too sharply and harshly with them, they must excuse me, for I profess I have no ill will at all against their persons—no more than against a non-entity—but I was justly zealous for the truth and bitter against such opinions as they have expressed. To me, these seem dangerous and in some respects impious, as (I believe) I have fully proved. This was another reason for my writing about this subject.

3. Another reason that made me undertake this subject was the horrid absurdities that the belief <note>original: "tenent"</note> of the common witch-mongers brings with it. This belief not only tends to promote superstition and Popery but is also very derogatory to the wisdom, justice, and providence of the Almighty. It serves to exalt the power of the kingdom of darkness and to question the truth of the principal article of the Christian faith,

If anyone is disturbed that I seem to maintain some things that are *paradoxes*, I hope I may ask leave to depart from the opinions of others, just as others have departed from those who went before them. And I ask them not so much to consider either the novelty or strangeness of the opinions, but rather the weight and strength of the reasons that are laid down to support and sustain <note>original: "statuminate"</note> them; for if the arguments are sound and valid, the *tenets* built upon them cannot be weak and tottering. And although I acknowledge that I have human frailties and so may err, yet I have no mind or will stubbornly to persevere in an error; and since these things that we have treated lie so far from the range <note>original: "ken"</note> of our senses, and experiments of this nature are either so rare or uncertain, we may rationally expect pardon rather than criticism.

But I shall say no more, but let the book speak for itself, only desiring the *readers* first to read and seriously consider before they judge, so that I may have cause to bid them *farewell*.

Dated *February* 23, 1673.

## CHAP. I.

*Of the false, irrational, and unchristian criticisms that have been, and still are, cast upon learned men for writing about obscure subjects: as also for treating of apparitions and witchcraft, especially if they went against the common stream of popular opinion.*

SINCE I am about to treat the mysterious and obscure subject of witches and witchcraft, I cannot but think it necessary (especially to make the things we handle more plain and evident) to imitate architects, who, when they intend to raise some fine building or edifice, do not only provide themselves with good and lasting materials, but above all take care to lay a firm and sure foundation. This they cannot well accomplish unless the earth and rubbish are removed, so that firm ground for a foundation may be found. So, before I lay the foundation of what I intend in this discourse, I shall labor to remove some criticisms and slanders that are usually cast upon those learned persons who labor to unchain imprisoned truth, and who dare to cross the stream of popular opinion backed by apparent authority, antiquity, or the universality of votes—especially if they have involved themselves in occult and mysterious subjects.

<margin>Reason 1.</margin>
1. Because the best part of a man, from a natural perspective, is his courage, resolution, and magnanimity, which should make him resolute and courageous to declare and maintain what he, upon sound and rational grounds, understands to be truth. He should not at all fear the censure or judgment of others, who may have had no better means to inform themselves, or perhaps have been less diligent, and regardless are subject to the same errors and mistakes as all of humanity—who must all confess the truth of that unerring oracle, *to err is human.* And therefore, he must certainly be a person of a poor, base, and low spirit who conceals his own sentiments regarding the truth for fear of the censure or slanders of others.

<margin>Reason 2.</margin>
2. He that is afraid to declare his thoughts for fear of censure or scandal must necessarily be very weak in his morals, as having little affection for truth, which is the chief object of the intellect and consequently ought, above all things, to sway and lead the emotions. To be frightened from owning or declaring the truth for fear of the vain, airy, groundless, and erroneous censures of others must certainly show a man to be weak in the grounds of morality and to have small affection for virtue, whose guide is truth. <margin>Augustine, *On the Christian Combat*.</margin> The learned Father said exceedingly well to this purpose: *He who hides the truth and he who utters a lie are both guilty: the former because he does not wish to be helpful, the latter because he desires to harm.*

<margin>Reason 3.</margin>
3. He that conceals the truth he knows for fear of the censures of others must certainly have little of Christianity in him, <margin>Proverbs 23:23.</margin> for we are commanded to buy the truth and not to sell it. For a Christian to conceal the truth, and not to dare to declare and defend it for fear of the vain and perishing censures of men, is to make an absolute sale of the truth—and that for the worst of all prices that can be. For what a weightless and worthless price are the judgments and opinions of vain man, whose breath is in his nostrils and whose life is but a vapor, that a Christian should, for fear of such vain censures, be afraid to declare or defend the truth? Therefore, let the subtle politicians and *Machiavellians* of this age (who have in a manner turned the truth of the Christian religion and the most certain rules of Providence into atheism, and become vain idolaters who sacrifice to the falsely adored and deified fancies of their own craft and cunning) think or say what they <margin>Gregory, *Homilies*.</margin> please; yet the rule of pious *Gregory* will ever hold true: *He ought to be a defender of the truth who, when he thinks rightly, is not afraid to speak, nor is he ashamed.* <margin>Chrysostom, on Matthew.</margin> And the words of *Chrysostom* ought never to be forgotten by a good Christian and one who fears God, who says: *Not only is he a betrayer of the truth who speaks a lie as truth, but also he who does not freely pronounce the truth which he ought to pronounce, or does not freely defend the truth which he ought to defend.* But as there have been some who have been frightened by the feigned

Bugbears of malevolent men's criticisms and scandals; so there have been others, to whom Nature has given greater courage, who were better principled in their morals, and better grounded in the Christian religion, who have scorned and undervalued those criticisms as vanities and trifles, and these were those

> ———— Quos Jupiter æquus amavit,
> Et meliore luto finxit præcordia Titan.

These were those who for the advancement of truth and learning, and the benefit of mankind, dared undertake
->*Ire per excubias, & se committere Parcis.*<-
And feared not the tempestuous storms of venomous tongues or malicious minds, of which we shall here list a sufficient catalogue.

1. In the first place, we need not travel far, either in regard to time or place, to find precedents of those who have undergone no small criticism and derision for vindicating truth and laboring for its advancement, even against common and deep-rooted opinion. So poorly have new inventors and inventions always been received among the current masters of various professions, and those who made the world believe that they alone had gained the monopoly on all learning. Our learned countryman Doctor Hakewill, in the preface to his *Apology*, has sufficiently proved this point: his profound work proving no decay in nature (a truth now sufficiently known and agreed upon) found no small opposition, both from those learned in theology and other persons, and underwent many sharp criticisms, until men had more carefully weighed the strength and persuasiveness of his arguments, which carry sufficient evidence to convince rational people. Our learned and most industrious anatomist *Dr. Harvey*, who (despite the recent quibbles of some) first discovered and demonstrated to the world that rare and profitable discovery of the *circulation of the blood*, underwent a similar fate: for eighteen or twenty years together, he groaned under the heavy criticism of almost all the Galenists and expert anatomists in Europe, and was railed upon and bitterly written against, not only by men like *Alexander Ross* and *Dr. Primrose*, but by *Riolanus* and others, and was not even spared by that famous physician of Rotterdam, *Zacharias Sylvius*, who honestly confesses this much:

<margin>Preface to Harvey’s Anatomical Exercises.</margin>

> *Primum mihi inventum hoc non placuit, quod & voce & scripto publicè testatus sum; sed dum postea ei resultando & explodendo vehementiùs incumbo, refutor & ipse & explodor : adeò sunt rationes ejus non persuadentes, sed cogentes : diligenter omnes examinavi, & in vivis aliquot canibus eum in finem à me dissectis, verissimum comperi.*

Which was a most sincere and free retraction and confession of his own errors, and may be proposed as an example to all rash and ill-advised critics. Neither could this most clear and evident truth (which is subject to visual demonstration and manifest experiments) find support in the world, until Walæus, Plempius,

*Plempius*, and various other judicious and accurate anatomists, had found the truth of *Harvey*'s opinion through their own trials and visual inspection; so difficult it is to overthrow an old, deep-rooted opinion. For I knew years ago that a person, for admitting or maintaining the circulation of the blood, would have been censured and derided as much by other *physicians* as one would be now for denying it. It is so hard to root out an opinion (no matter how false and groundless) once it is settled in the minds of many and has had a long period of continued reputation and belief. And it is even more important to consider the ignorance, stupidity, and perverseness of those who, in this age of *knowledge*, dare to take it upon themselves to censure (nay, to condemn) that *society* of persons and their endeavors. This society has a just, pious, merciful, and learned *king* as their founder, and counts as its members the greatest number of *nobility* and *gentry*—renowned for both divine and human *knowledge*—that can be chosen from the three *nations*. Their undertakings and goals are the most high, noble, and excellent that the *world* has ever yet witnessed. And yet (which is quite surprising), I have not only met many who censure and misjudge their vast and praiseworthy enterprise, but some have even been bold enough to appear in print to criticize and scandalize their proceedings. This is evident in that work titled *Plus Ultra*, written by Mr. *Stubbe* of *Warwick*, in which he has achieved as much as dogs do by barking at the moon. But it is plain that high social status or great talents exempt no man from malicious tongues or bad criticisms. And for this purpose, I cannot help but add Dr. *Casaubon*, who, as he suffered from a long physical illness, undoubtedly also suffered from some mental disturbance when, in his *Treatise of Credulity and Incredulity*, he stated this:

<margin>Page 3.</margin>
> "If I may speak my mind," he says, "without offense, I do not know what we should more likely attribute it to than some unfortunate constellation or influence—this enormous tendency toward innovation of all kinds, but particularly in matters of learning, with which so many are possessed without any basis or appearance of reason that I can see."

Alas, poor man! He was so blind that he could see no basis or appearance of reason for the usefulness of experimental philosophy, nor for the establishment of the Royal Society, but instead had to attribute it to the stars. It is a wonder why he does not attribute it to natural melancholy, as he does with almost all strange occurrences in his *Book of Enthusiasm*, or why not to demons or witches, as he does with most things in the treatise quoted.

yet this man's philosophy has had the luck to triumph in that university where so much contempt was poured upon him; for *Henricus Regius*, the public professor of medicine there, has published a book of natural philosophy consistent with the principles and design of *Descartes*: and it is in a manner generally received and applauded; and is much used by the honorable Mr. *Boyle*, who styled it the *Corpuscularian Philosophy*. This is despite the fact that at their inception, their first author and user was so much opposed and punished; for all inventions that are new (as well as opinions) are in their beginnings opposed and censured, not considering that all acquired knowledge and all arts and sciences were once new and had their beginnings.

3. When *Josephus Quercetanus* and Sir *Theodore Mayern* labored to introduce the practice of chemical medicine into the city of *Paris*, what cruel censures and scandals did they endure from all the rest of the physicians of the College, so that they were accounted unlearned and ignorant fellows and dangerous empirics, not fit to practice in the King of *France's* dominions, and so were sentenced by the College and prohibited from practicing? So far did ignorance, self-interest, and blind malice prevail against these two persons of so much worth and learning, that the former was made physician to the King of *France* and lived to see despised chemistry flourish where it had been most condemned, himself to be honored, and his chemical works to be published and held in great and general esteem with all who were lovers of learning. The latter likewise outlived the malice of all his enemies and saw himself advanced to be physician to two powerful and renowned Kings of *England*, and to have the general practice of most of the nobility and gentry of the kingdom, and to live to a fair old age and to die immensely wealthy. Thus even the bravest men, for their noble endeavors for the good of mankind, have always found harsh treatment.

As for example: suppose a man to be well read in school theology, metaphysics, logic, grammar, rhetoric, ethics, and physics; yet for all this, how unable would he be to resolve one of the most difficult propositions in *Euclid*? 5. *Roger Bacon*, our countryman, who was a *Franciscan Friar* and Doctor of Divinity, was the greatest <term>chemist</term>, astrologer, and mathematician of his time. Yet he could not escape the injurious and unchristian censure of being a <term>conjurer</term>. He was so hard-pressed that, as *Pitts* says, he was twice cited to *Rome* by *Clement IV* to purge himself of that accusation, and was forced to send his optical and mathematical instruments to *Rome* to satisfy the Pope and the Conclave. This he performed amply and came away with honor and applause. To vindicate him I need say little, because it has already been done by the pens of those learned persons *Pitts*, *Leland*, *Selden*, and *Naudæus*. I shall only add one sentence from that most learned treatise, *On the Marvelous Power of Art and Nature, and on the Nullity of Magic*, where he says: "Whatever is beyond the operation of nature or art is either not human, or is fictitious and full of fraud." 

Another of our countrymen, Dr. *John Dee*—the greatest and ablest philosopher, mathematician, and <term>chemist</term> that his age (or perhaps any age since) produced—could not evade the censure of the monster-headed multitude. Even in his lifetime, he was accounted a <term>conjurer</term>, of which he most sadly (and not without cause) complains in his most learned preface to *Euclid*, translated into English by Mr. *Billingsley*. There he strongly apologizes for himself with such zeal and fervency as may satisfy any rational Christian that he was no such wicked person as to have visible and familiar converse (if any such thing can exist nowadays) with the Devil, the known enemy of mankind. ### Chapter I: Supposed Witchcraft.

*Melchior Adam, Naudæus*, and others. Who has not almost read or heard of the horrid and abominable false scandals laid upon that *totius Germaniæ decus* <note>The glory of all Germany</note>, *Paracelsus*, by the malevolent pen of *Erastus*, and afterward swallowed up with greediness by *Libanius, Conringius, Sennertus*, and many others? For not only laboring to bring in a new theory and practice into the art of medicine, but also for striving to purge and purify the ancient, natural, laudable, and lawful magic from the filth and dregs of imposture, deceit, ceremonies, and superstitions; yet he has not lacked most strong and invincible champions to defend him, such as *Dorne, Petrus Severinus, Smetius, Crollius, Bitiscius*, and many others. Our countryman Dr. *Fludd*, a man acquainted with all kinds of learning, and one of the most Christian philosophers that ever wrote, yet did not lack those snarling animals, such as *Mersennus, Lanovius, Foster*, and *Gassendus*, as also our *Casaubon* (as mad as any) to accuse him vainly and falsely of diabolical magic, from which the strength of his own pen and arguments did discharge him without the possibility of replies. We shall now come to those who have treated of witchcraft, and strongly opposed and confuted the many wonderful and incredible actions and power ascribed to witches; and these, crossing the vogue of the common opinion, have not lacked their loads of unworthy and unchristian scandals cast upon them, of which we shall only name these two: *Wierus*, a learned person, a German, and in his time physician to the Duke of *Cleve*; the other our countryman Mr. *Reginald Scot*, a person of competent learning, pious, and of a good family. What is said against them in particular, I shall recite and give a brief response to it.

1. There is a little treatise in Latin titled *Dæmonologia*, attributed to King *James* (how truly we shall not dispute, for some ascribe it to others) wherein in the preface these two persons are hinted to be witches, and it is claimed that they wrote against the common opinion concerning the power of witches the better to shelter and conceal their diabolical skill. But indeed this groundless accusation needs no confutation, but rather scorn and derision, as having no rational ground of probability at all that they should be such cursed hypocrites or dissembling politicians—the one being a very learned and able physician, as both his writings do witness, and that upright and impartial author *Melchior Adam* in his life has most amply declared; the other known (as not living so very many years ago) to be a godly, learned, and an upright man, as his book which he calls *The Discovery of Witchcraft* does most largely make it appear, if his adversaries had ever taken the pains to peruse it. So that all rational persons may plainly see that it is but a lying invention, a malicious device, and a mere forged accusation.

2. These persons are accused to have absolutely denied the existence of witches, which we shall demonstrate to be notoriously false by these following reasons.

1. Could any rational man have ever thought or believed that Mr. Glanvill—a person who claims such high intellectual abilities—would have expressed so much weakness and impudence as to have charged Mr. Scot with the outright denial of the existence of witches, as he does in these words when speaking of him? He pretends this to be a refutation of the existence of witches and apparitions, and he hints at this in various other places, but without any quotation to show where or in what words Scot simply denies the existence of witches, which he nowhere maintains. So many are confident enough to charge others with views that they neither hold nor write.

2. Mr. Scot and Weyer do not frame the question as *An sint* <note>Whether they exist</note>, but *Quomodo sint* <note>In what manner they exist</note>, or how they act. So their question is only: what kind of power supposed witches have or act by, and what are the things that they do or can perform? Therefore, the phrasing of the question is not simply about the existence of witches, or *de existentia*, but only *de modo existendi* <note>concerning the manner of existence</note>. In this, it is plain that every dispute *de modo existendi* necessarily grants and supposes the certainty of the existence; otherwise, the dispute over the manner of their being, properties, power, or acts would have no ground or foundation at all. It is as if I and another should dispute about the extent, buildings, and location of the great city of Peking in China, or about the length, breadth, and height of the Great Wall dividing China from Tartary; <margin>it</margin> we both take <insert>it</insert> for granted that there is such a city and such a wall, otherwise our dispute would be wild, vain, and groundless. It would be like the two Wise-men of Gotham, who strove and argued about driving sheep over a bridge; one affirmed he would drive his sheep over the bridge, and the other protested against it, and so they began—one as if to drive, and the other to stay and stop them—when there were no sheep between them. And this might be a sufficient lesson to Mr. Glanvill to have been more sensible than to have charged Scot so falsely. Do not the ancient Fathers differ in their opinions *circa Angelorum modum existendi* <note>regarding the manner of the existence of angels</note>, some of them holding them to be corporeal and some incorporeal? Yet both these parties firmly held their existence. So this is a false and improper charge and has no basis to stand upon at all.

3. What man of reason and judgment could have believed that Mr. Glanvill or Dr. Casaubon—being persons who claim a great share of learning and to be exact in their ways of arguing—would have committed such a pitiful and gross error as the *fallacia consequentis* <note>the fallacy of the consequent</note>? For if I deny that a witch can fly in the air, or be transformed or transubstantiated into a cat, a dog, or a hare, or that the witch makes any visible covenant with the Devil, or that he sucks on their bodies, or that the Devil has carnal copulation with them; I do not thereby deny either the existence of witches, nor other properties that they may have for which they may be so called. This is no more than if I deny that a dog has rugibility <note>the ability to roar like a lion; from the catchword "lity"</note>—

And if the tales that *Scot* tells are odd and silly, most of them are taken from those pitiful, lying witch-mongers, such as *Delrio*, *Bodinus*, *Springerus*, *Remigius*, and the like—the authors who are most esteemed by Dr. *Casaubon* and other witch-mongers, of whom we shall say more hereafter.

For *<term>dolus versatur in universalibus</term>* <note>deceit deals in generalities</note>, and no man ought to be condemned without particular and precise proof regarding the time, place, and all other circumstances. This Mr. *Glanvill* could not do, and therefore he only gives general slanders without ground; and if *Scot* were little better than absurd, then he better agrees with Mr. *Glanvill*, whose Platonic whimsies are as absurd as any, as we shall sufficiently prove hereafter.

## The Displaying of CHAP. I.

4. Dr. *Casaubon* must have been highly driven by the desire to criticize when he would condemn a man without reading his book or seriously weighing the force of his arguments. This proves him to be very weak and of great perversity of mind, as all rational men may judge; for in effect it is this: *Scot* is an illiterate wretch, and his book is full of errors, but I never read it except as I have glanced at it at a friend's house or a bookseller's shop. Although Dr. *Reynolds* was a learned man, it does not appear for what particular point or error he criticized *Scot*; therefore, it is but a general and groundless charge, sheltered under the pretense of Dr. *Reynolds'* reputation—evidence which, in reason and law, is of no weight or validity.

5. For Dr. *Casaubon* to rank him among illiterate wretches is against the very rule of the Law of Nature, which teaches all people that they should not do to another what they would not have another do to them. Surely Dr. *Casaubon* would not want another to judge and condemn him as an illiterate wretch, and therefore he ought not to have condemned Mr. *Scot* as such. And as it is against the Law of Nature, so it is contrary to the rules of modesty and morality to give a man such stigmatizing labels. Indeed, it is even against the rules of good manners and civil education, except that some men think it is lawful for them to say anything, and that nothing they say misbecomes them. Lastly, let all good Christians judge how far it is against the rules of Christianity and piety.

6. The falsehood of this foul scandal is manifest in both the particulars contained within it. 1. For Mr. *Scot* was a learned and diligent person, as the entire treatise will bear witness; he understood the Latin language and something of Greek, and as for Hebrew, even if he knew nothing of it, he had obtained very good helps, as appears in his expounding the various words used in the Scriptures for supposed witches and witchcraft. This is also shown by his quoting of various Church Fathers, reformed ministers, and many other authors besides, which sufficiently prove that he was not illiterate. 2. And that he was no wretched person is apparent, as he was a man of a good family, a considerable estate, a man of very commendable conduct, and a very godly and zealous Protestant, as I have been informed by people of worth and credibility, and as is sufficiently proved by his writing.

I have not been so tedious in gathering these examples of men who have been criticized for opposing vulgar opinions or writing on obscure subjects merely as incidental or for show, but purely because they are introductory, necessary, and pertinent to the purpose I intend in this treatise. <meta>This page transitions from the defense of Reginald Scot's character and education to the first chapter of the work, which addresses the nature of "Supposed Witchcraft." # CHAP. I. Supposed Witchcraft.

<margin>Rule 1.</margin>
1. That the general prevalence of an opinion, or the large number of people who hold and maintain it, is not a safe and justifiable ground to accept it or to adhere to it; nor is it safe or rational to reject an opinion simply because there are but few who hold it, or the number who maintain it is small. And this I shall work to prove by these sure and firm arguments following.

<margin>Exodus 23:2</margin>
1. Because the Scriptures tell us this much: *You shall not follow a multitude to do evil.* And that there are many deceivers: <margin>Matthew 24:5, Luke 6:26</margin> *For many shall come in my Name, saying, "I am Christ," and shall deceive many. And woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you: for so did their fathers to the false prophets.* From which it is plain that, first, we are to consider and be assured that the matter is not evil; for if it is, we are not at all to be swayed by the multitudes that follow it or uphold it. So if the opinion is evil, erroneous, or false, we ought not to accept it or adhere to it, no matter how many hold or maintain it. So in truth and substance, we are not at all to consider whether there are few or many who hold it, but simply whether it is true or not. For as Plato tells us: *Neither should it be considered what was said, but whether it is said truly or not.* For the multitude have always been esteemed by all good authors and learned men as the most erroneous, as Seneca says: <margin>Book on the Happy Life. Lactantius, Divine Institutes, book 2, chapter 3.</margin> *We should seek not what pleases the common people, who are the worst interpreters of truth.* And Lactantius teaches us this: *The unlearned common people rejoice in empty displays, watch everything with childish minds, are delighted by frivolous things, and cannot weigh each matter for themselves.* And our Savior gives us proof and an instance of the error of the multitude, specifically in a matter of fact. Did not almost all the Jews under various kings applaud and approve of the doctrine and opinions of the false prophets, though they were utterly erroneous? This went so far that Elijah said he alone was left of the true prophets, though the false ones were many and numerous. So the Rule is proven to be true, both by the precept and the example of the Scriptures.

2. If we consider the generality of mankind, either in respect to their inclinations and dispositions, or their upbringing and education, we shall not find one in a hundred who is either naturally inclined or qualified by education to seek out and understand the truth. And then if there are a hundred to one drowned in ignorance and errors, and so few fitted to understand the truth of things—whether divine or natural—then it must necessarily follow that it is not safe to embrace or adhere to an opinion because of the great number of those who hold or maintain it, but rather to stick to the smaller number; though neither simply ought to be regarded, but only the truth itself.

3. Again, if we consider those numbers who are either naturally inclined or trained by education in learning to enable them to judge rightly between truth and truth-likeliness, how few of these prove to be at all excellent in those areas of learning

wherein they are bred, we may easily see the truth of this Rule sufficiently proved: that it is not safe to embrace or adhere to an opinion just because the numbers are great of those who hold or maintain it.

4. If the multitude that hold opinions—whether of spiritual or natural things—were to be followed merely because of the great numbers that hold them, then if we look and consider the writings of the best geographers, travelers, and navigators, we would have to be of the opinions of the Pagans (who are the most numerous part of mankind) or the Muslims (who are many in comparison to the small number of Christians). And then what horrid, blasphemous, idolatrous, impious, and diabolical opinions must we receive and hold, both concerning God, Angels, the Creation, and most of the operations that are produced by Nature? So, the arguments of Dr. Casaubon and Mr. Glanvil, drawn from the universality of the opinion and the great multitudes of those that hold it, are vain and groundless.

5. If the comparison I use is thought to be too broad, and the rule is applied only to the greater part of the learned who are in Europe, it will still hold good that the greatest part of the learned are not to be followed because of their numbers, nor are the rest to be rejected because of their small number. For it is known sufficiently that a Bishop of Mentz was censured and excommunicated for holding that there were <term>Antipodes</term> by some hundreds of those who were accounted learned and wise; so it is plain that the greater number may be in error, and those who are few may be in the right. And did not the greatest number of the physicians in Europe altogether adhere to the doctrine of Galen, though now in Germany, France, England, and many other nations most have rejected it? And was not the Aristotelian philosophy embraced by the greatest part of all the learned in Europe? And have not the Cartesians and others now sufficiently demonstrated the errors and imperfections of it? Especially the endeavors of the honorable and learned members of the Royal Society here in England, and similar societies overseas—by their continual labor and vigilance regarding experiments—have made its errors and defects obvious to all inquisitive persons. So, a multitude, as a multitude, ought not to lead or sway us, but truth itself.

6. If to all this we add that truth in itself is but one—for <term>unum</term> (one) and <term>verum</term> (true) are interchangeable—and that error or falsity is various and manifold, and that there may be a thousand errors about one particular thing and yet but one truth; it will necessarily follow that it cannot be safe to follow the greatest number holding an opinion because of their multitude, and the reason is that error is manifold, and truth is but one.

# CHAP. I. Supposed Witchcraft.

things) but it has once been new; and if an opinion should be rejected merely because of novelty, then it will follow, that either all opinions might have been rejected for that very reason, or that novelty is no safe ground alone, why an opinion should be opposed or rejected.

2. Antiquity and Novelty are but relations *with respect to our understanding, not with respect to nature*; for the truth, as it is fundamentally in things *outside the understanding*, cannot be accounted either old or new. And an opinion, when first found out and published, is as much a truth then, as when the current of hundreds or thousands of years have passed since its discovery. For it was no less a truth, when in the infancy of Philosophy it was held, that there was generation and corruption in Nature, in respect of Individuals, than it is now: so little does Time, Antiquity, or Novelty alter, change, confirm, or overthrow truth; for *veritas est temporis filia* <note>truth is the daughter of time</note>, in regard of its discovery to us or by us, who must draw it forth *è puteo Democriti* <note>from the well of Democritus</note>. And the existence of the *West-Indies* was as well before the discovery made by *Columbus* as since, and our ignorance of it did not impeach the truth of its being, neither did the novelty of its discovery make it less truth, nor the years since make it more: so that we ought simply to examine, whether an opinion be possible or impossible, probable or improbable, true or false; and if it be false, we ought to reject it, though it seem ever so venerable by the white hairs of Antiquity; nor ought we to refuse it, though it seem ever so young, or near its birth. For as St. *Cyprian* said: *Error vetustatis est vetustas erroris* <note>An error of antiquity is the antiquity of error</note>.

3. In regard of Natural Philosophy, and the knowledge of the properties of created things, and the knowledge of them, we preposterously reckon former Ages, and the men that lived in them, the Ancients; which in regard of production and generation of the Individuals of their own Species are so; but in respect of knowledge and experience, this Age is to be accounted the most ancient. For as the learned Lord *Bacon* says: <margin>Advancement of Learning, book 1, chapter 5.</margin>
> "Indeed to speak truly, *Antiquitas seculi, juventus mundi*, Antiquity of time is the youth of the World."

Certainly our times are the ancient times, when the World is now ancient, and not those which we count ancient, *in reverse order*, by a computation backward from our own times; and yet so much credit has been given to old Authors, as to invest them with the power of Dictators, that their words should stand, rather than admit them as Consuls to give advice.

<margin>Rule 3.</margin>
3. It is not safe nor rational to resolve to stick to our old imbibed opinions, nor willfully to reject those that seem new, except we be fully satisfied, from indubitable grounds, that what we account old is certainly true, and what we reckon to be new is undoubtedly false. And this will appear to be a truth, partly from the weakness of their arguments, that seem utterly to condemn all withdrawal from ancient opinions, as vain, foolish, and unnecessary; as also from other positive reasons.

# The Displaying of CHAP. I.

1. Some give the reason why they will not turn away from an opinion that their predecessors held: because their forefathers were as wise, if not wiser than they. But this, if strictly considered, is very weak and defective; for their predecessors were only men, and so were liable both to active and passive deception, and were not exempt from the common frailty of mankind, who are all subject to errors. And therefore, unless they were certain that their ancestors in former ages held the certain and undoubted grounds of truth, there is no reason in them, but mere perverseness of will, rather to obstinately *errare cum patribus* <note>err with the fathers</note> than to learn to follow the truth with those who are contemporary with them, which is foolish and irrational. Furthermore, there are more helps and means now to attain the knowledge of truth than there were in the days when their ancestors lived, and it must be a kind of the greatest madness to shut their eyes so that the light of truth may not appear to them.

2. This kind of reasoning has no more reason in it than if one should say that because his grandfather and great-grandfather were blind or lame, therefore they will be so too; or that because their ancestors never learned the Greek or Latin tongues, nor to write or read, neither will they learn any more than they did; or that their predecessors were bad managers and spendthrifts, and that therefore they will continue the same courses; or that because their forefathers followed drunkenness and luxury, therefore they will continue the same career of vices, as many of our debauched persons do nowadays, having no better reasons to allege for their excessive and vicious courses than what the Prophet condemned: *The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge.*

3. How far would they run back to establish the beginning of their ancestors? If as far as their first origins, then they must all be savages, barbarians, and heathens. And if they establish it distant from their first origins, then their predecessors had the same reason to have continued as those did who preceded them. But if their ancestors varied from and left the steps and opinions of those who went before them, then if they will do as their ancestors did, they must leave their courses and opinions, just as they had done regarding those who preceded them.

<margin>August. book on Free Will.</margin>
4. Some say they cannot turn away from the opinions of their predecessors because it would be a shame and disgrace to them. But that which we call shame and disgrace consists in the opinion of others, and we ought not to receive error or reject truth because of the censures or opinions of others: *Si de veritate scandalum sumitur, utilius permittitur nasci scandalum, quàm veritas relinquatur* <note>If a scandal is taken from the truth, it is better to allow the scandal to arise than for the truth to be abandoned</note>. And to leave an error to embrace truth is so far from being a shame and a disgrace that there cannot be a greater honor or glory; for *errare humanum est, sed in errore perseverare belluinum ac diabolicum est* <note>to err is human, but to persevere in error is beastly and diabolical</note>.

1. It has been common in almost all ages, not only for the common people, but also for the whole rabble of demonographers and witch-mongers to ascribe those strange and wonderful effects—whether arising from Art or Nature—to the worst of God’s creatures, if they did not themselves understand their causes, and to censure the authors who wrote of them as conjurers and magicians, as I have made manifest in my former instances. This might be further proven and illustrated by the effects of healing by the *weapon-salve*, the *sympathetic powder*, the curing of various *diseases* by *appensions* <note>objects or charms suspended from the body</note>, *amulets*, or by *transplantation* <note>a supposed medical method of transferring a disease from a person into another object or organism</note>, and many other most admirable effects both of Art and Nature. These are all thrown upon the Devil’s back by these self-conceited, ignorant people, and he is made the author and producer of them, as though he had a kind of omnipotent power. Concerning this, the learned philosopher and physician *Van Helmont* gives us this account: 
<margin>Concerning injected matter, page 597.</margin>
> “Indeed, I believe it conflicts with piety if a power surpassing nature is attributed to the Devil. But those ignorant of nature presume themselves to be nature's secretaries through the reading of books; however, whatever is hidden from them, let it be considered either impossible, or false, or deceptive and diabolical.” 

And a little after he adds this: 
<margin>Ibid. page 598.</margin>
> “For it was at least an invention of immense laziness to have referred everything we do not understand to the Devil, nor would I wish the Devil to be invoked to satisfy our questions through a rash attribution of powers.”

2. Whoever shall read *Pancirollus* concerning *memorable things recently discovered* <note>De rebus memorabilibus noviter repertis</note>, may easily be satisfied as to what strange and stupendous things Art and the inventions of men have produced in these latter ages. And no man can rationally doubt but that many more just as strange or far more wonderful things may be found out and discovered in ages to come; for there is a kind of bottomless depth in the Arts, whether liberal or mechanical, that has not yet been sounded, but lies hidden and unknown to men. And if these, because of their wonderful nature, should be ascribed to the power of *Satan* (as former ages have ignorantly done), and their authors accused of conjuring and diabolical magic, no greater wrong could be done to Art and artists. It would be a kind of blasphemy to attribute these stupendous effects (as the common people and witch-mongers usually do) to the Devil, the worst of God's creatures and the enemy of mankind.

5. The last rule I shall observe is that if people mean to profit from reading controversies of this nature, they must prudently and deliberately consider the goal that authors have had in writing. For though it is the general pretense of all that they write to refute errors and to maintain truth, yet very few in disputes of this nature have sincerely fulfilled this intended goal. For some have written (as we shall hereafter make manifest in the proper place) for the designed purpose of establishing certain points in their corrupted and superstitious religion. Some wrote because of their own gain and profit arising from upholding these opinions of the great power and deeds of witches, as did all the Inquisitors and their followers, who had a share in the condemned witches' goods. Others have written on these subjects merely for ostentation and vanity, to get a name for being learned and capable people; the judicious reader ought to beware of and consider all of these. Whereas, what is more necessary and commendable for those who treat any controversial point in writing or in other disputations than a clear and easy-to-understand method, a right and exact stating of the question in doubt, defining or describing the terms that are or may be ambiguous, and dividing the whole into its proper and genuine parts—distinguishing one thing from another, limiting things that are too general, and explaining everything that is doubtful? I have premised this much because most of the authors who have treated this knotty and thorny subject of witches and witchcraft have been as confused and unmethodical as any. For whereas the learned orator *Cicero* tells us that *every discourse ought to proceed from a definition*; and that it is also true that what is not aptly and fitly defined or described, as far as the subject will admit, is never perfectly understood: yet most of these authors (who are numerous) have laid down no perfect description of a witch or witchcraft, nor explained fully what they meant by that name, notion, or conception. *women who enchant little children by their touch, and by the offering of milk and their breasts.* So that if the comparison were appropriate in any proportion or detail, those women whom they consider witches only hurt little children with the virulent vapors of their breath and the emanations that issue from their filthy and polluted bodies. Thus, they work by contact and handling, by which the contagious poison is conveyed, but not by witchcraft.

3. There is another word they apply to witches, as insignificant and improper as the other, and that is *Sortilegus*, *Klēromantēs*, a teller of fortunes by lots or cuts. And *Lambertus Danæus*, who in other things was a judicious and learned person, yet doted extremely upon this opinion, calling a witch *Sortiarius*, deriving it from *Sortilegus*, which the French call *Sorcier*. Now what affinity or consistency does the casting or using of lots have with that which these men call *witchcraft*? Surely none at all. For though lots may, like the best things, be abused and twisted to a vain or evil end, yet they are not altogether evil; rather, a civil and lawful use may be made of them, as is manifest today in the famous city of *Venice*, where their chief officers are chosen by them. And also there has been a godly and divine use made of them even by the Apostles themselves in deciding the election of *Barsabas* and *Matthias*; the lot fell upon the latter, and so he was numbered with the eleven Apostles.
<margin>Acts 1:26.</margin>
And *Solomon* tells us, *The lot is cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof is of the Lord.*
<margin>Prov. 16:33.</margin>
And surely these men were at a loss to find a suitable word to fix upon these creatures—to whom they ascribe such impossible and incredible actions—when they were forced to bring in this title of *Sortilegus*, which has no kinship at all with such witches as they mean and intend.

4. Sometimes they call them by the name *Saga*, which means no more than a wise and subtle woman, being derived from *perceiving* (*à sagiendo*) to perceive quickly, or to scent a thing out quickly, which the Germans call *Unhold*, which is no more than *malevolent* or ill-willed.

5. They use the words *Veneficus*, *venefica*, and *veneficium*; and these, in their proper meaning and derivation from Latin, import no more than a poisoner, or to make poison (*venenum facere*). And so these names might perhaps be given to them because by tradition they had learned several ways to poison secretly and strangely. For as there may be various hidden and not ordinarily known ways (as we shall show hereafter) by which—either by smelling, tasting, touching, or perhaps by sight—they could kill and destroy, though the means they used and the effects produced were merely natural; yet because the manner was very hidden and imperceptible, it was, through ignorance and a lack of proper inspection into the matter, accounted diabolical. There was no more of a devil in the business than there is in a thief or murderer, except only in the use and application, which is to steal, kill, or de-

And this, though now improperly and abusively called witchcraft, only signifies poisoning; so the French call it *Empoisonnement*, the Italians *Veneficio* or *Avenenatione*, and the Germans *Vergifftung*, which all amount to the same purpose. And this *Veneficium* or poisoning the Greeks call Φαρμάκευσις and Φαρμακεία, from Φάρμακον, *Medicamentum vel Venenum*; for sometimes it was taken in a better sense for a curing and healing medicine, and sometimes in a worse sense for poison that did kill or destroy. Nor can it be found in any Greek author to signify any more than such men or women who used charms and incantations, and were believed by the vulgar to effect strange things by them, when in truth and indeed they effected nothing at all except by natural means and secret poisons, and from there they took these names. And the poets spoke of them to adorn and embellish their poems, according to common opinion; not that they themselves believed the things were done as the vulgar believed, nor to give credit to such false fables and impossibilities, but to make their poems more delectable and welcome to the common people, who are usually taken with such foolish romantic stories and lies. But after the year 1300, when the Spanish Inquisitors and the Popish doctors and writers had found the sweetness and benefit of the confiscated goods of those they had caused to be accused and condemned for witches, in their sense then these words—either in Greek or Latin—were twisted to signify a witch who made a visible and corporeal league with the Devil, when in the true sense of them they only signified a secret poisoner. So all things were hurried, however improper and dissonant, to be made serviceable to their filthy lucre and avaricious self-interest. *Templum venale Deusq;.* <note>The temple and God are for sale.</note>

6. Common opinion will object and say that it is harsh and severe that cheaters and impostors should be ranked with enchanters, and those who converse with devils and with idolaters, and that it is difficult to give a reason for this. To this, we shall give this full response.

<margin>Leviticus 20:10. Deuteronomy 22:22, 23, 24.</margin>
1. We are to consider in what precise respect actions are called sinful and wicked in Sacred Writ, and why they have such severe punishments attached to them; we shall find that this is not *by reason of the means or the act, but of the end* <note>ratione medii vel actûs, sed finis</note>. For instance and illustration: we shall find that the Law was peremptory regarding adultery, which says: *If a man be found lying with a woman married to a husband, then they shall both of them die.* Now the act of copulation, as it is an act, is the same with a lawful wife as it is with the wife of another man (that is, when considered generically), and yet one is lawful, as it agrees with God’s Law and Ordinance, and the other is unlawful, sinful, wicked, and therefore to be punished with death, because it is a deviation from the Divine Ordinance and contrary to the Command of God, who says, *Thou shalt not commit adultery.* So though the things committed by these persons were or might be performed by natural or artificial means that simply in themselves were not sinful or so severely punishable, yet they were evil in regard to the end, which was to deceive and seduce the people into idolatry.

<margin>2 Chronicles 33:1-8.</margin>
<margin>Psalms 115:4-7. Ibid. Psalm 135:17.</margin>
2. Therefore the true and precise reason why these persons (termed witches or diviners) are to be so severely punished by the Law of God is because they drew the people to idolatry, the thing that God most hates, and against which he has pronounced the most severe and most terrible judgments of all. Indeed, these people were the very false prophets—especially of one sort—and the very priests of the idols, as is manifest in the wicked and filthy idolatry of all sorts set up and practiced by *Manasseh*, including almost all the types mentioned in the Scriptures. And God declares himself to be a jealous God, and that he will not give his glory to another, but is the only Lord God, and him only we ought to serve; and therefore he will most severely punish those who attribute that to idols which is only proper to himself. For this cause, and upon this ground, are all those terrible warnings <note>comminations</note> used in the Scriptures, especially against this sort of people, who were the chief instruments in promoting idol-worship, ascribing the power of a Deity to them. As the Prophet tells us, *Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands; they have mouths, but they speak not; eyes have they, but they see not; they have ears, but they hear not; noses have they, but they smell not; they have hands but they handle not; feet have they, but they walk not, neither do they speak through their throat, neither is there any breath in their mouths.*

Now, if he had been any great magician, or could have performed any great things, he could not have wondered so much at those things that *Philip* worked; or if he could have flown in the air, as *Eusebius* (or those who have foisted such incredible lies into his writings) pretends, then he would not have been so amazed at the miracles and signs that the Apostles worked, nor would he have offered to buy the gift of bestowing the Holy Ghost, except for the reason that he was a notorious dissembler and impostor. And if he had been in league with the Devil, surely he might have cast out devils by the power of *Beelzebub*, the prince of devils; all of which plainly concludes him to be an absolute cheater and impostor. And the story of *Bel* and the *Dragon* (though but an Apocryphal piece, yet very ancient, and of sufficient credit regarding matter of fact) evidently demonstrates that these sort of people were abominable cheaters and impostors, and were not endowed with any supernatural power, nor had the assistance of any visible demon, but only the devil of deceit and cheating in their own breasts, and so were, as *Cardan* says, *Carnales Dæmones ipsis Dæmonibus callidiores* <note>Fleshly demons more cunning than the demons themselves</note>.

5. And though by the laws of our own nation these kinds of people were to be severely punished, as appears by the Statute 1 *James I chapter* 12, yet they had respect in that Act not only to the punishment regarding what these persons could or did do, but also in regard to their being impostors and deceivers of the people; <margin>Institutes part 3, p. 46.</margin> for so the Lord Chief Justice Sir *Edward Cook* <note>Sir Edward Coke</note>, the best expositor of law who has written in our language, explains it in these words: The mischiefs before this part of this Act were:
> “ *That various impostors, men and women, would take it upon themselves to tell or do these fine things specified here, in great deceit of the people, and cheating and swindling them of their money or other goods: therefore was this part of the Act made, wherein these words* [*take upon him or them*] *are very remarkable. For if they take it upon themselves, etc., though in truth they do it not, yet are they in danger of this first branch.* ”

6. And whereas in the objection Mr. *Glanvil* mentions converse with devils, if he means mental, internal, and spiritual converse, such as murderers, adulterers, thieves, robbers, and all wicked persons have with Satan, we grant it; for so did the Jews and the High Priests in conspiring and acting to put our blessed Savior to death: *it was their hour, and the power of darkness*. But if he means a visible and corporeal converse, then we plainly affirm that there is not, nor can be any such, by which any such strange things (as witchmongers foolishly and falsely believe) can be performed or effected. Therefore, by way of conclusion in this particular, we grant that there are many sorts of such kind of witches,
