2. And just as there is a numerous crew of active witches, whose existence we freely acknowledge, there is another sort who are under a passive delusion and do not know—or at least do not observe or understand—that they are being deluded or deceived. These are those who confidently believe they see, do, and suffer many strange, odd, and wonderful things that have no real existence at all, but exist only in their depraved imaginations and are merely *melancholic figments* (*melancholiæ figmenta*). And yet the confessions of these people, though absurd, idle, foolish, false, and impossible, are accepted as truths by common witch-hunters without any ground or reason. These confessions are falsely attributed to demons and are used as sufficient grounds to proceed with condemning the confessors to death, when it is all merely a passive delusion wrought within the depraved imaginative faculty through these three ways or means.

1. One of the causes that produces this depraved and passive delusion is a poor education. They are raised in ignorance of God, the Scriptures, or the true grounds of the Christian religion; furthermore, they are not even taught the common rules of morality or other human literature. Instead, they only absorb and suck in, along with their mothers' and nurses' milk, the common, gross, and erroneous opinions held by ignorant commoners, who are generally enchanted and bewitched by the belief in strange stories regarding devils, apparitions, fairies, hobgoblins, ghosts, spirits, and the like. Because of this, a very deep impression of the truth of these gross and impossible things is stamped into their imaginations, making them almost impossible to erase or wash out for the rest of their lives. Custom and upbringing from a young age are so powerful that even though the things received, stubbornly believed in, and adhered to are abominable falsehoods and impossibilities—having no other existence but in the brains and fantasies of old, ignorant, and doting people—they are merely *the terrors and figments of women and nurses* (*muliercularum & nutricum terriculamenta & figmenta*). Therefore, *Seneca* said: *The power of custom is most heavy* (*Gravissimum est consuetudinis imperium*). That this is one main cause of this delusion is manifest from all the best historians; where the light of the Gospel has appeared the least, and where there is the greatest brutish ignorance and heathenish barbarism, there the greatest number of these deluded witches or melancholics are to be found—such as in the North of *Scotland*, *Norway*, *Lapland*, and the like, as may be seen at length in *Saxo Grammaticus*, *Olaus Magnus*, *Hector Boetius*, and similar authors.

But besides these two sorts of witches, whose existence we do not deny, there is an interpretation of the word witch in another sense, the existence of which I absolutely deny, and that is this according to Mr. *Perkins*: "A witch is a magician who, either by an open or secret league, knowingly and willingly consents to use the aid and assistance of the Devil in the working of wonders."

But the full description and notion that common witch-hunters give a witch is this: "That a witch is such a person to whom the Devil does appear in some visible shape, with whom the witch makes a league or covenant, sometimes by a bond signed with the witch's blood; and that thereby he does afterwards suck upon some part of their bodies, and that they have carnal copulation together; and that by virtue of that league the witch can be changed into a hare, dog, cat, wolf, or similar creatures; that they can fly in the air, raise storms and tempests, kill men or cattle, and perform such wonders." This notion of a witch may be gathered from the writings of these persons: *Delrio* the Jesuit, *Bodinus*, *Jacobus Springerus*, *Johannes Niderus*, *Bartholomeus Spineus*, *Paulus Grillandus*, *Lambertus Danaeus*, *Hemmingius*, *Erastus*, *Sennertus*, and many others. It is also found in the writings of our own countrymen: Mr. *Perkins*, Mr. *Bernard* of *Balcombe*, the author of the book called *Demonology*, Mr. *Gaule*, Mr. *Giffard*, and various others, who have one after another licked up the vomit of the first promoter of this vain and false opinion, and without due consideration have labored to force it upon others.

It is against their arguments that we now principally direct our pen, and after answering their groundless and unjust scandals, we shall labor to overthrow their chief bulwarks and fortifications.

# CHAPTER III.

*The denial of such a witch as was last described in the preceding chapter does not imply the denial of angels or spirits. Apparitions are no warrantable ground for a Christian to believe in the existence of angels or devils; only the Word of God is.*

Having declared in what sense and understanding we accept the existence of witches, and in what sense we deny them, lest we be misunderstood, we shall add this: That we do not (as the Schools speak) deny the existence of witches *absolutely and simply*, but *in a certain respect*, and that they do not exist *in such a manner*—that is, they do not make a visible contract with the Devil, he does not suck upon their bodies, they do not have carnal copulation with him, and similar things mentioned before. In these respects, and no other, did *Wierus*, *Gutierrius*, and Mr. *Scot* deny witches; that is, that neither they nor their supposed familiars could perform such things as are ascribed to them. And that Dr. *Casaubon* and Mr. *Glanvil* should charge those who hold this opinion with atheism or <term>Sadducism</term> <note>A term referring to the denial of the existence of spirits or the immortality of the soul, named after the ancient Sadducees.</note> is very strange to me, as there is no ground, connection, or rational consequence for doing so. <header>38 The Displaying of CHAP. III.</header>

purpose, and the state of the question we lay down thus:

That denying the existence of angels or spirits, or the resurrection, does not imply the denial of the being of God; nor does denying the existence of witches (in the sense previously established) imply the denial of angels or spirits. Furthermore, we shall prove with irrefragable arguments that they unjustly charge the authors of this opinion with <term>Sadducism</term>.

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
1. No correct deduction can be made, nor any right consequence drawn, where there is no causal dependency nor any connection of dependency. For just as with a relative and its correlative, the denial of one necessarily destroys the other, yet the *foundation of the relation* <note>Latin: *fundamentum Relationis*</note> is not destroyed; so a father without a child, as a father, neither exists nor is known, and yet the foundation of those two terms—paternity and childhood—which is man, remains. So he that denies creation destroys the relative, which is Creator; yet the foundation, which is God, remains. And the denial of creation does not imply the necessary conclusion of denying the being of a God, because there might be a God even if there were no creation, because God is supposed to exist, both in respect to causality and duration, before creation. So, what relation can Mr. *Glanvill* imagine between the being of God and the being of angels or spirits? For they both belong to the category of substance, and not that of relation; and there is even less relation between the being of a witch and the being of spirits. Thus, the denial of one does not imply the denial of the other. And even if there were a relation (which Mr. *Glanvill* cannot show), the foundation of that relation (which is so necessary that relatives cannot subsist without it) might remain, even if the relatives were taken away. Therefore, the denial of the existence of angels or spirits does not imply the denial of the being of God; and therefore, the authors of this opinion are wrongfully and falsely charged with atheism. Likewise, the denial of the existence of a witch (in the sense specified) does not imply the denial of the being of spirits; and therefore *Scot*, *Osborne*, and their like are falsely and wrongfully charged with Sadducism.

<margin>
Argument 2.
Matt. 22:23.
Acts 23:8.
</margin>
2. Though it is a true maxim that *an argument from possibility to actual existence is not valid* <note>Latin: *de posse ad esse non valet argumentum*</note>; yet, on the contrary, the possibility of something can never be rationally denied if it has once existed in *reality* <note>Latin: *esse*</note>. But it is apparent that the Sadducees denied the resurrection and the existence of either angels or spirits; that is, they denied that angels or spirits, whether good or bad, existed separately, and held that they were nothing but the good or bad impulses in men's minds. Yet these men were no atheists; for though they denied the resurrection and held that there were no angels or spirits, they still held and believed there was a God, and they accepted and believed the five books of *Moses*. Otherwise, our Savior would not have used an argument whose only strength was drawn from a sentence in the third chapter of *Exodus*, the sixth verse. So even the denial of

the existence of angels and spirits does not imply the denying of a God; much less does denying the existence of a witch imply the denial of the existence of angels and spirits. Therefore, the charge of atheism and <term>Sadducism</term> is false, injurious, and scandalous.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
3. Regarding those things that in their beings have no dependence on one another, the denial of one does not take away or deny the existence of the other; but where a being exists merely in dependency upon another superior cause, there if you take away or deny the existence of the first cause, you thereby take away and deny the existence of all the rest that depends upon it. So he who denies the existence of a God necessarily denies the existence of angels or spirits; but not the other way around. For he who denies the existence of angels and spirits does not therefore necessarily take away or deny the existence of a God, because the being of a God is independent of either angel or spirit and exists solely by itself. Therefore, even if *Wierus* or *Scot* had denied the existence of angels and spirits (which they did not), it would not have implied that they were atheists; thus, they are falsely accused by Dr. *Casaubon* and Mr. *Glanvil*. And though they might have denied the existence of witches (which they did not *simply, but in a certain manner* <note>Latin: simpliciter, sed tali modo</note>), it would not have implied that they were guilty of <term>Sadducism</term>, because spirits or demons have their existence without any dependence on the existence of witches. Therefore, it is but a poor *fallacy of consequence* <note>Latin: fallacia consequentiæ</note> to say that he who denies a witch denies a demon or spirit.

<margin>Argument 4.</margin>
4. Denying the existence of spirits does not imply denying the existence of a God, because in the priority of duration, God existed when spirits did not, for they are not immortal *from the beginning* <note>Latin: à parte anté</note>. Likewise, denying the existence of witches does not imply the denial of the existence of spirits, for in the priority of duration, spirits existed before witches; for *Adam* and *Eve* could not have been ignorant that there were spirits, both good and bad, and yet at that time there were no witches. So, since a spirit has, in respect to duration, a being before a witch can have any, denying the existence of the latter does not imply denying the existence of the former; it is merely illogical, agreeing with no rules of logic except those of "Logger-head College."

<margin>Argument 5.</margin>
5. Many properties or proper adjuncts may be ascribed to a substance, the denial of which does not imply the denial of the existence of the substance itself. Thus, to deny that a horse has fins like a fish or wings like a bird does not imply the denial of the existence of a horse. Therefore, it is injurious and scandalous of Dr. *Casaubon* and Mr. *Glanvil* to charge Dr. *Wierus* and Mr. *Scot* with atheism and <term>Sadducism</term>, when indeed (as we shall prove hereafter) their own tenets tend toward blasphemy, impiety, vanity, and uncharitableness.

Another thing that we oppose is that apparitions are not warrantable

<margin>Argument 1.</margin>
1. For to say that the apparitions of spirits, good or bad, prove their existence is only a *petitio principii* <note>Latin: a begging of the question</note>, a begging of the question that is initially in doubt and ought to be proved. For how are we to be assured that the apparitions that are made—and really attested as truth by unquestionable witnesses (not to speak of melancholy fancies and fables, tricks of knavery and imposture, and other ignorant and gross mistakes which are often believed to be apparitions when they are no such thing)—are made by good or bad spirits? For that is the matter in doubt, and so it is only a circular way of arguing by way of begging the question, or proving *ignotum per ignotius* <note>Latin: the unknown by something even more unknown</note>; for apparitions do not prove the being of spirits, unless it is first proved that those apparitions are made or caused by spirits.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
2. There are many apparitions that are produced by natural and artificial causes and do not need to be referred to supernatural ones, such as all those *idola* <note>images or appearances</note>, images, or forms that we see in mirrors, which cannot be denied to be apparitions, and yet arise from natural causes. Likewise, the apparition of comets, new stars, and many other sorts of strange meteors—as sometimes three suns, the rainbow, *halones* <note>halos</note>, and the like—have natural causes to produce them and are no proof of the being of spirits. Indeed, as the best and most credible historians have left on record, and as it has been known to be a certain truth in various parts of these three kingdoms within the space of these last forty years, strange and various sights have been seen in the air—of men, horses, and armies fighting one another. And yet these were no proof of the existence of spirits, because they may (and doubtlessly do) proceed from other causes, and not from the operation or efficiency of angels or spirits, whether good or bad.

<margin>Argument 3.</margin>
3. It is not certainly known what diversity of creatures there may be that are *mediae naturae* <note>Latin: of a middle nature</note> between angels and men, which may sometimes appear and then vanish. So, even if it is granted that there are apparitions really and truly, it does not necessarily follow that these are caused by good or bad angels, because they may be effected by creatures of another and middle nature; and thus apparitions are no certain ground for believing in the existence of angels or spirits. ### CHAP. IV. Supposed Witchcraft.

These two details are fully sufficient as an argument to deny whatever is not contained in them as being unfit to be accepted for either purpose. Thus, regarding a Christian's warfare, everything necessary for obtaining a perfect and complete victory, and for standing firm and persevering, is fully declared in them. Whatever they do not mention is to be rejected as lacking the seal of Divine Authority, whether it concerns avoiding what is prohibited or following what is commanded. And therefore we affirm that what the Scriptures have not revealed about the power of the Kingdom of Satan is to be rejected and not believed. Whatever weapons we are to use against the wiles of the Devil, we are to be provided with, but we need no others except what the Holy Spirit has made known to us in the Scriptures. If what they relate was not from their own certain knowledge or <term>αὐτοψία</term> <note>autopsia; first-hand observation</note>, then it is of little or no credit at all; for the person who relates it might be guilty of either active or passive deception and delusion, or might have heard it from another, or by common report. In all of these, there is no certainty; instead, it leaves sufficient grounds for doubt, and is enough to caution a prudent person to completely suspend his belief until better proof can be brought. <margin>Epist. book 7, page 252.</margin> There is a story related by *Plinius Caecilius* to his friend *Sura* regarding a house in *Athens* that was haunted by a spirit in so terrible and frightening a manner that it was left utterly forsaken, and no one would live in it until *Athenodorus* the philosopher ventured into it. He waited for the coming of the apparition or phantom, and following its signs, he followed it to a place below where it vanished. He marked the spot, went to the magistrate, and had the place dug up; they found the bones of a person chained or fettered. He had the bones buried, and so the house remained free from spirits afterward. It is a wonder to think how many authors have swallowed this account (even *Philip Camerarius* himself, who though a very learned man, was yet extremely credulous in things of this nature) and urged it for proof as a matter of great credit and authority, when we cannot see that it affords any credible ground for a rational man to believe it. This is not only because the matter itself and its circumstances yield sufficient grounds for suspecting its truth, but chiefly because *Pliny* relates it only by hearsay—*exponam ut accepi* <note>I will explain it as I received it</note>—and he desires the opinion of his friend *Sura* regarding it and the rest, from whom we find no answer. The testimony of one is the testimony of none.

And even if his authority had been great, or of weight in such matters as these, he was still only a <term>singularis testis</term> <note>single witness</note>, which is not sufficient to be relied upon in these things. And lastly (for our present purpose here), he does not record it as a thing of his own certain knowledge, but as hearsay from *Epitherses*, who was only a single relator and a man of no certain truthfulness; therefore, we can have no rational ground to believe the truth of the story, but it may be rejected with more reason than it can be supported by.

<margin>
Plutarch, in the *Life of Marcus Brutus*, page 361.
</margin>
His story of *Brutus*'s <term>malus Genius</term> <note>evil spirit or phantom</note> appearing to him can be of no greater credit, because he received this merely by tradition and hearsay. It could have no other origin than the account of *Brutus* himself, whose guilty conscience and troubled brain imagined such vain things; for those who were near *Brutus* neither saw nor heard any such matter, and therefore it must have been a deception of the fancy, and no real apparition <term>ad extra</term> <note>external to the mind</note>.

2. And just as evidence of a matter of fact recorded from the account of others is of no validity to a judicious person, so if the matter of fact is witnessed by only a single testimony (even if by an eye or ear-witness), it is not sufficient. This is because a single person may be imperfect in some senses or under some distress, and so be no proper judge of what he sees or hears. The Word of Truth tells us, *That in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall be established*; and therefore we are not (especially in such obscure matters as these) to trust the evidence of a single testimony.

<margin>
*The Invisible World*, pages 245, 246, 247.
</margin>

For (says he) if any of her sisters spoke during the set hours of their silence, she used to remind them of their required silence by three knocks at the door of the cell. And once, appearing (as she often did) in a luminous brightness to a certain Carmelite, she is said to have addressed him thus:"

3. But if matters of fact are witnessed and attested by many or various persons who were ear and eye-witnesses, their testimony may still carry no weight in the balance of Justice or right Reason. This is because they may be corrupt in their interests, and so have their judgments misguided and biased by the corruption of their desires and affections, or they may relate things out of bitterness, envy, and malice. Thus, in these mysterious matters, they may not be a fit authority to rely upon, nor competent evidence in these particulars, as Dr. Casaubon is forced to confess in these words: 
<margin>Of *Credulity* and *Incredulity*, page 159.</margin>
> "In the reporting of strange things, whether natural or supernatural, one must know the character of the reporter, if it can be known: and what interest he had, or might probably be supposed to have had, in the report, to have it believed. And again, whether he claims to have seen it himself, or taken it on the credit of others. And whether a man, by his profession, is in a capacity likely to judge the truth of those things to which he bears witness."

Every one of these particulars would require individual consideration. For if there is interest in terms of Religion, then all authorities and every appearance of reason are drawn in to support this interest. Truth is commonly stifled in this contest for self-interest, and opposing parties are stigmatized with all the filthy lies and enormous crimes that can be invented, as is most evident in these instances.

The Catholic party, finding themselves hindered and opposed in matters of the highest interest, have forged a thousand false stories and tales to support their party's interests. They have left no dirt or dung unscraped to throw in the faces of their opponents. There, they drew thousands of people into the snare of the Inquisition for alleged witchcraft, which they defined as heresy. They wrote and bore witness for their own ends, interests, and profit, having a share in the goods and estates of all who were convicted and condemned. These were nothing else but a jumble of horrific and abominable lies, not to be believed, because the authors only invented them to promote their own base ends and wretched interests.

4. But even if the authors who report matters of fact regarding these four particulars we have named were ear- and eye-witnesses—and not just one, but a great number—and were not swayed by any corrupt or self-interest whatsoever, all this is still not sufficient to provide evidence in these matters unless they are rightly qualified in other things necessarily required to enable a person to judge these subtle and difficult matters. Some of the chief qualifications we shall enumerate here: 

1. The persons fit to give a perfect judgment of these matters ought to have perfect sensory organs; otherwise, they may easily be deceived and perceive things differently than they actually are. Thus, some defects or distempers in the ears, eyes, or the rest of the senses may hinder the true perception of things performed or done. 

2. ### CHAPTER V.

*That these things now in question are only merely supposed, and were yet never rationally nor sufficiently proved: And that the allegations brought to prove them are weak, frivolous, and absolutely invalid. With a full refutation of all the four particulars.*

Having in the preceding chapter proved that the Scriptures and sound reason are the proper mediums to decide these difficulties by, and also laid down the necessary qualifications required in an author or witness that would evidence these things as matters of fact: We shall here once again repeat the four particulars which we are about to refute, which are these. 1. That the Devil does not make a visible or corporeal league and covenant with the supposed witches. 2. That he does not suck upon their bodies. 3. That he has not carnal copulation with them. 4. That they are not really changed into cats, dogs, wolves, or the like. And these four particulars we affirm were never matters of fact, nor ever had a being, except only in the fancy as mere chimeras, nor that they ever were or can be proved to have been brought to pass or acted; and <note>concerning things which do not appear and things which do not exist, the reasoning is the same</note>, says the great maxim of our law. But in the first place let us hear what the patrons of this wretched and execrable opinion have to say to prove that they are matters of fact, or were ever acted or performed. And first we have Mr. Glanvill arguing at this rate:

<margin>Page 5, 6.</margin>
> "All histories are full of the exploits
> of those instruments of darkness; and the testimony of all ages,
> not only of the rude and barbarous, but of the most civilized and

These objections at first view seem very plausible, and appear to carry with them a great splendor and weight of truth and reason; but if they are looked into and narrowly weighed in the balance of sound reason and unbiased judgment, they will be found too light, and will soon vanish into rhetorical fumes and frothy vapors. So that this may be more clearly performed, we shall rank them into three points, in which all their seeming strength lies, and they are these:

1. They pretend that these things are sufficiently proved by historians of unquestionable credit and reputation.

2. That the confessions of witches themselves, in different regions and at several times and places, who have all acknowledged these details, are sufficient evidence of the truth of these performances.

3. That so many wise and grave judges and honest juries could not have been deceived into putting to death such great numbers of these kinds of people, called or accounted witches, without sufficient proof of the matters of fact. To all of these we shall give a full response, in respect to the four details mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, and shall combine and add such positive arguments as will be compelling to all rational persons whose corrupt wills have not perverted their judgments.

1. It is much to be wondered at that Mr. Glanvill (but especially Bishop Hall, a very reverend and learned person) should place any great emphasis upon such a weak foundation. For there is none of these three objections that will amount to a necessary proposition, but only to a contingent one, which will infer no certain and necessary conclusion, nor bring forth any certainty or science, but only bare opinion and probability. <note>A contingent proposition is one that is true in such a way that it could be false</note>: and at best the strength of all these are but <term>testimonia humana</term> <note>human testimony</note>, which are but weak and no sufficient ground for a rational man to believe them to be true, because <term>humanum est errare</term> <note>it is human to err</note>. ...professed Christians too, and therefore does require stronger arguments than contingent propositions to establish a firm ground for the belief in this opinion.

2. It is one thing barely to affirm, and another thing to prove sufficiently and fully. For though they boldly allege that these things are sufficiently proved by authors of unquestionable credit and truth, we must return a flat negative, and that for these reasons. 1. Let them show us any one author of credible truth who was ever an ear- or eye-witness of the Devil making a visible and corporal league or bargain with witches, or that he ever sucked upon their bodies, or that he had carnal copulation with them, or that by the experience of his senses ever certainly knew a man really transubstantiated and transformed into a wolf, or a wolf into a man, and we will yield the whole cause. But we must assert and truly affirm that this pretense of theirs—that these things are sufficiently proved by historians of good credit—is a mere falsity and a lying flourish of vain words. There are (we confess) a multitude of vain and lying stories amassed together in the writings of demonographers and witch-mongers concerning strange and odd apparitions, feats, confessions, and such like; but never any one positive proof of any of these four particulars by any authors of credit and reputation; and this we dare boldly declare to the world.

2. Let them produce any two witnesses who were of honesty and integrity, sound understanding, and ability, who were ever present and were ear- and eye-witnesses of a visible, vocal, and corporal league made between the Devil and the witch; or let them tell us who was nearby and watched, and really and truly saw the Devil suck upon some part of the witch's body; or who were the chamberlains, pimps, or panders when the Devil and the witch committed carnal copulation; or who were ever present when a witch was changed into a cat, a dog, a hare, or a wolf. If they can only bring forth any two credible witnesses to prove these things, then we shall believe them; but we must assert that no such two could ever be produced yet. Therefore, we cannot but wonder at the shameless impudence of such persons who dare affirm these things that never were nor can be proved, and yet have not blushed to vent and trumpet forth such execrable and abominable lies to the world. Mr. *Glanvill* confidently affirms these things to be matters of fact, and *affirmanti incumbit probatio* <note>the burden of proof lies upon the one who affirms</note>; let him produce his witnesses, and if they be persons of judgment, truth, and impartiality, then we shall accept their proof. But it is not figments, suppositions, weak presumptions, or apparent falsities that will achieve it; for that which was never acted can never truly be proved, and things that do not appear are as though they were not. Therefore, he must produce his testimonies or lose both his cause and credit, and must be taken for an asserter of never-proven fables.

### The Displaying of CHAP. V.

Now we know they usually do in this case as soldiers do, who, when they are driven out of some outwork or trench, then retreat into another that they think is stronger and safer. And being driven from their weak hold of a bare affirmation without proof—that these things are verified to have been matters of fact and actually performed, both by authority and the evidence of sense (which are both utterly false)—then they fly to this assertion: That the confessions of so many witches in all ages, in several countries, at various times and places, all agreeing in these particulars, are sufficient evidence of the truth of these matters. To this we shall rejoin that the confessions of witches, however considered, are not of credit and validity to prove these things; but are in themselves null and void, as false, impossible, and forged lies, which we shall make good by the following reasons.

<margin>Reason 1</margin>
1. The witch must be taken to be either a person *insanae, vel sanae mentis* (of insane or sound mind); and if they are *insanae mentis*, their confessions are not sufficient evidence, nor worthy of any credit; because there is neither reason, law, nor equity that allows the testimony or confession of an idiot, lunatic, mad, or doting person, because they are not of a right and sound understanding, and are not to be accounted as *compotes mentis* (of sound mind), nor governed by rationality. For as by the <term>Civil Law</term> mad folks, idiots, and childish old men, bond-slaves, and peasants are not capable of making a will to dispose of goods, lands, or chattels; so much more are all these sorts of persons barred from giving evidence by confessions or otherwise in matters concerning life and death, which are of far greater weight and concern. And that these persons are of unsound understanding is manifest in all the points they confess, and therefore they are no proof, nor ought to be credited; and that for these reasons. 1. Because the things they confess are not attested by any other persons of integrity and sound judgment, and they must of necessity be liars, because they are the bond-slaves of the Devil, whose works they will do, and he was a liar from the beginning. 2. Because they confess things that are impossible (as we shall prove shortly) and *confiteri impossibilia insanientis est* (to confess impossible things is the mark of a madman). 3. There is no good purpose for which they make these confessions, nor do they receive any benefit by them, either spiritual or temporal, internal or external. And this sufficiently shows that they are deluded, melancholy, and mad persons, and so their confessions are of no credit, truth, or validity.

<margin>Reason 2</margin>
2. Their confessions will be found null and false if we consider the impulsive cause that moves them to make them, and the purpose for which they declare such false and lying matters, specifically in these particulars. 1. The moving cause is not, nor can be, the Spirit of God, which is a spirit of truth and righteousness, nor any motion of true remorse for their sins, or anything flowing from repentant hearts, because they are persons forsaken by God and His grace, and given over to reprobate minds and senses, and therefore

<summary>The author argues that confessions of witchcraft are legally and rationally invalid because they typically come from individuals of unsound mind or are driven by delusion. He asserts that confessing to impossible acts is proof of madness and that such testimony would be rejected even in minor civil matters, let alone capital cases.</summary>

Thus, no more credit is to be given to them than to the maddest <term>melancholic</term> who was ever read or heard of.

<margin>Reason 3.</margin>
3. That there is not any jot of truth in these confessions is manifest if we consider the subject matter of them, as is plain by these following grounds. 1. For most of them are not credible because of their obscenity and filthiness; for chaste ears would tingle to hear such bawdy and immodest lies; and what pure and sober minds would not be nauseated and startled to understand such unclean stories, as of the carnal copulation of the Devil with a witch, or of his sucking the teat or wart of an old stinking and rotten carcass? Surely even the impurity of it may be sufficient to overthrow the credibility of it, especially among Christians. 2. There are many things that have no truth in them at all, which nevertheless have a likelihood of truth; but these are void of both truth and likelihood. For it is neither truth, nor has it any likelihood of it, to believe as a truth that the Devil should carry an old witch—one who can hardly crawl with a staff—through the air into foreign regions to dancing and banqueting, and yet have her return with an empty belly, and the next day be forced, like old *Dembdike* or *Elizabeth Sothernes*, and *Alizon Denice*, to go begging with a sour milk can. Is this either probable or likely? Would it not have much more advantaged the Devil's interest and his kingdom to have furnished them with good and true meat and drink, and not with such imaginary foods, which would neither fill the stomach nor satisfy the appetite? Had it not been more for the Devil's benefit to have furnished them with plenty of gold and silver, than to let them go ragged and tattered, begging their bread from door to door? 3. As these confessions have no likelihood of truth in them, so they are things that are simply impossible to be performed by any created power, and therefore must necessarily be false and fictitious accounts; for no creature can perform anything except that for which it was ordered and designed by Creation. We told her that her body had never stirred out of the chamber; she maintained the contrary. We showed her the blows we had given her; she persisted even more stiffly in her opinion."

By the testimony of this author, who was an ear- and eyewitness of this event, along with other persons with him—which manifests it to be good and sufficient evidence—it appears that the witches are under a melancholic and passive delusion, promoted by the help of sleep-inducing ointments, whereby they fancy and think they are carried to far remote places where they hear and see strange things, and do and suffer that which is not performed at all, but only as in a dream. Their bodies, in the meantime, lie immovable, and so they relate only falsehoods and lies, which is an unanswerable proof of the absolute falsity of their confessions—the thing that we undertook here to prove. And some recent learned men (including *Mr. Glanvil* himself), giving too much credit to the things related by the witches in their confessions as being true stories of things really performed at a great distance, have been forced to revive that old Platonic whim of the soul’s real exit from the body into far distant places and its return again, with the certain knowledge of things done or said there, according to the account that *Pliny* gives us in these words: <margin>Natural History, book 7, chapter 52, page 103.</margin> *We find (he says) among the examples that the soul of Hermotimus of Clazomenae used to wander, leaving the body, and traveling far, reported many things that could only be known by someone present, while the body in the meantime was half-dead; until, having been burned—*

Another apparent ground for the invalidity of the truth or credit of these confessions is that which a learned divine gives us in his letter to Dr. *Wierus*, the substance of which we shall provide in English as follows:

> "I have known," he says, "the year before (he wrote his epistle in the year 1565) many foolish things from the private confession of a certain old woman, an enchanter, who, when she had heard in my sermon the passage in the 19th chapter of the *Acts* explained—*That many of the Ephesians, being of those who had exercised curious arts, had brought their books and burned them openly, etc.*—she immediately," he says, "came to me with a clearly troubled mind; and with tears pouring forth into my bosom the secrets of her breast, she received Christian instruction. And when she had understood, by the blessing of God, the vanity of diabolical impostures, and perceived them with opened eyes, she was easily converted to the light of truth, the smoke of lies being set aside. Once the truth was received, she most constantly confessed that it appeared to her clearer than the light at noonday that Satan did only deceive and blind the eyes of his vassals, and that there was nothing done in reality; and this she declared with a detestation of her diabolical art."

And so he concludes it in these words: *Uno verbo dicam, me satis experientiâ didicisse, bonam partem incantationum mera esse insomnia.* <note>In one word, I say that I have learned enough by experience that a good part of incantations are mere dreams.</note> And whoever shall read and seriously consider the epistle of that excellent and learned divine will find most of those vain illusions exposed and refuted. So that in all (or most) of the things attributed to witches, we shall find no more diabolical operation in them than an internal, mental, and spiritual delusion, in making the witches believe—and leading others to the same opinion—that the Devil has a kind of omnipotent power and sovereignty. Therefore, *Aristotle* rightly concluded: *Incantamenta esse muliercularum figmenta.* <note>Incantations are the fictions of silly women.</note>

# CHAP. V. supposed Witchcraft.

The argument concerning confessions is this: Is it possibly credible to a rational and unbiased judgment that the witches (no matter how many, at various times and places) having made themselves the slaves and vassals of the Devil, both in soul and body, and being led by his lying and deceitful spirit (though making large and voluntary confessions) can be conceived to have any spark of truth in them at all? Surely there is no more truth in these confessions than there is in the Devil, who was a liar from the beginning; and therefore we argue thus. Such kind of will, affections, and inclinations as are in the Devil himself, such kind are in his children. But the will and affections of the Devil are against God, His Truth, and against all God's people, and his inclinations tend to continual lying. Therefore the will, affections, and inclinations of his children (such as the witches are, and are granted to be) are against God, His Truth, and against all God's people, and their inclinations tend to continual lying. The proof of the major and minor proposition is the plain words of our Saviour,

<margin>John 8:44.</margin>
> *You are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father the devil you will do, θέλετε ποιεῖν, and he was a murderer from the beginning, and stayed not in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks of his own: for he is a liar, and the father of it.*

And again St. *John* tells us:

<margin>1 John 3:8.</margin>
> *He that commits sin, is of the devil; for the devil has sinned from the beginning.*

<margin>Psalm 62:4.</margin>
So that it may truly be said of them, *They delight in lies, and their confessions are nothing but lies.* And if they object and say that here we admit a league between the Devil and the witch—otherwise the witches could not be his children, vassals, and bond-slaves, which elsewhere we deny—we answer, it is a gross mistake, in not observing the distinction we make between a mental and spiritual league, such as the Devil and *Judas* made, and such as all wicked men make with him, and under this league we acknowledge all witches to be; but a visible and corporeal league we positively deny, and so the objection is of no validity. And thus we suppose we have sufficiently proved that there ought to be no credit at all given to the confessions of witches, any more than to devils, who are all liars.

Now let us proceed to their third main objection: That so many wise and grave judges and honest juries could not have been deceived to put to death such great numbers of those kind of people without sufficient proof of the matters of fact. Against which we oppose these following reasons.

<margin>Reason 1.</margin>
1. It is but an argument at best to drive the other party into an absurdity, which is not of any such dangerous consequence as may be supposed; for it would but conclude that many grave and wise judges and juries have been imposed upon and deceived, which is but *argumentum ad homines* <note>An argument directed at the people involved rather than the logic itself.</note>, and doubtless many might have been, and have been. And do not we Christians hold that the gravest and wisest judges among the *Turks* and *Persians* have been, and are deceived, and have done unjustly in persecuting and

<meta>The text ends with the catchword "putting", leading into the next page's discussion on the persecution of Christians.</meta>

Now, if the witnesses, out of malice, envy, ignorance, or mistake, swear to matters of fact for which death or other punishments are allotted by the law, both the judges and the jury are absolutely excusable; and if there is any guilt in the witnesses, or falsehood in their evidence, it lies at their own doors and upon their own consciences, and the judges and jurors are clear and not to be blamed, for no human prudence can altogether prevent witnesses from erring or swearing falsely.

# The Displaying of CHAP. V.

Instead, the answers given were only of their own devising and framing to maintain their reputation. And so, all the various types of diviners or witches mentioned in the Old Testament were under a spiritual league with the Devil. They knew very well that what they did was not by the power of God, but rather through the help of art, nature, sleight of hand, conspiracy, or similar impostures and cheats. Yet they pretended, as *Simon Magus* did, and claimed to be great men, thereby to deceive others, when they clearly knew themselves to be nothing but hypocrites and liars. For the sake of profit, reputation, and vanity, they pretended to do those things which they could never truly perform.

They know well they have no power to perform these things, but they willingly and knowingly pretend to do them for the sake of vanity and dirty profit. The supposed witches of Samlesbury in the County of Lancaster, in the tenth year of the reign of King James, were so far from this confession that they were cleared, and the accusation found to be false, and all driven by the imposture of one Thompson, or Christopher Southworth. But if there be any such league or covenant between the witches and the Devil, how does the truth of this matter of fact (if ever there were or could be any such thing) come to be certainly known and revealed? Have any of the penmen of the Holy Scriptures recorded that there ever was, is, or can be any such league or contract? Also, in this I appeal to all learned physicians, who know the way that Nature breeds human seed, the causes that make it prolific, and the members fit for its generation and reception; who (I doubt not) will deride this tenet and condemn it as false and abominable. We find also external Transfiguration, as of Christ on the Mountain; for the text says, in St. *Matthew's* Gospel: *And he was transfigured before them, and his face did shine as the Sun, and his raiment was white as the light.* And *Mark* says: *And he was transfigured before them, and his raiment became shining, exceeding white as snow: so as no fuller on earth can white them.* And St. *Luke* says: *And as he prayed, the fashion of his countenance was altered, and his raiment was white and glittering.* The word used in those places for the transfiguring or altering of his face by St. *Matthew* and St. *Mark* is <term>μετεμορφώθη</term>, from <term>μετὰ</term> (trans/across), and <term>μορφὴ</term> (forma/shape), the outward form, shape, figure, or lineaments; and this word is also used for the change or transforming of the mind, will, desires, and affections. For so the Apostle says: *And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.* And again he says: *We behold as in a glass the glory of the Lord with open face: and are transformed into the same image from glory to glory.* But St. *Luke*, instead of this word, expresses it thus: <term>τὸ εἶδος τοῦ προσώπου αὐτοῦ ἕτερον</term>. *Tremellius* renders it: *Transformatus est aspectus vultûs ejus* <note>The appearance of his face was transformed</note>. And *Beza*: *Species vultûs ejus alia* <note>The appearance of his face was different</note>, which is nearest the Greek. So *Moses'* face, when he had been with the Lord upon the Mount, the skin of it did shine, so that he put a veil upon it when he spoke to the people, and put it off when he went in to speak unto the Lord. So these were external alterations of both Christ's and *Moses'* face, by appearing glorious, resplendent, and shining like the Sun; and this was wrought by a divine hand and power. From which we may note,

1. That though Christ was thus gloriously transformed (for so the word carries it), yet we are not to imagine that Christ was essentially changed into some other substance or nature; no, but that he was rather made most resplendent in glory there.

2. And where the Apostle wishes the *Romans* to be transformed: Is it to be essentially transformed into any other substance or natural thing? No, not so, but effectively into some other more sacred qualities, by the renovation of their inward mind. And again where he says: *And are transformed into the same image from glory to glory.* His meaning is not that we are essentially transformed into the very image of God; for if so, he would very sharply confirm that foolish opinion of some who hold that men are deified in God, and that God also is <term>hominified</term> in men. But his purpose is that we (by the operation of the holy Spirit) should proceed and grow (by degrees) from glory to glory, until we be truly conformed to the likeness of that same glorious Image of God wherein we were first created; and so he intends no essential transformation at all.

3. Satan is transformed into an Angel of Light in the same way that his ministers are transformed into the apostles of Christ. But Satan's ministers are not essentially transformed into the apostles of Christ. Therefore, neither is Satan essentially transformed into an Angel of Light. For though Satan’s ministers may pretend to any amount of piety and zeal, and labor to personate and imitate the true ministers of Christ, yet despite that pretended transformation, they still really and essentially remain as they were—that is, deceivers and hypocrites. And Satan, for all his seeming and apparent personating and imitating of the angels of light, still remains in his essence and nature an angel of darkness, and a lying and accursed wretch.

5. The best and most sound expositors—ancient, medieval, and modern—explain this passage as we have argued it, of which we shall name only two or three. St. *Chrysostom* tells us this: *Operarii dolosi: nam operantur quidem, sed revellunt ea quæ sunt plantata: nam quoniam sciunt se aliter non posse esse acceptos, personâ veritatis sumptâ, erroris actum simulantes peragunt.* <note>Deceitful workers: for they indeed work, but they tear up those things that are planted; for since they know they cannot otherwise be accepted, having assumed the persona of truth, they perform the act of error by pretending.</note> And a little after he says this: *Et multos Diabolus sic decipit, personâ in se acceptâ, & non factus Angelus lucis: sic illi personam Apostolorum circumferunt, non ipsam potentiam, neq; fortes sunt.* <note>And the Devil deceives many in this way, by a persona assumed in himself, though not having become an Angel of light; so they carry around the persona of the Apostles, not the power itself, nor are they strong.</note> Dr. *Hammond* gives the paraphrase of this passage thus: 

> "For the truth is (he says) these men that come to infuse false doctrines into you behave themselves as cunningly as they can, and labor to imitate and seem to do those very things that we true Apostles do. And it is no unusual matter for deceivers and seducers to do so; for Satan himself pretends to do those things that the good angels do, and acts as if he intended you all kindness when he comes to destroy you. And therefore it is not at all strange if seducing heretics, employed by him, imitate the actions of the Apostles of Christ; but according to the hypocrisy of their actions, so shall their ends be. See *Theophylact* and *Calvin* on the passage." 

So we positively conclude that from this passage of Scripture, no real or essential transformations of devils can be proved at all.

6. There are natural transformations by progression to perfection, as is manifest in insects, which at first to our view appear to be worms, maggots, creepers, or caterpillars, and yet afterwards become several sorts of winged creatures, such as butterflies of many and various kinds, flies, and the like. For example, that creature which fishermen here in the North call a <term>May-Fly</term> is at first but a little creeper enclosed in a hull made of pieces of straw or the like; and similarly, that which they call a <term>cod-bait</term> is like a yellow maggot with a black head enclosed in a sandy, crusty husk, and yet toward the middle of *August* or the beginning of *September* becomes a fine yellowish fly, which the fishermen use as bait; and these are but gradual progressions toward the perfection of the <term>animalcule</term>, as the learned author *Johannes Swammerdanus* has declared in these words, as we find it laid down in the *Philosophical Transactions*:

Since these are natural transfigurations (for so they may be properly called), we cannot rationally suppose that any person of judgment will imagine that any such can be produced by devils or witches. This is because they are brought forth by natural principles and agents, which devils or witches cannot overrule, alter, nor hinder. Otherwise, the whole and certain course that the Creator has set in the order of the production and generation of natural things might be suspended, which is not possible to be performed without an omnipotent power, which the devils and witches do not have. Besides, most of these require a suitable time for their production and perfection, which must only be performed by the internal operation of nature, or by art accelerating the works of nature, which devils and witches cannot bring to pass.

7. There are several other transformations (at least so accounted and called) which, because they are not absolutely relevant to our purpose, we shall only mention briefly. 1. So a stage-player transforms himself, sometimes to represent one person and sometimes another; and though his outward habit, speech, and action be changed, yet he remains the same in nature and person that he was before those changes, and so this proves nothing for witchcraft at all. 3. Now we must conclude that because this boy lived and lay in the open air, was fed with raw meat, and went on all fours, was he therefore really and essentially changed into a wolf? No, that would be illogical and ridiculous; and so it would be if, because *Nebuchadnezzar* lay in the open field, was wet with the rain and dew, and ate grass like an ox, we concluded that he was therefore really changed into a beast; the absurdities are both alike. This is as mad a kind of inference as if we should say that rabbits and geese eat grass like an ox, therefore they are oxen or asses, when they nevertheless still retain their essential beings and shapes without any essential transformations at all.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
2. Because the hairs of his head (as the text says) had grown like eagles' feathers, and also because the very nails of his hands and feet were like the claws of a bird, yet it does not prove that he was really changed into a beast, for these reasons. 1. Because it would be more consistent to conclude that he was rather transformed into some bird, having feathers and claws, than into a beast that has horns and hoofs, though there was in him no physical transformation at all, but only a changed mind.

2. The text does not use the Hebrew phrase employed when there is real transubstantiation, as with *Lot’s* wife: *Et fuit statua salis* <note>And she became a pillar of salt</note>; but as *Tremellius* translates it: *Usquedum pili ejus ut Aquilarum plumæ crevissent, & ungues ejus ut avium* <note>Until his hair had grown like eagles' feathers, and his nails like birds'</note>. And *Arias Montanus* thus: *Donec capillus ejus sicut Aquilarum crevit, & ungues ejus sicut avium* <note>Until his hair grew like that of eagles, and his nails like those of birds</note>; which is exactly consistent with the Hebrew. So the assertion is not that his hairs were changed into eagles' feathers, nor his nails into birds' claws, but that they were *sicut*, or *as*, the feathers of eagles, and *as* the claws of birds; the hair having grown tangled, filthy, and rough, and the nails having grown long, hard, and curved for want of cutting, grooming, combing, and maintenance; the words or sense do not support more change than this.

3. There was no other change but what occurred by natural growth; for the Hebrew word רבה <note>rabah</note> properly means *it was many, it grew in multitude*: so that the hairs were naturally increased in number and length, and the nails in size and length. Thus, there was no essential change at all, but only an excessive growth of them both, as he had lost the use of reason and therefore could not take measures to cut, clean, and maintain them. So they only grew filthy and ill-favored for want of grooming and care, just as many who have been lost or left in deserts and desolate places have, after some time, been found to be overgrown with hair and ugly nails, so that they have scarcely been taken for men, but have appeared as savage and feral monsters.

> "A certain countryman was seen in the springtime at Alkmaar with a horrid look, and mad, staying about the churchyard, and afterward entering the church; and he leaped upon a seat or plank (as we have seen him), only climbing upward, and another while downward with great fury, and never resting in one place. He carried a long staff in his hand, but struck nobody, though he used it to beat off the dogs; for he had his thighs and legs black and ulcered with black crusts or scabs from the biting of dogs. His whole body appeared squalid, very black, and melancholic, but pale in the face, and his eyes exceedingly hollow. From the aforesaid signs (he says), I judged the man affected with lycanthropy or wolfish melancholy. He never used any physician that I know of. And this both this author, *Schenckius*, and *Sennertus* sufficiently confirm from *Paulus*, *Aetius*, *Avicenna*, and the like."

From all this it is clear and manifest that *Nebuchadnezzar’s* distemper was only a kind of melancholy, whereby the imagination was corrupted and the use of reason and right understanding was for the time taken quite away, as the text says: *Let his heart be changed from man's, and let a beast's heart be given unto him.* That is, let his thoughts, desires, and affections be made brutish; for by the heart in Scripture the thoughts, will, and affections are understood, as in "my son, give me your heart," that is, the love and affections of your soul and heart. So when it is said, *Let a beast's heart be given him*, that means let his mind, thoughts, and affections be made bestial; and so there was a change of the conditions and qualities of his mind and heart, but no real or essential change of his natural heart at all.

<margin>See Polanus, Rollock, and others on Daniel, chapter 4, verse 16.</margin>
And in this sense *Tremellius* takes it, saying: *Let him grow brutish, let him understand nothing human*; and so do *Polanus*, *Rollock*, and others understand it. For *Polanus* says: *His soul ought to have become completely brutish, and his mind and judgment of the human soul lost; for this is not to be understood as some metamorphosis made in the body, but only as the soul becoming brutish.* So that from these examples it appears that many persons, by reason of melancholy in its several kinds, have been mentally and internally (as they thought, being depraved in their imaginations) changed into wolves and other kinds of creatures, and have acted their parts as though they had been really so, when the change was only in the qualities and conditions of the mind, and not otherwise. And so only was the change of *Nebuchadnezzar*, which notwithstanding *Bodinus*, the Popish writers, and witchmongers have falsely and ignorantly taken to be a real transubstantiation, when it was only mental: so apt are men to mistake and urge things amiss when it serves their own gain or interest. But if these persons who thought themselves really changed into wolves had been covered with a wolf's skin fitted to their bodies, and gone upon all fours, and so had acted the parts of wolves, then it might in all likelihood have more strongly induced

So having sufficiently disproved their supposition or assumption that *Nebuchadnezzar* was essentially transformed into a beast, we shall also show the consequence that (if it had been true) they would draw from it: namely, that if *Nebuchadnezzar* were really transformed into a beast, much more may the Devil transform himself into the shape of any creature, and may change witches into cats, dogs, hares, and the like. This can by no true rules of argument be valid, because it stands upon diverse, or rather contrary agents—namely, God and the Devil. The one has of himself an absolute and indeterminate power, and therefore is of himself able to work what he will, where, when, and however it best pleases himself. And so by consequence he might (if it had so seemed good in his wisdom) have essentially transformed *Nebuchadnezzar* into an ox. The other (the Devil, I mean) has only a finite and limited power, and therefore is utterly unable of himself to accomplish any one work beyond the bounds of that power; and so by consequence he cannot possibly transform himself essentially into any creature whatsoever, without a special power from God. Lastly, we shall conclude all with this binding argument: whatever transubstantiations are wrought, the thing transformed ceases to be what it was before, both in nature and properties. For instance, as *Lot's Wife* being transubstantiated into a pillar of salt ceased to be flesh, blood, and bones as she was before, and lost all the properties of human nature. So if devils or witches be transubstantiated into other creatures, they cease to be what they were before, both in nature and properties. And then by consequence the Devil would cease to be a Devil in nature and properties, and the witches would cease to have human nature and properties in them.

Having laid down these positive arguments, we shall in the next place show the horrid absurdities of these tenets—to wit, of holding a visible contract, that the Devil sucks upon the witches' bodies, that they have carnal copulation together, or that they are essentially changed into cats, dogs, or hares, or that they can fly in the air, or raise storms or tempests, and kill men or cattle, and the like—and that in this order:

But however it was, the disciples did not then believe that it was Christ with his individual body in which he suffered, but either (as some of the Church Fathers believed) that it was his very spirit that he yielded up upon the Cross, appearing in his figure or shape, which was so pure, fine, and penetrable that it could pass through any medium, no matter how dense or solid; or some other spirit that assumed his form and shape, which is far more probable and sound. But however it was, they believed that it was some spirit in his likeness and not he himself in that very identical body in which he suffered, as may be clearly gathered from the words of *Thomas* called *Didymus*, who strongly affirmed, saying:

> *Unless I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my fingers into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe.*

4. To the grounds of all these doubts our Savior gives a demonstrative and infallible solution, which we shall explain in these particulars. 1. He does not at all deny the existence or beings of spirits, nor that spirits do not or cannot make visible apparitions, but rather grants both. 2. But he limits these apparitions to those inseparable properties that belong to bodies and spirits; that is, a body (that is to say, a human body) has flesh and bones, but a spirit has neither, as *Christ’s* or human bodies have. Therefore, a learned person says regarding the passage: <margin>Rollock, as above</margin> "He teaches that he is not a spirit in this way: A spirit, he says, does not have flesh and bones. But I, as you see, have flesh and bones; therefore I am not a spirit. Look, therefore, to the senses and things perceived by the senses—namely, the sense of sight and the sense of touch—from things visible and tangible, he teaches that he is a body and not a spirit. For by the senses, faith is both born and confirmed." So whether spirits are taken to be corporeal (and so appear in their own bodies) or to be incorporeal (and so appear in assumed bodies), yet they are both to sight, and especially to touch, not as human bodies are that have flesh and bones. So, however they do, may, or can appear (for it must be considered in that breadth, otherwise our Savior's argument would not be irrefragable and convincing), they cannot be like flesh and bones in their resistance to touch, for flesh and bones resist the sense of touch, and

By this, Thomas’s great unbelief and doubting was unquestionably satisfied, by putting his fingers into or upon the very prints of the nails, and by putting his hand into or upon the wound or scar on his side. And therefore, though the same power that raised him from the dead and rolled the sealed stone from the sepulcher could have perfected his body to be without prints or scars of the wounds, yet divine Wisdom reserved them, thereby to cure the unbelief of his disciples and undeniably to confirm the truth of his resurrection; to which <margin>See Thomas Aquinas's *Catena Aurea* on this passage.</margin> purpose one said well: *there, to heal the hearts of the doubters, the traces of the wounds were preserved.* And further to establish and settle their faith, he took a piece of a broiled fish and of a honeycomb and ate before them; all of which concluded him to have a true body, and that he was not a spirit, from which we draw these conclusions.

1. That however spirits do or may appear, they do not, or cannot, have such a body that, in respect to tangibility, is like flesh and bones. For flesh and bones are dense, solid, and make a sensible resistance to the touch; but the bodies of spirits in their apparitions are not, nor can they be so. For while we do not deny that there are and may be apparitions in any figure or shape, yet they can only be like the figures and shapes in the clouds, which are often seen and cause much wonder, though (we suppose) many of them may be attributed more to the projections of men's imaginations than to their real existence in those forms or shapes. So they may be like shadows, or the appearances of bodies that we see near or far off, or like the images that we behold of ourselves and other things in mirrors or looking-glasses; which, though they are certainly not non-entities (for *nothingness has no operation*), yet they affect the senses, which is an operation or action. Still, they all easily yield to the touch and have no firmness or solidity as flesh and bones have; and this is all that can be justly deduced from our Saviour’s argumentation.

2. Either we must believe that our Saviour’s argument has no force or validity—which is blasphemous and horrid to affirm or imagine, he being the way, the truth, and the life, and in whose mouth there was found no guile—and thereby overthrow the whole foundation of the Christian religion; or else we must certainly believe that spirits, whenever they appear, have no such solidity or resistance to touch as flesh and bones have. And consequently, that whatever strange things we may, by sight and touch, take to be the apparitions of spirits, which to the touch have the solidity of flesh and bones,

## CHAP. VI.

->*That various places in Scripture have been mistranslated, thereby to uphold this horrid opinion of the Devil's omnipotence and the power of witches, when there is not one word that signifies a familiar spirit or a witch in that sense that is vulgarly intended.*<-

<margin>*Wierus*, book 2, page 89.</margin>
<margin>*A Candle in the Dark*, p. 10.</margin>

Concerning the words in the Hebrew and Greek that are commonly alleged to prove these things, they have been wrested and strained to uphold these tenets by those translators who had imbibed these opinions; and so instead of following the true and genuine significance of the words, they hauled them to support a preconceived opinion, and did not simply and plainly render them as they ought to have been. This has been observed by many, especially by *Wierus*, who got the learned *Masius* (a great <term>Hebrician</term> <note>a scholar of the Hebrew language</note>) to interpret them, of which he has given a full account, which was followed by Mr. *Scot*. Also Mr. *Ady*, who has perfectly rendered them according to the translation of *Junius* and *Tremellius*, and likewise Mr. *Wagstaff* has neatly explained most of them. So that our attempt here might seem to be superfluous and unnecessary, and may be condemned as arrogance and vain confidence. To which we reply: that it is far from us to compare ourselves with those learned men who were masters of the Hebrew and Greek tongues, being in comparison but a smatterer in those languages; yet we have in our younger years both studied and taught them to others, and as far as we undertake, we hope we need not fear the censure of the most rigid critic, intending to note some things that others have omitted, and to handle them fully, which others have only done briefly. 4. And even if there were no other means to distinguish a true miracle from a false one, this would still be infallibly sufficient to instruct and direct us.

<margin>See the Polyglot Bible on this passage.</margin>

The Septuagint renders it for the most part as κληδονιζόμενοι <note>omen-seekers</note>, sometimes as οἰωνιζόμενοι <note>augurs</note>, and sometimes as ὀρνιθοσκοπήσεσθε <note>bird-watchers</note>, which are all of different derivations and meanings. Others render it in other ways, such as: *neither shall you seek omens, nor shall you observe times, do not prophesy, do not predict, let him not observe dreams and auguries, nor he who practices astrology*, etc. Now, from such a diversity, no man is able to draw a positive certainty.

2. They do not stick to one specific word appropriate to the Hebrew, which they would have done—had they not forgotten themselves—rather than leaving it uncertain. For *Arias Montanus*, in the 19th chapter of *Leviticus*, verse 26, renders it as *neither shall you practice enchantments*, and in the 2nd chapter of *Isaiah*, verse 6, translates it as *augurs like the Philistines*. Now, what a great difference there is between any sort of augury and juggling, or sleight-of-hand, is known to anyone of average reading. Even Junius and Tremellius, who of all others one might have thought would have been more circumspect, still fall into the same uncertainty; for in Deuteronomy 18:10, they translate it as *Planetarius*, but in the place previously cited in Leviticus, they translate it as *neque utemini præstigiis*, though in the margin they correct it with this note: <note>neither make conjectures from the clouds, nor grant more than is right to the observation of time</note>. And in Isaiah 2:6, *Et præstigiatores sunt ut Polischtai*.

<margin>
See John Weyer, *De Praestigiis Daemonum*, book 1, p. 91.
Of Divination, book 4, chapter 10, p. 183.
</margin>

3. But if there is any certainty in adhering to the original meaning of the Hebrew root, which plainly signifies *obnubilavit* (to cloud over), then it is without question most safe and genuine to translate it as *Planetarius*. To this, the most learned Andreas Masius (as he is quoted by Weyer) inclines in these words: "The ancient Hebrews say that word properly pertains to those who superstitiously observe moments of time, and prescribe some things as lucky and others as unlucky for carrying out affairs." To which Mr. Thomas Goodwin agrees, saying: "But of all, I approve those who derive it from ענן, a cloud, as if the original signified properly a planetary or star-gazer."

4. But however, thus far there is no word found that signifies a witch in the sense we have defined, nor any such person who has a real familiar spirit, either within them or attending upon them, ready to appear visibly at their command; this has not yet been found.

4. The next is וְנִחֵשׁ from the root נחש *nichesh*, *auguratus est*, *observavit*, *augurium fecit*. Our English translators have erroneously rendered this as an "enchanter," which it in no way signifies, nor has any relation to. Having named a "charmer" in the next verse, it is as though "enchanter" and "charmer" were not the same thing, when the word plainly (as Mr. Goodwin and the learned Masius confess) implies an augur or soothsayer: that is, one who from his own experience draws observations of good or evil to come. Regarding this, we may note these things:

1. Most of the translations given to us in the *Polyglot* Bible translate the Hebrew word as *auguratus est*, and so understand it to be an augur or soothsayer, a conjecturer, or an observer. This is based on whatever source he takes his observations from, such as the flight, cries, or motion of birds or beasts, looking into their entrails, and the like; and from there taking it upon themselves to foretell good or evil to come, or what was hidden and secret.

2. The Hebrew word נחש is rendered by the Septuagint as οἰώνισμα, *Augurium*, *Auspicium*—that is, an augur, an observer, or a conjecturer—which Luther translates as: <term>eyn de up Voegell geschrey achtet</term> <note>one who pays attention to the cries of birds</note>.

3. This Hebrew word is taken in a positive sense, meaning to heedfully consider, mark, or observe, as Laban said when he labored to stay Jacob from going from him:

So that though Laban’s heart was not upright toward Jacob, nor was he a sincere worshiper of the God of the Jews; yet so far had the Lord convinced him, by the faithful and industrious service of Jacob that he had experienced, and by trial found that the Lord had blessed him for Jacob’s sake.

<margin>Gen. 44:5, 15.</margin>
And the same word is used when Joseph said:

> Is not this the cup wherein my Lord drinks, and whereby indeed he divines, or makes trial?

And again:

> Do you not know that such a man as I can certainly divine, or make trial?

And though Pererius has made a large dispute about this matter, and recites the opinions of many authors concerning it; yet it is manifest that Joseph knew his brothers before, and had caused the cup to be put into Benjamin’s sack, and that all this was only done in a just and prudent way, the better to prepare his brothers for his revealing of himself to them, and so had reference to no unlawful conjecturing at all, though it was plain that he had the special gift from God of interpreting dreams and foretelling things that were to come.

4. It is too hard a task to enumerate all the several ways that the heathens used, by observation, to foretell things to come, and more difficult to declare all the subjects from which they gathered the signs of their predictions. The chief ones that the old Romans used were *Augurium*, said as if it were *Avigerium* or *Avigarium*, namely from the chirping of birds (*ab avium garritu*) which those taking auspices observed: and so *Auspicium*, as if it were *Avispecium*, from watching birds (*ab avibus spectandis*). And these observations were taken either from the feeding, flying, or noise of the birds. So they had their *Haruspices, Harioli*, and *Haruspicina*, which was derived from *haruga* (a sacrificial victim), from *hara* (the pen in which it is confined and kept).

5. But all these sorts of observations, guessings, and conjectures may be considered in these three ways: 1. Some of them are natural, rational, and legal; such as the prognostic part of the art of medicine, and political predictions of the change, fall, and ruin of kingdoms, states, and empires. Some are civil, taken from the course and conduct of men; as when one sees a rich young heir who follows nothing but vice, luxury, and all sorts of debauchery, it is easy to foretell that his end will be beggery and misery. Some, from the due observation of beasts and fowls which live in the open air (*sub dio*), may easily conjecture the alteration of the weather. And so by observing

# CHAP. VI. supposed Witchcraft.

Observing the change, or color of the stars and planets, the clouds and elements, may easily foretell the change of weather. And we find that these predictions from the signs gathered from natural causes are not condemned by our Blessed Savior, who says: <margin>Matt. 16:2, 3.</margin> *When it is evening, you say it will be fair weather, for the sky is red. And in the morning, it will be foul weather today, for the sky is red and lowering.* And again: <margin>Luke 12:54.</margin> *When you see a cloud rise out of the West, straightway you say, there comes a shower, and so it is. And when you see the South wind blow, you say, there will be heat, and it comes to pass.*

2. There are some conjectures that are false, groundless, and superstitious, as were, and are, all the predictions taken from the feeding, flying, or noise of fowls, or the signs appearing in the entrails of beasts; for in all such things, there is no connection between the cause and effect, and they therefore are false and vain, and this was one of the reasons why they were forbidden among the Jews.

3. There were some that in regard to their use and end were wicked and idolatrous, and in this respect all divinations and predictions are wicked and unlawful if they be used (as was and is yet among the Heathen) to lead the people to, or confirm them in, the worship of idols and false gods. And from all this it appears that yet we can find no proper or fit word for such a kind of witch whose existence we have denied and are disproving.

5. The next word in this place of *Deuteronomy* is ומכשף *Umechafcheth*, which our translators render as a "witch," but in what sense or propriety, I think few can conjecture; for it comes from the Hebrew root, כשף *Coscheth*, which *Avenarius* renders as *Fascinavit* (he fascinated) or *effascinavit* (he bewitched), but *Schindlerus* translates it as "practiced illusions, mischief, or magic; he changed something natural in the sight of the eye, so that it appeared other than it is." And by *Buxtorfius* it is rendered *Præstigiæ* (illusions), and the derivations from it through the whole Old Testament, which is the most certain propriety of the word, as these following considerations will make manifest.

<margin>Exod. 7:11, 22.</margin>
<margin>2 Chron. 33:6.</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 9:22.</margin>
1. That most of the translators, in rendering this word whether in this place or in others, have been very inconstant, one place not agreeing with another; as *Arias Montanus* in this place gives it as *maleficus* (evildoer), but in *Exodus* he makes it *Præstigiatores* (illusionists), and in the 22nd and 16th [chapters] of the same book he makes it *Præstigiatricem*; and in another place where the very same word is used in the Hebrew, he says of *Manasseh*, *& Præstigiis vacabat* ("and he was occupied with illusions"). And yet in another place, he renders the very same word as *veneficia* (sorceries or poisonings). So uncertain was this learned man, and so inconsiderate in his versions, wherein he ought to have had a more special care. Now *Tremellius*, in all the places named before, does use the word *Præstigiatorum* and words from the same derivation in Latin, which shows certainty and constancy.

This is spiritual rebellion, just as the divinations of idol-priests and idol-worship were.
