# CHAP. VI. *Supposed Witchcraft.*

...associates or gathers many animals into one place, or associates them so they do not cause harm. From this we may note the following:

<margin>Chap. 14. 3. Exod. 36. 10.</margin>
1. That it primarily signifies joining together, as in that passage of *Genesis* speaking of the kings who went to war: *All these were joined together in the vale of Siddim, which is the salt sea.* And in another place: *And he coupled the five curtains together*; and in the same sense in various other places. By all of which it appears that when it is used for incantation or charming, it is because of some conjunction or coupling together.

2. It is very remarkable that in all the translations in the *Polyglot*, there is no variance; neither do *Arias Montanus*, *Buxtorfius*, or *Tremellius* differ at all, and the Greek translators agree with them, who render it <term>ἐπαίδων ἐπαοιδώ</term>, and the *German*, *Dutch*, *French*, and *Italian* translators agree with this. It is likewise so rendered in *Isaiah* 47:9, 12 and in other places. So it is plain that it signifies those who took it upon themselves, through strange words and charms, to prevent venomous beasts from hurting, biting, or stinging, and many other wonderful things; but what they actually brought to pass, or achieved—besides deluding and deceiving the people and leading them to idolatry—is hard to determine, which we shall discuss in another place.

3. There are various opinions concerning this incantation or charming, as to why it should be accounted as "conjunction" or "association." Some, such as *Schindlerus* and *Bithner*, judge it is because they associate or bring together many serpents or harmful creatures into one place and then destroy them. But this is merely a conjecture, for it is strongly disputed by the best learned on both sides whether charms and enchantments can really and truly perform any such effects; various instances and examples are brought forward both ways, some for the affirmative and some for the negative, so that the matter of fact is not certainly known or granted. Others understand "association" to mean the league or compact made between the charmer and the Devil, by virtue of which such strange things are brought to pass by them. This was the opinion of Mr. *Perkins* (if that book on witchcraft that goes under his name is truly his) who, strengthening his notion with that verse in the 58th *Psalm*, thought that he had found an invincible argument to prove the compact between witches and devils. Therefore, it is necessary and expedient to examine that text to the bottom to sift out the true translation and sense of that passage, which we shall do at length in the following particulars.

1. Our *English* translators render it thus, speaking of the deaf adder or asp: *Which will not listen to the voice of the charmers, charming ever so wisely*; and in the margin, *or be the charmer ever so cunning*, where they take no notice of the joining of conjunctions, and consequently none of such a league or compact.

2. *Tremellius* gives it thus: *Which does not listen to the voice of those who mutter, using*

# The Displaying of CHAP. VI.

We shall leave this to the judgment of critics and provide the marginal note that is added there. <margin>*surda*] that is, acting craftily against incantations, as the following words explain; for she stops both her ears by fixing one to the earth and covering and stopping the other with her tail.</margin> Of the deaf adder: "acts craftily against the incantations, as the following words do expound: For she stops both her ears, by fixing one to the earth, and covering and stopping the other with her tail; and that Hierome, Augustine, Cassiodorus, and others do so expound the place." Whether this be true of the asp or not is much to be doubted, for I find no author of credit who avers it from his own knowledge, and the thing is very difficult to bring to experiment; and the Psalmist might speak according to vulgar opinion, for which there was no necessity that it should be literally and certainly true. Further, he goes on and says, *mussitantium*] "That is to say, pronouncing their incantations to charm her, whispering and very low"; which study of charming—lest any should think that David approves of them in this place—he learnedly uses the very words of the prohibition which God laid down in Deuteronomy 18:11. For (he says) these fascinators in the Hebrew name are said to associate society, because they apply the society of the Devil to their arts.

3. Those we call the Septuagint render it thus: Ἥτις οὐκ εἰσακούσεται φωνὴν ἐπᾳδόντων, φαρμάκῳ τε φαρμακευομένῳ παρὰ σοφῷ. And that which is ascribed to Hierome in the eighth volume of his works printed at Basil in 1525, gives two Latin versions of this, one answering to the Septuagint which is this: *Quæ non exaudiet vocem incantantium & venefici incantantis sapienter.* The other according to the Hebrew thus: *Ut non audiat vocem murmurantium, nec incantatoris incantationes callidas.* So this makes the meaning to be that the deaf asp is so cunning in stopping her ear that she does not hear the voice of those who murmur and mutter charms, even if it is a charmer that utters the most cunning and powerful charms. So here there is no regard given to joining or associating either serpents together, or the society of the charmer and the Devil.

### CHAP. VI. Supposed Witchcraft.

(that the witch and the devil were in a pact and sworn together) and that they were most skilled in that art. But this only begs the question, in a way, and does not prove it; for all it amounts to is this: that the asp cannot be charmed, not even by those who have the greatest skill in the matter of incantation.

5. The *French* Translators render it thus: *Le quel n'écoute point la voix des enchanteurs, ni du charmeur fort expert en charmes*, which is: "Who will not at all hear the voice of the enchanter, nor of the charmer who is expert in charms." And this proves nothing at all regarding joining societies or making pacts. The *Italian* version gives it this way: *Accioche non oda la voce de glivoce incantatori, del venefico incantante incantationi di dotto*. In *English* thus: "So that it does not hear the voice of the enchanter, of the witch (if that is the meaning of the word *venefico*, a poisoner) enchanting with the incantations of the learned." And this is the closest to the *Hebrew* of all the others, and conveys this much: that the asp does not listen to the voice of the enchanter, or of the charmer who uses charms that were framed and joined together by a learned scholar. So, if "associating" is included, it must be understood as the framing and joining of the charms, which undoubtedly was the composition of those who were very learned, especially if they work by a natural operation, which we shall discuss hereafter.

6. But now we come to the *Hebrew* itself, which *Arias Montanus* renders thus: *Quæ non audiet ad vocem mussitantium: jungentis conjunctiones docti*. And in the margin thus: <margin>*Quæ non obtemperabit voce incantantium, incantantis incantationes sapienter*</margin>. Which we may translate into English as: "Which listens not to the voice of the mutterers, of the learned joiner of conjunctions." And the other thus: "Which obeys not the voice of the charmers, of the person charming charms wisely." So it may mean that the asp listens not to the voice of those who mutter or whisper the charms of the charmer who uses them wisely, or of him who is a wise charmer. But it is unnecessary and improper to make a half-stop at *mussitantium* [mutterers], for then there will be no coherence in grammatical structure between the former and latter part of the verse. Therefore, according to the rules of grammar, it should be rendered thus: *Quæ non audiet ad vocem mussitantium incantationes, docti incantantis*. And so the meaning is plainly this: that the asp does not listen to the voice of those who mutter the charms of a learned charmer. And thus there is no intimation of an association or pact either one way or the other, but it merely implies that the asp resists and frustrates the charms of the mutterers who use them, even though they are wise in their use, which is undoubtedly the most natural rendering and the true meaning of the passage. Or else it may be aptly translated this way: *Quæ non audiet ad vocem mussitantium conjunctiones jungentis docti*; that is: "Which listens not to the voice of those who mutter the conjunctions of a learned joiner." So in this way the sense will be, that the

We may note that these words (that is to say, the *genii* divining from the belly) which we have enclosed in parentheses are not found in the Greek written by *Plutarch*, but are only added as the conjecture of *Turnebus*. 4. *Plutarch* holds it childish to believe that God hides himself and speaks in the belly of these cheating diviners, and in this, though a pagan, he was wiser than many who profess Christianity now, who believe it to be some spirit, when it is nothing but the cunning imposture of those persons who through practice have learned that artifice of turning their voices back into their throats and breasts. 5. As for matter of fact, it is manifest that in the time of *Plutarch* there were those who practiced this cunning trick to gain credit or money by the pretense of predictions and divinations; such a person was doubtless the woman at *Endor*, and the maid mentioned in the *Acts* of the Apostles, of whom we shall speak shortly.

whether it was a natural illness or not. The father and the boy, along with an old "cunning woman" (an accomplice brought in to emphasize the certainty of his possession and the truth of a spirit speaking within him), came to see me; they all appeared to my judgment and best reason to be fitting persons to perform a planned imposture. The father had been one who lived extravagantly and spent most of his wealth, being quite profane and irreligious. The boy, by his face, appeared to have a melancholy temperament and a subtle and crafty disposition. The woman was cunning and tried to force me to believe whatever she recounted, thinking she could deceive me as she had done others. I immediately judged it to be neither a natural disease nor a supernatural affliction, but only trickery and imposture; thus, I silenced the woman and told her she was a cheat who deserved proper punishment, and that most of the things she told were lies of her own invention. I told the father and the son that I could soon cast out all the devils he was possessed with, but that I must have him in my own custody, and none of them were to come near him or speak with him. I waited for a long time to see him in one of his fits, but his "devil" was too fearful of my stern face and harsh behavior. Well, after those three had consulted together, the lad could by no means be persuaded to stay with me, not even for that night, nor could he be convinced to be brought into my presence again. Instead, they went away, the lad riding behind his father; and when they were about a quarter of a mile from the town and the father turned the horse to come back to me, the lad leaped off the horse and ran away from the town as fast as he could. That night, they went to a Catholic house where there was a large enough gathering of people, and many tales were told of the spirit’s divinations in the boy, but not one word was said either about me or against me. Soon after, the gentleman who was related to the boy came over, and I satisfied him that it was a contrived trick. After he returned, he tried to persuade them to send the boy to me, but he could by no means accomplish it; therefore, he never paid them any regard afterward, and soon after, the matter vanished into nothing.

<margin>History 4.</margin> I myself also knew a person in the West Riding of *Yorkshire* who, about forty years ago or more, for the sake of making sport, would put a blanket over himself and then make anyone who did not know the truth believe that he had a child with him. He would converse so lifelike with two voices and would imitate crying and the like. Also, the same person, under a blanket and moving on all fours, would so exceedingly aptly—even realistically—act out a skirmish between two mastiffs, both by baring his teeth, snarling, and all other motions and noises, that several sensible people were deceived and truly believed there were two mastiffs under the blanket, until their eyes convinced them of their error. So deceptive can art or skill be when supported by practice and agility.

5. But to come to the heart of the matter, these things are to be considered. 1. Some thought that they were really and essentially possessed with an evil spirit that spoke in them and gave forth answers, and this is the most common, though most false, opinion. If it were true, it supports nothing regarding those familiars that are attributed to our witches; for by that they mean a visible devil outside of them in the shape of a dog, a cat, or the like, and both of these are equally absurd and false, as we shall show shortly. 2. Some thought that an evil spirit from the outside merely worked upon their minds, and so inspired them with these divinations, and this seems to have been the opinion of *Plutarch* and some others of the heathens. 3. But others (which is the view we maintain) held that they were counterfeiting, deluding impostors, and what they did was only by <term>ventriloquy</term>, juggling, and conspiracy, and that all their pretended divinations and predictions were nothing but lying conjectures and ambiguous equivocations. But to explain it fully, we must understand that they pretended and took it upon themselves to foretell and declare things to come, which nonetheless were but false forgeries and lies. For if they had really had any certain foreknowledge of things to come, then when *Jehu* was made king and subtly pretended to sacrifice to *Baal*, and so gathered together all the priests to sacrifice—if these base, lying, cheating impostors had really had any skill in divination—then they might have known that their assembly was not truly to advance their idolatry, but to take their lives. And it may safely be concluded that those who could not foresee the danger threatening their own lives could not truly foretell contingent events to others. And though the Scripture gives us many such examples as these, yet to avoid wordiness, this may suffice to demonstrate that all their pretended predictions were nothing but conjectures or lying forgeries.

And as they took it upon themselves to foretell things to come, so this Woman of *Endor*, and likely the rest, pretended to do it by raising up, or causing the dead to ascend, to give answers to the things demanded.

4. <margin>2 Chron. 33:6.</margin> Among all the various ways of Idolatry that *Manasseh* set up, or caused to be set up, this is one: וַיַּעַשׂ אוֹב, and *fecit Pythonem*, or *fecissetque Pythonem*; he made *Ob*, or *Pytho*. And though translators have been much perplexed and hard-pressed to give a meaning agreeable to their preconceived opinion, yet they have—whether right or wrong—brought it to fit their minds, though it is utterly false and erroneous. For *Tremellius* renders it *instituitque Pythonem* <note>and he established Python</note>, which, though fairly close, is still short of the proper meaning, and most of the others have gone quite the opposite way. But our *English* translators are the worst of all, who translate it: *and dealt with a familiar spirit*. When it is plain that this word must be taken in this place as it is in the third verse of this chapter: *he made groves*, *fecitque lucos*, because the words are both from the same root, which is עָשָׂה *fecit*, *confecit*, *perfecit* <note>he made, completed, or finished</note>. This is how it is and must be understood in other places, and it is especially clear in these: <margin>Gen. 6:14, 16.</margin> *God said to Noah, make for yourself an Ark of Gopher wood, and after, a window shall you make for the Ark.* <margin>Psal. 115:3.</margin> The Psalmist says: *But our God is in heaven, he has done whatever he pleased*, and again, *To him who alone does great wonders.* <margin>Id. 136:4.</margin> We might add forty more places where the word is used that comes from this root and has the same exact meaning; so from this we may conclude: 1. That *Manasseh* could not make a Devil or a Spirit, and therefore the word *Ob* does not intend or represent any such matter in its true and genuine meaning. 2. That he could not make a man or woman, and therefore the word properly signifies neither. 3. That he could only make and cause to be constructed the groves in such an order as the idol-priests might direct, as most fit for them to perform their deceptive and juggling tricks and delusions. So he might make or cause to be constructed the <term>μαντεῖον</term> <note>manteion; a place of divination</note> or place for the oracle, and prepare those gadgets and tools with which the diviner—either by him or herself, or with the help of accomplices—might bring about strange things. These things were made to lead the blind and ignorant people to believe they were performed by the God worshipped in and by those idols, or by demons and spirits, or by calling up the dead. When in truth, nothing at all was performed except through raptures, faked and forced furies, or trances; and by these means, lying predictions and ambiguous equivocations were uttered, by which the people were deluded and drawn into idolatry. Or, they gave dark and obscure responses by <term>Ventriloquy</term>, speaking into bottles, or through hollow pipes and cavities, through which they would "peep and mutter." 8. The next word that follows in this passage of *Deuteronomy* is וְיִדְּעֹנִי from the root יָדַע *he knew* or *he perceived*; it properly refers (as Avenarius says) to the mind and intellect. Our translators (contrary to their usual custom) have maintained consistency here and have always translated it as a Wizard, a name (as we conjecture) that is not improper. For we, in the North of *England*, call those who take it upon themselves to foretell where things are that have been stolen, or to take upon themselves to help people or property that the foolish credulity of the common people has thought to be bewitched—we (I say) call them Wise Men or Wise Women, without regard to the way or means by which they undertook to perform these things. Many others translate it as *sciolus* <note>A pretender to knowledge or a smatterer.</note>, which is proper and consistent with the former. The other translations that we have either seen or were able to understand are so uncertain, various, broad, and wild that it would be a waste of labor to examine or recite them; and the word Wizard (though a general one) is the most proper that we can find. But we must conclude that so far we find no such word that signifies a Witch in the sense we have allowed and endeavored to disprove.

9. The last word mentioned in this text of *Deuteronomy* is a Necromancer, or one who consults with the dead. Now whether there was some special kind of divination, or merely a grouping of all the kinds—being in all their various sorts merely a way of leading the people to inquire of dumb and dead idols—may be a significant and important question. And though no interpreter or commentator whom we have seen, read, or remember suggests any such matter, but instead they all keep to the common theme—that it should be some kind of magic by which they could make the dead appear and consult with them—nevertheless, despite all this, we cannot but propose our doubts for the following reasons.

1. *Moses* in this text undoubtedly did not set down all the particular types of divinations and deceptions used among the Heathen, for that would hardly have been possible, but only the primary kinds of them. And it is not rationally probable that he would do it by a tautology, or a repetition of the same thing twice. For inquiring of the dead, or consulting with them, was intended in the word *ob*, and the woman of *Endor* said: *Whom shall I raise up, or cause to ascend to you?* By this it appears that she pretended (and *Saul* also vainly believed, who said: *Divine for me in or by ob*) that she could cause the dead to ascend and receive answers from them about things to come, as is manifest in the story of the pretended apparition and prediction of *Samuel*. And so this thing would be twice repeated in this place, which is not probable that *Moses* would have done.

1. It is the opinion of *Masius* and Mr. *Ady* that it is a general word, and signifies one who has skill in many of these kinds of arts (if they may be so called). The latter of these says: "**It is taken in the general sense for *magus*, a Magician; one who has one or all of these crafts or impostures.**" And the former, quoting the sentence of Rabbi *Isaac Natar*, says: <note>By this name, the Hebrews called anyone among the nations who professed singular wisdom, especially when it pertained to superstition.</note>

By this it appears plainly that it is a general name, and may most properly be rendered as "magician."

3. It may most properly be taken for a magician because those who acted before *Pharaoh* are called by that name; and, except for their opposition to *Moses* and their superstition, it does not appear that they dealt with unlawful magic, as we shall prove undeniably hereafter.

II. There is also another word which is used in various places, which is <note>לחש</note> *mussitavit*, "he has muttered" or "murmured." It is taken generally for any kind of murmuring for any cause whatsoever, as in this place: *But when David saw that his servants whispered.* And again: *All that hate me, whisper together against me.* And in another place: <note>They poured out a low prayer</note>, a low whispering prayer. In these places, it is taken for any kind of low speaking, whispering, or muttering. Regarding this, we may observe these things:

1. Sometimes by a metonymy <note>a figure of speech where a concept is referred to by the name of something closely associated with it</note> it is taken for a low and modest speech, the art of oratory, or eloquence, as in *Isaiah* 3:3: <note>and one who is intelligent or skilled in eloquence</note>, and sometimes for an earring, *inauris*, as in the 20th verse of the same chapter.

<margin>Psalm 58:6.</margin>
2. It is also ascribed to charmers or enchanters, as in the Psalm: *That does not listen to the voice of the charmers*. Here it is plain that all charmers were whisperers and mutterers, but not conversely that all whisperers or mutterers are charmers.

<margin>Eccles. 10:11.</margin>
3. And whereas our English translation reads it: *Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment, and a babbler is no better*; it may as well be read as *Arias Montanus* translates it: <note>If the serpent bites without hissing or sibilance.</note> And *Schindlerus* to the same purpose: <note>If the serpent will bite without incantation, or murmur—that is, a hiss.</note> And so *Avenarius*: <note>If the serpent bites without whispering—that is, without a hiss.</note> And though *Tremellius* and the whole troop of translators do render it as our English translators do, yet that will not make sense. For it would imply that just as a serpent will bite unless it is charmed, so will a babbler also do. But who ever heard of babblers being charmed? So, truly considered, that cannot be the sense of the passage.

Thus we have reviewed all the words in the Old Testament that can in any way relate to this subject, and yet among them all there is not one that properly and genuinely—without stretching, distorting, or mistranslating—does or can signify any such Witch or Diviner that can kill or destroy men or beasts, or that makes a visible pact with a Devil, or whose body he sucks, or that they have sexual intercourse together; or such a Witch as is or can be actually changed into a cat, dog, or something similar, which was the task we undertook in this chapter. And as for the words that are in the New Testament, we shall handle them when we answer the objections made from there. Therefore, we would warn Mr. *Glanvill*, and all other honest and sober persons, to beware of false translations or mistranslations, and not to labor to establish dangerous and erroneous tenets upon such slippery and sandy foundations: For one falsehood once assumed or accepted as truth brings a numerous train of absurdities following after it.

## CHAP. VII. *Supposed Witchcraft.*

...power in those particulars that we have opposed. And because the whole stress lies upon the true interpretation of those places pretended to prove such matters by, we think it convenient and very conducive to the task at hand to lay down those rules of interpretation that the most learned theologians have declared and assigned; specifically in these particulars.

1. That to truly understand the Scriptures according to the mind of the Holy Spirit who gave them forth, and by whose inspiration they were written, it is most necessary that we implore the help of that blessed Spirit who revealed them to those who penned them; because, as St. James says:
<margin>James 1:5, 17.</margin>
> *If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all men liberally and without reproach, and it shall be given him. For every good gift, and every perfect gift is from above, and comes down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation, nor shadow of turning.*
And it is said of the disciples of Christ:
<margin>Luke 24:45.</margin>
> *Then opened he their understandings, that they might understand the Scriptures.*
So that all men, whether wise or unwise, learned or unlearned, have need of the teaching and Spirit of Christ to open their understandings to understand the Scriptures; and therefore all men have need of faithful and fervent prayers, so that God may enlighten their minds in the understanding of them; otherwise, they are but like blind men who go without a guide, and so must necessarily fall into the ditch of ignorance and error.

2. That a most due and diligent collation and comparison be made of the several versions with the sources and originals themselves, so that the accuracy of the translations may be determined. For if an error in this point is committed, all the expositions and deductions drawn from there must necessarily be erroneous and faulty.

3. That there be a due comparing of the antecedents and consequents in the context, so that the purpose, scope, theme, arguments, disposition, and method may be perfectly and maturely considered: otherwise, by slighting or omitting any one of these particular points, the whole passage may be mistaken, and an error easily fallen into.

4. There must be a due and serious consideration of the phrases and manner of speaking, especially in regard to that language in which it was first written: For every distinct language has its peculiar phrases and forms of speaking, which may not be proper in another tongue; ignoring this may more quickly lead to a great deviation from the genuine sense of the passage.

5. That there be a most diligent comparing of the passage of Scripture to be explained with others of the same similarity or difference. For oftentimes one Scripture unfolds and opens another, and one text clarifies and makes plain another: for want of a due comparison of one with another, the true sense of the passage that is to be expounded may be mistaken.

6. And especially when explaining any passage, regard must be given to the <term>Analogy of Faith</term>: because the Scriptures do not contradict one another, especially in the articles of faith and the chief points necessary to be believed.

<margin>2 Peter 1:20.</margin>

7. A proper comparison ought to be made with the judgments and sentiments of other interpreters, as the Apostle says: *That no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation*: which ought to be translated as the learned Beza and Dr. Hammond provide: "No prophecy of Scripture is *propriæ incitationis*, of a man's own or proper incitation, motion, or releasing; for so the Greek is, <term>ἰδίας ἐπιλύσεως οὐ γίνεται</term>." Regarding this, Beza provides this learned note: "The Prophets are indeed to be read, but in such a way that the gift of interpretation is asked of God, so that the same God may be both the Author and Interpreter of the prophetic writings. For though a man has by nature ever so great endowments of understanding, judgment, and reason, or has ever so large and ample acquirements, or presumes ever so highly to be assisted by the Spirit; yet his own single judgment ought not to be relied upon in the exposition of the Scriptures; but he ought to call for aid and to consider the sentiment and opinion of others." For it is obvious into what dangerous errors the <term>Arians</term>, <term>Pelagians</term>, and <term>Antitrinitarians</term> of old, and the <term>Socinians</term> and <term>Arminians</term> of later years have fallen, by making their innate notions and the strength of natural reason the chief and principal rules for interpreting the Scriptures. And there is hardly any one thing that the Scriptures are more against, or do more condemn, than the too much extolling and idolizing of human and carnal reason. Because *the carnal mind*, <term>τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς</term>, *is enmity against God, and is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be*; of which Beza says: *Probatio cur intelligentia carnis sit mors, quia, inquit, Dei est hostis* <note>The proof of why the understanding of the flesh is death: because, he says, it is an enemy of God.</note>. And again, the text says: *For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,* <term>τὴν σοφίαν τῶν σοφῶν</term>, *and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent*; <term>τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν συνετῶν</term>. And again, *Has not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?* <term>σοφίαν τοῦ κόσμου τούτου</term>. And the words of the Hebrew in that passage of *Isaiah* signify all that height of wisdom or understanding that men either have by nature or acquire by art and industry. Nor is it safe for a man to rely upon his own single acquired talents, be they ever so vast or great; because in most ages, the most destructive errors and damnable heresies have been voiced and maintained by men who were of the greatest acquired endowments. And that it is often as vain to presume upon having the guidance of the Spirit, as it is the other two, is manifest in the recent times of rebellion and confusion; where every man pretending the Spirit made such wild and extravagant expositions of the Scriptures as few ages have known before; and this is still kept up by the giddy troop of fanatical <term>Quakers</term> and the like.

Whereby allegorical, metaphorical, mystical, and parabolical expositions are not only cried down, but by some even abhorred and detested, which thing ought not absolutely and simply to be approved of; and therefore we shall make it plain in some few particulars.

1. In historical relations of matters of fact, we ought to keep close to the literal meaning, and not to deviate a jot from it; otherwise we should overthrow the best part of the Christian faith, and destroy the chief foundation of Scripture truths. But notwithstanding this, though we ought to hold to the literal sense in respect of the matter of fact, yet we are not always to be bound to the bare letter in the mood, means, or manner of the performance. It is apparent that our Saviour Christ cured the man that was born blind, and the means and manner is described: *He spat on the ground and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay. He went his way therefore and washed, and came seeing.* Now as to the matter of fact, that the man born blind was cured and had his sight restored, is a truth according to the sense of the letter; and that the manner, which was by spittle and earth made into clay, and his eyes covered or anointed with it, and washing in the pool of *Siloam*, was also literally true, is manifest. But it were absurd so far to stick to the letter as to believe that clay, and spittle, and washing in the pool of *Siloam*, were true and real natural means to produce that effect; no, that would be absurd, and therein the literal sense is not to be followed.

So when the angel tells the Virgin *Mary* that she should conceive in her womb, and she, not understanding how that should come to pass because she had not known a man, the angel answered, *the Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the highest shall overshadow you.* Though the matter of fact is an undoubted truth and an article of faith, literally taken, yet the manner of the Holy Spirit's coming upon her and the power of the highest overshadowing her cannot be understood in a literal sense—as though it were by that natural and human way that men and women beget and conceive children, for that would be horrid and absurd (as some recent profane, wretched, and debauched atheists have spattered forth)—but rather in a metaphorical sense and a most mystical meaning. So it is plain that where a matter of fact may be literally and historically true, yet the manner in which that matter of fact is brought to pass may be—nay, must be—metaphorical, or else an absurdity will follow, which was the thing undertaken to be proved.

But just as that which is literally and historically true in matter of fact or meaning is not to be departed from, so that which is a metaphor ought not to be turned into a literal thing; nor, on the contrary, should the literal sense be made metaphorical.

5. Parables are similarities taken from things that may have been done, or that are supposed to have been done; thus, the thing to which the comparison is made, or from which the similarity is drawn, does not always need to be a thing that has been performed in all its circumstances and manner. It is sufficient that the thing was possible, or rationally probable to have been performed, or at least was supposed to have been so. For instance, in that parable where our Savior says:
<margin>Matthew 7:24, 25, 26, 27</margin>
*That those who hear his words and do them are like a wise man who built his house upon a rock; and he that hears them, and does them not, is like a foolish man, who built his house upon the sand:*
Now, it is not necessary that there should have been two such men who, in matter of fact, acted in that manner (though there might have been many men before the time of our Savior who might have done so); rather, it was sufficient that the thing from which the comparison was made was possible, rational, and probable. But the truth intended by the parable or similarity is always a spiritual truth and certainty. Concerning this, the learned *Beza*, upon the Parable of the Rich Man and *Lazarus*, gives us this remarkable note: “Although Christ relates a history, nonetheless he writes of spiritual things under figures which he knew were suitable to our senses. For souls are neither endowed with fingers and eyes, nor do they suffer thirst, nor do they have mutual conversation with one another. Therefore the summary is that faithful souls, after they have departed from their bodies, lead a pleasant and blessed life outside the world; and that most horrible torments are prepared for the reprobates, which can no more be conceived by our minds than the immense glory of heaven.”

6. For instance, when the Apostle, speaking of the two sons of *Abraham*—one from *Hagar*, a bondwoman, and the other from *Sarah*, a free woman—says: *These things are an allegory*, <term>ἅτινα ἀλληγορούμενα</term>, which things express one thing by another. In the *Apocalypse*, the Devil (by a perpetual allegory) is called a *Dragon* or *Serpent*. 5. Again, how can *Judah* literally be a lion's whelp, or *Christ* be called the *lion of the tribe of Judah*? Even so, it must be accounted most absurd and abominable for *Pererius* or any other to fancy that the Devil may not properly enough, in an allegory or mystical sense, be called a serpent in that act of tempting *Eve*, without either assuming the shape of a serpent or entering into the body of a natural one. I appeal to all rational men to judge if the absurdities of both are not alike, if taken barely and literally. Must it not be understood that they were called so because of their poisonous and wicked minds, by way of metaphor? 8. The Serpent that tempted *Eve* in Paradise is said there to be more subtle than any beast of the field. *Moses*, therefore, purposely attributes speech to the serpent which tempted *Eve*, so that we (knowing by experience that speech cannot properly belong to a natural serpent) might be more easily persuaded to believe that this must be understood metaphorically as the spiritual serpent.

<margin>Judg. 9:7, 8, 9, 10, etc.</margin>

It takes its name from its creeping condition, for *Serpens* is derived *à serpendo* <note>from creeping</note>, and in Hebrew it is called נחש (*nachash*) <term>reptile</term> from נחש, *reptavit, serpsit* <note>he crawled or crept</note>. *Moses* makes no mention at all of the serpent's coming to *Eve* for that business, nor of its departure after the action, nor of any one special property by which it might be essentially recognized as indeed a true natural serpent. Nor does he mention any amazement or sudden fear in *Eve* at its sudden approach and extraordinary speech—even though *Moses* himself was afterwards horribly afraid at the mere sight of a serpent.

Neither is this way of metaphorically expounding the Scriptures—where the literal sense includes an apparent absurdity—either unique or new, for both **Ancients** and **Moderns** have allowed the same course; for *St. Augustine* says:

<margin>Augustine, *On Genesis*, book 11, chapter 1.</margin>
> "When anything is found in the Scriptures which cannot (without an absurdity) possibly be interpreted literally, that thing without doubt is spoken figuratively, and must receive some other signification than the bare letter seems to import."

And *Gregory* says:

<margin>Gregory, *Morals on Job*.</margin>
> "When the order of the history becomes defective in itself in the literal sense, then some mystical sense, as if through wide open doors, offers itself; indeed, that mystical sense must be received instead of the literal sense itself."

And therefore (says *Peter Martyr*):

<margin>Peter Martyr on Genesis 3:1.</margin>
> "That malediction or curse which the Lord cast on the Serpent must be allegorically understood of the Devil; and those things which seem properly to accord to the serpent indeed must metaphorically be transferred to *Satan*, understood in the Serpent."

So then, by all the premises, it is very apparent that it was the Devil himself, and no natural serpent, who set upon *Eve* in that temptation, he being only metaphorically set forth by the name of a serpent. And therefore, he had no need in that action to essentially take upon himself the body of a natural serpent for the better accomplishment of the intended business.

The next step is to lay down positive arguments to prove that the Devil did not essentially enter into the body of the serpent; and if he did, that neither he by himself, nor the serpent and he joined, could thereby make any articulate sound or discourse. If the Devil in the serpent is supposed (as he is) to perform any such matter, it must be by considering him as either an incorporeal or a corporeal creature; but we affirm he could perform it neither way, and that for these reasons:

<margin>Reason 1.</margin>
1. If the Devil is considered simply and absolutely as an incorporeal creature, then it follows that he cannot act upon any corporeal matter, because an incorporeal substance can make no contact with a body unless it were itself corporeal; for, *quicquid agit, agit per contactum, vel mediatum, vel immediatum* <note>Whatever acts, acts through contact, whether mediated or immediate.</note>. But both of those are caused by the touch of one body upon another, as when one’s hand, by touching a straw, immediately moves it out of its place, or else by blowing moves it, which is through the mediation of the air; but that which is merely incorporeal can perform neither. Because that which is merely incorporeal has no surface [superficies] by which to touch the body to be moved, and therefore can cause no motion of it at all; and where there is no motion, there can be no alteration, and consequently no speech nor articulation at all. And therefore the Devil (if incorporeal) could not move the organs of the serpent at all, and so could not speak in the serpent nor move its organs, even if they had been fit for articulate speech [prolation], which they were not. This was the thing required to be proved.

<margin>Reason 2.</margin>
2. The Serpent, by the ordinance of God at the Creation, was limited to an inarticulate sound, not an articulate one; but the Devil neither has, nor ever had, any power to change and overturn the course of God's ordination in nature. Therefore, he does not have the power, nor ever did, to make the Serpent speak articulately; for that would be to overthrow the inviolable order God set at the Creation, which no man of sound judgment ever claimed the Devil could do.

<margin>Reason 3.</margin>
3. I take it to be one of the most firm maxims that the Schools ever had: *immateriale non agit in materiale, nisi eminenter ut Deus* <note>immaterial things do not act upon material things, except eminently as God does</note>. Therefore, since the Devil is incorporeal and immaterial, he cannot act upon that which is material, as was the body of the Serpent, unless he had possessed a super-eminent and omnipotent power—which would be blasphemous to attribute to him. Therefore, he could not articulately speak in the Serpent to *Eve*, because he is immaterial and had no omnipotent power.

<margin>Reason 4.</margin>
4. And if he is conceived to be corporeal, then he could either speak articulately and audibly by himself, or else he could not. If he could do so by himself, then entering into the Serpent was needless and superfluous. And if he could not, then entering into the Serpent would not have granted that faculty to him, and so either way he could not have performed it; for a frog creeping into the body of a man will not cause the frog to speak, though it may make some noise or croaking.

<margin>Reason 5.</margin>
5. Even if the Devil, being corporeal, had entered into the body of the Serpent, yet by no motion that could be made with or upon her organs could they have been framed to utter an articulate sound, because they were not fitted for that purpose, but only to make a sibilation or hissing. For in instruments that are artificial, the various sounds and tunes made by them are only agreeable to the diversity of their parts and their various constructions; so a harp (once made) cannot be ordered to give forth a sound like a trumpet, nor the noise of a pipe organ, nor vice versa. And if any of their parts are wanting, defective, or broken, then the orderly sound and music is spoiled. And though a parrot or parakeet may, by vocal and external teaching, be brought to learn and speak some words, yet it is not by the teacher entering into its belly, but by his outward, vocal teaching, by which its senses and imagination are audibly acted upon, and not otherwise. But in this action ascribed to *Satan*, he is not supposed to be able to speak articulately, nor to have taught the Serpent vocally and audibly; even if he could have done so, her organs were not capable of any such matter. Therefore, it would have been more subtle of the Devil to have chosen a parrot rather than a serpent.

<margin>Reason 1.</margin>
1. It is but a bare assertion without any proof at all, and he only shelters it under the authority of *St. Augustine* and *Gregory*, whose authority in many other matters he often rejects when they do not agree with his humor, purpose, and interest. But regardless, they are but *testimonia humana* <note>human testimonies</note>; and we are not to regard who the men are that speak, so much as to consider the weight and reason of what they say.

<margin>Reason 2.</margin>
2. He proceeds upon a false supposition: that the sensitive appetite, and consequently the fantasy, could not be wrought upon nor drawn except by a sensible and exterior object, when it is manifest that the sight of the serpent alone could not have stirred the sensitive appetite; for it is rationally to be supposed as a certainty that *Eve* had seen the serpent before that time. Neither could it be the conversation with the serpent, considered merely as conversation, that could have moved it; for it is certain she had heard, and had had audible, vocal, and articulate conversation with her husband before this time of the temptation. Neither could it be the beholding of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for by the conversation it appears that she had seen it before, and it is probable that the temptation occurred in the view of it, and the appearance (species) of the said tree that appeared to her eye was the same as it was before. So it is most manifest that the temptation took effect from the strong lie that Satan told her, *that their eyes should be opened and they should be as gods, knowing good and evil*, and so her deception was first made in her mind and understanding, and thereby the will was drawn, and the sensitive appetite moved, whereupon *she took of the fruit of the tree, and did eat.* And this may far more reasonably be thought to have been brought to pass by a mental discourse and internal motions, rather than by external arrangement, which must first work upon the mind before the fantasy or sensitive appetite could be moved or drawn at all.

<margin>Reason 3.</margin>
3. If the temptation had happened in the way that *Pererius* supposes, our first parents could not have been seduced; for Satan's argument was not to persuade *Eve* that it was pleasant to the taste or good for the stomach (thereby to have drawn the sensitive appetite and the fantasy), but that it was good and profitable to make them wise, and to be like *gods*, whereby he ensnared her understanding with a fallacious and lying argument, thus framed, as the learned *Piscator* lays it down:

If this opinion were true—that *Eve*, by reason of her perfection in the state of innocence, could not be tempted nor seduced except by an external way and means—then how could it come to pass that the angels in their original state (which was as perfect, if not more so, than *Eve's*) were drawn into that defection without a tempter or any external means, leaving their state and station and not remaining in the truth? 2. How could the defection have been so general (for multitudes of them fell) if they had not had some way or means to communicate their thoughts and intentions to one another? For though we are not able to understand the manner in which they discourse or commune with one another, yet it must be taken as a truth that they have a way and means to manifest their thoughts to one another, which is in some way analogous to what we call speech or discourse. Therefore, con-

<margin>Volume 3, Book 3, Chapter 19, Page 156.</margin>
cerning this point, the learned and judicious *Zanchy* concludes thus:
> "Therefore," he says, "that which we do by a physical voice, the same thing the angels and blessed souls in heaven—yes, the devils in the infernal pit and in the air—do perform, but without a voice, in a spiritual manner."

3. If this opinion were true, then the blessed souls, being divested of their bodies, would not have communion with one another, nor would they jointly praise and glorify God together, which would be false and absurd; and therefore,

<margin>Jerome on Job, Chapter 24.</margin>
<margin>Volume 7, Page 187.</margin>
the learned Father said well:
> "It is to be held steadfastly that the offices of the heavenly host are by no means performed in silence; seeing we may read that the angelic powers before the throne of the Lord sound forth his praise with unwearied voices."

<margin>2 Corinthians 2:11.</margin>

The sleights and subtle machinations (for he has his <term>Νοήματα</term> or devices) of Satan's kingdom could not be carried on if he did not have a way and means to communicate them to the rest of the crew of his inferior fiends; and this, therefore, plainly proves that there is a way of hidden, mystical, and spiritual discourse which the Devil could and did represent to the mind and understanding of *Eve*, by which she was seduced, and that there was no need for a vocal and audible conversation; and so much in answer to his objection.

### CH A P. VII. *supposed Witchcraft.*

...of Pharaoh's Magicians, from which they argue this way: If the Magicians of Pharaoh were able, by the power and assistance of the Devil, to change their rods into serpents, the water into blood, and to produce frogs; why may not witches, by the power and assistance of the Devil, change themselves and other things into various and strange shapes, and perform the rest of the feats that are attributed to them?

But though this is only a <term>petitio principii</term> <note>a begging of the question</note>—that they did these things by the assistance of the Devil, which is neither supposed nor granted, but ought first to have been proven; and though in the case of hardening Pharaoh's heart, there might have been (and was) a unique dispensation from God at that time—yet it does not follow that God always allows, or gives the Devil leave to operate similar things; and so nothing can be firmly concluded from this. Yet, though these things are so, we shall set them aside and come to the full opening and discussion of the matter, specifically in these two particulars: 1. How far the Devil's power and assistance concurred with the actions and performances. 2. And where he did not concur or act at all.

<margin>Ephesians 2:2</margin>
<margin>2 Timothy 3:8</margin>
1. We shall grant that since Pharaoh and the Magicians were idolaters and worshippers of false gods, their primary goals were to magnify the power of their idols and to show that their supposed gods could work and bring to pass as strange miracles or wonders as Moses and Aaron could perform by the assistance of the God of the Hebrews. Regarding this goal, they had all the assistance that Satan and his dark kingdom of angels could afford them in a spiritual and hellish way; for *he is the Prince of the power of the air who works in the children of disobedience*, which both Pharaoh and his Magicians were. To this purpose, the Apostle tells us, speaking of false and seducing teachers: *That they were like Jannes and Jambres who withstood Moses in their resisting of the truth*. So, the Magicians of Pharaoh were condemned for resisting the truth of the message that Moses and Aaron brought, and the real miracles that they performed. Therefore, regarding the wicked end they aimed at, they were assisted with the power and concurrence of the Devil, and in that respect only were they his servants and instruments.

But as for the second particular—namely, the <term>efficient causes</term> and means of producing those things that the Magicians did—we affirm they were performed by the power of nature and art, and that the Devil was not an <term>efficient cause</term> of their production. We prove this by these irrefutable arguments:

<margin>*Argument 1.*</margin>
1. Those who affirm that the Devil did or can produce such strange effects also acknowledge that what he performs in natural and elementary bodies is done by applying natural agents to natural and suitable patients <note>the objects acted upon by an agent</note>, which truly bring to pass such strange effects; and that he does no more than simply make the local application of them.

From which it must necessarily follow that the effects flow from natural agents, and so no causality at all can be attributed to him, except for that fictitious one of being a *causa sine qua non* <note>a necessary condition without which the effect would not happen</note>, which is the same as being no cause at all. And besides that, there is no proof that he performs this local application; for if he is incorporeal, then it is simply impossible that he should perform any such task; and in any case, a man by natural power and means, if he knows the fit and apt actives and passives, may perform them himself, and so the Devil's assistance is unnecessary; and we have never yet met with any argument that carried any convincing force that might lead us to believe that he is such a great naturalist.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
2. There are many persons who think themselves significant sharers in most types of learning, and others who are very strait-laced in their pretended zeal for godliness and in detesting the works of Satan, who even flinch and show an abhorrence at the word magic, if it is even once named, as though there were no magic but that which is diabolical, or as if that which they call diabolical were evil in any other way than only in its purpose and use. For there are many plants and minerals that, though poisonous, are nonetheless good in respect of their creation and the good uses that may be made of them, such as to kill harmful animals that are hurtful to man. But if anyone out of malice and wickedness should use them to poison and destroy men and women, it would be wicked and diabolical in its purpose and use, yet the means were lawful and natural. So, whatever the Devil may do through wicked men, his instruments, in leading and drawing them to make use of the great *magnalia naturæ* <note>great works of nature</note> to work strange wonders, thereby to confirm idolatry and superstition, or to resist the truth and such devilish ends—though the end and use may be wicked and diabolical, yet the efficient cause is natural and lawful. And therefore we can find no other ground or reason for dividing magic into natural and diabolical but only that they differ in their purpose and use; for otherwise they both work by natural agency and means, seeing the Devil can do nothing above or contrary to that course that God has set in nature. Therefore, men may do without the aid of devils whatever devils can do, since they have no advantage over us but operate only by applying active things to passive, just as men do. And therefore that most learned philosopher, chemist, and mathematician, our countryman Roger *Bacon*, said excellently well in these words: <margin>On the Secret Works of Art and Nature, ch. 5.</margin> *non igitur oportet nos uti magicis illusionibus cum potestas Philosophiæ doceat operari quod sufficit* <note>Therefore we ought not to use magical illusions when the power of philosophy teaches us to perform what is sufficient</note>. Therefore, those men who came from the East to worship Christ are called magicians, not because the great knowledge they had in the secrets of nature was diabolical or unlawful—for the name of a magician was honorable and laudable until knaves and impostors made use of it to cheat and deceive, and for wicked and ungodly ends—but because they had made use of it for the glory of God and the good of mankind; therefore they were magicians in the genuine and best sense, as working by lawful and na-

Thus, the only difference in magic lies in its purpose and use, and not in the causes or agents, which are both natural. So Jacob, when he set the peeled rods with white streaks in them before the flocks in the gutters of the watering troughs—so that when the rams and the sheep came up to drink and coupled together, they might conceive and bring forth ring-streaked, speckled, and spotted young ones—it happened just so. This is admitted by *Pererius* himself and most learned expositors of that passage to be from natural causes, and was a strange feat of natural magic; but it was not evil because it was not directed toward a wicked end. But that of Pharaoh's magicians, though likewise wrought by natural causes (for it was so, whether ascribed to the Devil, who can only work by natural means, or not), was wicked and diabolical because they did it to resist Moses and Aaron, the messengers of the Lord Jehovah.

3. Most or all of the learned expositors who have commented on this passage in *Exodus* (as may be seen in Dr. Willet’s *Hexapla* and various other learned authors), although they attribute these things done by the magicians to the power and assistance of Satan, nevertheless acknowledge that, in terms of the manner of the act, they were not done really and in truth, but only in show and appearance. But what they mean by "show and appearance" is not so easy to find out and determine; for if by it they mean that they did it as jugglers and those who use the art of sleight of hand do—that is, by showing one thing and then by nimble skill and agility taking it away and suddenly and imperceptibly substituting another thing in its place, which they perform by leading the eyes and attention of the spectators another way with staring and the use of strange and insignificant words—then we would soon be in agreement. For they might probably and easily have been performed in that way, as we shall prove shortly, but this is not what they mean or intend. Instead, some mean that the Devil only deceived the fantasy and imagination of the beholders, causing them to imagine and believe that the rods were changed into serpents when they were not changed at all; rather, only their imaginations were deceived into thinking them to be serpents when they were only rods. This is similar to how melancholy persons, men in fevers, or those with frenzies and maniacal distempers often think and affirm that they see strange things when they see no such things externally, but the fantasy is only deceived with the species and images of those things within. And though we may be derided and laughed to scorn by the ignorant, or harshly taxed and censured by the majority of cynical critics, yet we cannot so far stifle the knowledge of our own brains, nor be so cowardly in maintaining the truth, but we must assert: That anciently there has been a certain lawful art, by which some sorts of metals might be mixed together under a proper constellation, and afterward engraved at similarly fit planetary times with various figures, that would naturally work strange things. And this piece of learning, although it may justly be numbered among the *Desiderata* <note>things desired but missing</note>, and might very well have been placed in the catalog of the *Deperdita* <note>lost things</note> of *Pancirollus*; yet it was well known to the ancient magicians, and by them often put into practice with happy success. This argument we desire that any of the witch-mongers or demonographers should answer before they conclude so strongly for the power of devils and witches.

So we conceive we have sufficiently proved that what *Pharaoh's* magicians performed might rationally and probably be brought to pass by natural magic, or collusion and sleight of hand, without any other diabolical assistance than what was mental and spiritual regarding their goal, which was the resisting of *Moses*. And by all they did—as in changing their rods, bringing in frogs, and changing water into blood—it does not rationally appear that they had any supernatural assistance; for if they had, they could not have been so amazed at the miracle of turning the dust into lice. For what skill did the Devil lack that he could not perform this?

If by his power the former things were brought to pass, could there be more difficulty in doing this than in the bringing of frogs? Neither could their *legerdemain* have failed them except that they were surprised and taken unawares, not being provided to play every kind of trick, but only some few for which they had made provision. And so to excuse their own inability, they cried out, *this is the finger of God*; a pitiful shift to excuse their own knavery and deception, for there could be no more of the finger of God in this than in the former, but only a shift to put off their own shame.

Another place from which they would draw arguments to maintain the power of the Devil and Witches is the story of *Balaam* in the *Book of Numbers*, from which in the first place they would conclude that he used wicked and diabolical divinations, and that by words he could either bless or curse. In answer to which we shall give these pressing reasons.

<margin>Reason 1. Numbers 22:6. Numbers 23:8, 23.</margin>
1. Though it might be granted that he used divinations that were not lawful, yet what is that to a killing and murdering witch? Surely nothing at all. And though *Balak* believed that *whosoever he blessed were blessed, and whosoever he cursed were cursed*, and therefore fetched him from so far, yet there is nothing apparent to prove that *Balaam* could do any such thing; and from *Balak's* belief to *Balaam's* performances, no argument proceeds, for his belief that he could either bless or curse did not confer any power to *Balaam* to produce such effects. And *Balaam's* blessings or cursings might be intentional and declarative, but could not be effective, for he confesses a great piece of truth: *How should he curse whom God had not cursed, or how should he defy whom the Lord had not defied?* He might have done it verbally, but it would have been frustrated and to no effect; and therefore he concluded: *Surely there was no enchantment against Jacob, nor any divination against Israel.*

<margin>Reason 2. Chapter 24:1.</margin>
2. And though it be said that he went not, as at other times, to meet auguries (for as we have shown before, the word does properly signify that), it must be understood, and is manifest, that at the former times he went to attend solitarily to what the Lord would say to him, and those two times that he went before were only to meet the Lord, to hear and receive what he would say to him. But here he did not, nor had need to go, for the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he took up his parable and prophesied. Where although his going to meet the Lord be called "meeting divinations," yet it cannot be taken in the worse sense for unlawful divinations, but for such as were sent to him and taught to him by God, by visions, angels, trances, or other such ways as God in those times used to reveal his will to his prophets. For from first to last, it appears that he neither professed nor did (in this case) utter anything but what the Lord commanded him, and so was no false prophet.

The Angel could not both stand in the narrow way and likewise be in the ass in the same moment of time, unless we should grant that absurdity that a creature may be in two distinct places at one and the self-same time, which was never yet allowed to any created being. But they openly belie and falsify the words of the text, for it does not say that the Angel spoke in the ass, but that the Lord (the word is *Jehovah*) opened the mouth of the ass. So that (we suppose) enough is demonstrated here that from none of the places of Scripture hitherto enumerated can any colorable grounds be drawn to uphold those particulars that we have labored to refute, and therefore we shall pass to another chapter.

mutter and murmur, and peep and chirp like a bird coming out of the shell, or that she spoke in some hollow cave or vault, through some pipe, or in a bottle, and so bewildered and deceived poor fearful and despairing *Saul*, or had a partner dressed like *Samuel* to play his part, and that it was neither *Samuel’s* body, soul, nor any ghost or devil, but only the cunning and imposture of the woman alone, or assisted by a partner. And though this might be fully satisfactory to all sound and serious judgments, especially if added to what Mr. *Scot*, Mr. *Ady*, Mr. *Wagstaff*, and the learned authors of the *Dialogue of Spirits and Devils* have written upon this subject: yet because we have promised before to speak something of the history and matter of fact, and that Mr. *Glanvill*, a minister of our *English* Church, has lately championed the cause, we shall refute his arguments and clear the case as fully as can reasonably be required, and that in these following details.

<margin>1 Sam. 3. 19. Id. c. 7. v. 13.</margin>
1. The certain and infallible prophecies of *Samuel*, coming to pass exactly as he foretold them—for it is said: *And Samuel grew, and the Lord was with him, and let none of his words fall to the ground*;—were clearly known to all *Israel*, as in the case of the destruction of *Eli* and his house, and by the defeat of the *Philistines* at *Ebenezer*, and in the anointing of *Saul* to be king, and in the case of sending thunder and lightning during harvest time, and such like. And as these were publicly known to all *Israel*, and they had seen and tested what infallible certainty followed them, so it was as generally known that *Samuel* had told *Saul* that God had rejected him from being king over *Israel*, and that he had appointed *David* to be king in his place; and therefore any rational man who knew these things, and also saw that *David* prospered in all things he did, and that it was quite otherwise for *Saul*, might certainly know that the kingdom would be transferred from him to *David*. Thus, there was no need to bring up a spirit or devil to predict this, as it was sufficiently known to all; of which the woman at *Endor* also could not be ignorant, as it was a matter of concern to her, especially regarding her practice, which was mere cheating and imposture.

<margin>Confid. about Witchcraft, p. 8.</margin>
And therefore Mr. *Glanvill’s* argument concludes nothing, where he says: "And this *Samuel* truly foretold his approaching fate, namely: 'That *Israel* should be delivered with him into the hands of the *Philistines*, and that on the morrow he and his sons should be in the state of the dead,' which doubtlessly is meant by the expression that [*they should be with him:*] which contingent details, how could the cheater and her partner foretell if there were nothing in it extraordinary and supernatural?" To answer which we say, that there was no contingent detail foretold that Mr. *Glanvill* could not have foretold himself if he had been there and known only what was publicly revealed in *Israel*, without incurring the danger of being considered a witch or a diviner.

If she saw *Samuel* (whom she could not help but know), why did she answer *Saul* when he asked, "What did *you* see?" She answered, *I saw gods ascending out of the earth*. Let Mr. *Glanvill* and all men judge if this is not gross and obvious lying; "*Gods*" is plural, but *Samuel* was only one.

3. Just as it is manifest that this woman was an active deceiver and one who intended to cheat and swindle, it is also plain that *Saul* was in a condition fit to be deluded and imposed upon, even by those who were less cunning and skillful than she was in the craft of cheating, which is apparent for these reasons: 1. The Spirit of the Lord had departed from him, and consequently wisdom, prudence, and discretion—and so that which should have guided his will, affections, and actions in the right way—had totally left him. And when these are gone, what is man but a fit instrument to undergo and suffer even the worst and lowest of delusions and abuses? 
<margin>1 Sam. 16. 14.</margin> 2. The Spirit of the Lord had not only left him, but an evil spirit from the Lord had come upon him that vexed and terrified him. And to what madness, folly, and wickedness is he not subject, who is led by the spirit of lies and darkness? 
<margin>1 Sam. 15. 23, 27.</margin> 3. The Lord had openly declared that because he had rejected the word of the Lord, the Lord had therefore rejected him from being King over *Israel*, and that the Kingdom should be torn from him and given to one more worthy than him. Now, it is easy to imagine what despondency of mind, what torture, and what vexation of spirit must have been in him, who, having been a King, is thus threatened to have his Kingdom torn from him and given to another. 
<margin>1 Sam. 28. 6.</margin> 4. He must have been under a most fearful consternation of mind, not only because of these things mentioned, but especially because, having previously received counsel and advice from the Lord in his dangers and straits, though he now *inquired of the Lord, yet the Lord answered him neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by Prophets*. The Lord did not answer him by dreams, for the union and converse that had existed between the Lord and him before was now broken by reason of his sins and rebellion. Neither did the Lord answer him by Urim, for the *Urim* was not in the possession of *Saul* then, but of *David* (Chapter 23, verses 6, 9). Neither did the Lord answer him by Prophets, for *Samuel* had left him after his last denouncing of judgment against him and never came to him again until his death. 5. He must have been in a most fearful state and a fit subject for even the most weak and simple imposture in the world, because the *Philistines* were upon him with a powerful and numerous army, and he was able to gather only a few and weak forces, as most and the best of the people had revolted from him and were, in their affections or in person, with and for *David*. And from this it may easily be gathered how easy a thing it was to delude and deceive *Saul*, even by those who had far less craft than this woman, who was undoubtedly devilishly cunning in her swindling tricks.

As yet *Saul* saw nothing, but stood waiting like a drowned puppet to hear what the outcome would be, for all he understood was from her cunning and lying account. Further, his question is not in the present tense but in the past: *“What did you see?”* or “What have you seen?” This could not be consistently said if they had both been in the same room, but in any case, it undeniably concludes that as yet he saw nothing at all. 4. But how did he know or perceive that it was *Samuel*? Not by the sight of his eyes, for we have made it plain that he was either in another room, or that no visible apparition presented itself before his eyes; rather, he only perceived it by the description of the crafty *Woman*, who knew well enough what habit or garments *Samuel* wore in his lifetime, as he was the most publicly known man in *Israel*. Surely, in rational consequence, it could be nothing else. For all that she had done and said before being undeniably lies and cheats, this also, in just and right reason, must be judged to be so as well. So it was either the *Woman* who, being in another room, changed and altered her voice and so played the part of *Samuel*, or else she had an accomplice whom she brought out to act the part of the dead *Samuel*.

1. It is manifest from these reasons that it was not the body of *Samuel* that was raised up, nor the soul joined with it that acted *Samuel’s* part. 1. Because *Samuel’s* body had lain too long in the grave—some account it nearly two years—and therefore it must have been largely corrupted, wasted, and disfigured, so that no one could have certainly known it was *Samuel*. 2. It must have been so putrefied and stinking that no one could have endured being near it because of the foul and horrible smell. 3. Who would have covered it with the mantle? If it had been buried with him, it must have been rotten and consumed in so long a time. Surely there were no tailors in the grave to make him a new one; rather, by reason and likelihood, if it had been his body, it should have appeared in linen or a winding-sheet, if that had not been rotten likewise.

<margin>Philippians 3:21.</margin>
4. To raise a body that had been dead so long would have required an omnipotent power, for it is the almighty power of Christ alone that raises up the vile bodies of his saints and makes them like his glorious body. And therefore neither the woman with all her divinations, nor all the devils in hell, nor any created power—but only the Lord Almighty—could have performed this miracle. He would never have done it to gratify the whim or to magnify the cheating craft of an idolatrous, wicked, and swindling witch.
<margin>Matthew 27:52, 53.</margin>
And if the devil or any created power could raise up the body of a departed saint, then the rising out of the graves of many bodies of saints who had slept, and their coming into the holy city and appearing to many after Christ was risen from the dead, would have been no certain or convincing argument for the undoubted truth of the divinity and resurrection of our most blessed Savior. But they were most infallible evidences of both, as the Father
<margin>Catena Aurea, Thomas Aquinas on Matthew 27.</margin>
*St. Jerome* says in these words: *“Thus many bodies of the saints arose to show the Lord rising; and yet, though the monuments were opened, they did not rise before the Lord rose, so that he might be the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead.”*

5. We argue thus that it was not *Samuel’s* soul joined with the body that acted this: any tenet that is flatly contrary to the plain doctrine of the Scripture must be false. But this tenet of *Samuel’s* soul acting in the body after death is flatly contrary to the plain doctrine of the Scripture; therefore, it is false. We suppose no orthodox Christian can justly deny the major premise, and the minor is proved thus:
<margin>Revelation 14:13.</margin>
The Scripture assures us that *those who die in the Lord* (as without all doubt *Samuel* did) *are blessed and rest from their labors.* Therefore, this tenet must be abominably false; for if the soul of *Samuel* had been brought back after his death to act in the body, then he would not have rested from his labors. Instead, he would have been disquieted and brought to new trouble, being vexed to see *Saul* committing more wickedness than before by taking counsel from a cursed, idolatrous woman—one such as the Lord had commanded to be destroyed. ...where this counterfeit *Samuel* says, *Why have you disquieted me?* As though the Saints of God after death could be disquieted by a Devil or a Witch—who (according to God's infallible truth) are blessed, rest from their labors, and are in the hands of the Lord, where no torments can touch them. And therefore, no one would have spoken those lying words but a devilish, cheating woman <note>Original: "quean"</note>, or a damnable, bribed <note>Original: "suborned"</note> accomplice.

6. If *Samuel's* soul was again joined to his body so long after separation, and thus performed vital actions, who was the author of this conjunction or union? Could the Witch, the Devil, or any created power effect that union? Surely not; none but the almighty power of *Jehovah*, who breathed into *Adam* the breath of life. And therefore we are bold to assert (with all the company of learned *Christians*) that this opinion is erroneous, impious, and blasphemous.

2. The second opinion—that it was *Samuel's* soul that appeared in his usual shape and clothing that he wore while he lived—has been strenuously maintained by the *Catholic* <note>Original: "Popish"</note> party and as strongly refuted by the *Reformed theologians* <note>Original: "Divines"</note>. But we shall not trouble ourselves and our readers with all of them, but only urge two or three that are most convincing, thereby to answer *Mr. Glanvill's* foolish notions <note>Original: "fopperies"</note>, and they are these:

1. If it were *Samuel's* soul that appeared, it cannot be supposed to have come against God's will, or whether God wanted it or not. For hardly any rational man (we believe) will affirm that, because God does whatsoever He will, both in *Heaven and Earth*, and who has resisted His will? 

2. And it cannot be rationally thought that *Samuel*—who while he lived was so meticulously careful to do nothing (especially in his prophetic office) but what he was commanded by God—would after his death run an errand without His consent or permission. 

3. And that his soul did not come by the command of God is most certain. Though *Mr. Glanvill* asks the question, "Who says that happy departed souls were never employed in any ministries here below?" to which (though we have answered it before) we now again reply: all learned *theologians* of the *Reformed churches* have said and maintained it, and so do we both say and affirm, that they never were, nor are, employed in ministries here below. This is because they were never created nor ordained by God for any such end or purpose; rather, there are legions of *Angels* who are ordained to be *ministering spirits*, and not the souls of the saints departed from this life. But *Mr. Glanvill* goes further and says that *Samuel* was not raised by the power of the Witch's enchantments, but came on that occasion on a *Divine errand*. And though we have before unanswerably proved in general that no souls of those who are dead appear or wander here below after death, nor come on such pointless <note>Original: "sleeveless"</note> errands as he supposes, yet we shall add one or two points here in particular to prove that *Samuel's* soul did not come on a *Divine errand* as sent by God—without which mission it could not have come at all.
