It is manifest that God in all His ordinances of providence, especially in the order of His miracles, works chiefly to confirm and witness truth, for that (as the worthy and learned *Stillingfleet* has observed) is the most proper *criterium* <note>A standard or principle by which something is judged.</note> of a miracle; and to send a soul from the dead must certainly be miraculous. Now if the chief end in God’s working of miracles (for none else but He can work them) is to establish truth and settle His own Divine and pure worship, then it cannot be to uphold lies and idolatrous courses. But if God should have sent *Samuel’s* soul on a Divine errand while the Witch was practicing her diabolical divinations and cheating tricks, it would have been to countenance and confirm both *Saul* and the Witch in their wicked ways, and to have contradicted His own law and command, which positively ordered that all who used divinations should be put to death, and all those who sought counsel from them should be severely punished. Now let Mr. *Glanvill*, or any other, prove that God orders that to be done by the dead which He forbade to be done by the living. 6. If it had been the true *Samuel* who appeared, it is not rational nor credible to imagine that he would neither rebuke *Saul* for consulting with a woman who practiced those things that were forbidden by the law upon pain of death, nor that he would either reprove or punish so wicked a woman, finding her in the very act. We say it is not credible, unless we suppose *Samuel* was less zealous for the law and commands of God being dead than he was while living. <margin>1 Sam. 15:33</margin> Surely he who, while living, *hewed Agag in pieces* only because God had commanded he should be slain, would (if it had been the true *Samuel*, which without all question it was not) have done as much or worse to the cursed and idolatrous cheating Witch, even after his death, if he had come upon a Divine errand. 7. God would have shown Himself very mutable if He had answered *Saul* in a miraculous way by a dead prophet, having refused to answer him by one living. 3. That the Devil assumed the shape of *Samuel* and acted out the whole business is the opinion of all, or most, of the learned Divines of the reformed Churches, of whom we shall ask pardon if we dissent from them, it not being a fundamental of Religion nor any Article of the Faith. And this we profess is not done out of a spirit of contradiction, nor for singularity, but only because (as we believe) the tenet has no sufficient grounds, neither from Scripture nor sound reason, to support it; and therefore we shall work toward its refutation by these following arguments.

1. Because this opinion—that the Devil should perform this apparition—assumes two suppositions never yet sufficiently proved, and that contain no certain truth. For first, they take as a hypothesis that Devils are merely and simply incorporeal Spirits, which we shall prove hereafter to be false. Secondly, they take for another hypothesis that Spirits and Devils can assume whatever bodies they please and appear in any figure or shape, which is a mere fiction invented by the foolish Schoolmen, as we shall sufficiently demonstrate hereafter.

But though fallen angels—with respect to their malice, wicked wills, and envious desires by which they seek (as much as in them lies) the ruin of all mankind, both in soul and body—may in that particular end and regard be said to be like roaring lions going about and seeking whom they may devour, and compassing the earth and walking to and fro in it; yet we must affirm that in respect of executing their wicked, envious, and malicious wills and desires, they are restrained, indeed kept in the chains of everlasting darkness. From these fetters and chains they do not go out, except when and as far as they are sent, ordered, licensed (or as some would have it worded) permitted, by the purpose and decree of the Divine and Almighty’s providence. So it is most certain that the fallen spirits cannot go forth from their chains when they wish to act whatever mischief they would, contrary to the will of the Almighty, who has fettered and still keeps them in those chains. But when they are at any time let loose, it is only by the will, decree, license, and order of Jehovah, who sends them forth to accomplish His will, either as a punishment to the wicked to inflict upon them His just judgments (for which they are the appointed ministers and executioners, and in the performance of these offices of His wrath, they are limited and bounded as to how far they shall proceed and no further); or else they are sent forth to tempt or afflict the godly for the trial of their faith. And in this, they are so restrained and bounded by the power of the Almighty that they cannot act one jot beyond the limit of His commands or commissions, as is manifest in the case of *David*, who was tempted by Satan to number the people, and in the affliction of *Job*, wherein he was bounded as to how far he should act and no further. And when the evil angels are thus sent forth and limited by God as to what and how far they shall act, it is always for just and righteous ends, as in the case of *Ahab*, when a lying spirit was sent by God into the mouths of his prophets so that he might be persuaded to go up to *Ramath Gilead* that he might be slain there; or as it was for a judgment and destruction upon *Sennacherib's* army, so that *Jerusalem* might be saved and freed, and he sent back with shame and confusion into his own country; or it is to manifest His glory, goodness, and mercy to His saints. Thus *David* was moved to number the people, so that falling under that temptation, and he and the people therefore plagued, they might be brought to a greater degree of repentance and to know that their defense stood not in the multitude of men, but in the benignity of Jehovah, who was their strength and defender,

# CHAP. VIII.

And so *Job* was so severely afflicted, that his faith and patience might be made manifest, and remain as an example to all succeeding generations. But it is utterly irrational and incredible that God would send the Devil (without whose mission he could not have done it) to appear in the shape of *Samuel*, either to magnify the skill or practice of a lewd, wicked, and idolatrous woman—a thing he had forbidden by his plain and open law—nor to gratify the curiosity of a wretched reprobate, such as *Saul*, whom he had refused to answer by living prophets, and therefore would not answer him by the apparition of a Devil, to have committed a counterfeit imposture in the shape of holy *Samuel*. And therefore we conclude that it was no apparition of the Devil, but merely the imposture of the woman, either alone or with a confederate.

There is also a fourth opinion concerning the transaction of this woman of *Endor*, which holds that it was neither the body nor soul of *Samuel* that was raised up, nor the Devil that appeared in his shape, nor that it was the imposture of the witch alone or with a confederate, but that it was the sidereal or astral spirit (as they are pleased to term it) of *Samuel* that was made to appear and speak by the art and skill of the woman. But because this tenet is not of much antiquity, nor has many supporters, and also because it takes for a hypothesis that there are three parts in man—the body, soul, and spirit—and that the soul goes immediately after death either to heaven or hell, the body to the grave, and that the spirit does for a certain time after death wander in the air and may be (by a certain kind of art) brought to appear visibly and to give answers concerning all things that it knew while living—which as yet has never been sufficiently proved—therefore we shall pass over it here, having (perhaps) occasion to speak of it more extensively hereafter.

We shall now come to mention some places in the New Testament that are produced by some to prove the great power of devils and witches in transferring and carrying bodies through the air, such as that of our Savior’s temptation, where it is said that the Devil took him into an exceedingly high mountain, and that he set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple in *Jerusalem*, from which they argue thus: that if the Devil had power to carry our most blessed Savior through the air into a high mountain, and to set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple, then much more does he have power to carry the bodies of witches, who are his sworn vassals, through the air wherever he pleases or they desire. To cancel the force of this objection, we give these reasons.

<margin>*Reas. 1.*</margin>
1. If it were granted that the Devil did transport our Savior through the air, yet it will not follow that he can at any time when he pleases carry the bodies of men or women likewise; for no particular proposition will, according to the rules of logic, infer a general or universal conclusion, nor can one example or instance inductively prove a general practice; one swallow does not make a summer.

For though once, when our blessed Savior was baptized, the Holy Ghost did descend like a dove and light upon him, it does not follow that in all his other actions of preaching or working miracles, the Holy Spirit should also appear in the form of a dove; nor when other saints are baptized will it follow that it does, or should always, appear in the same form. And though *Samson* did once slay a thousand of the *Philistines* with the jawbone of an ass, it does not follow that he did so in like manner in every battle, or that every man may do the same.

<margin>Reason 2.</margin>
2. If it were granted that the Devil did carry Christ's body in the air, it will not follow that he can do so at any other time when he pleases; because in the temptation of Christ, there was an extraordinary dispensation from God for the same, which cannot be presupposed in the ordinary transportation of witches, and therefore the argument falls quite to the ground.

<margin>Reason 3.</margin>
3. In the actions of Satan (especially in physical things, for we speak not of the acts of his will), the will, order, and permission of God are chiefly to be considered, because his power (in respect of execution) is under the power of the Almighty; so he can do nothing in this respect but what he is ordered and commanded to do. And therefore the purpose of the action is principally to be regarded; for if God should have given way for Christ to be carried by Satan in the air, it was for a glorious and good end: that the obedience of his will to the Father might be shown, and that his victory over the Devil might be made manifest. But in carrying the bodies of witches in the air, there can be no good, just, or pious end why the Devil should be licensed or permitted to carry them, except it were to promote filthiness and abominable wickedness—which would be absurd and blasphemous to imagine. And therefore we may rationally and plainly conclude that the carrying of the bodies of witches in the air by the power of the Devil is a false, wicked, and impious opinion.

4. Some are of the opinion that this whole transaction was visible, sensory, and physical, such as *Theophylact* and many others. Some are of the opinion that it was wholly in a vision. The great *Cameron* seems to be of this opinion, comparing it with that of *Ezekiel* who says: *And the spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the visions of God to Jerusalem.* And he shows that the word Ανηνεχθη <note>Greek: anenēchthē, meaning "carried up" or "brought up."</note> does agree with the Hebrew word נשא <note>Hebrew: nasa, meaning "to lift up" or "carry."</note>, which is as applicable to lifting up or carrying in a vision as it is to physical transportation. And in *St. Mark*, *Tremellius* says, *deduxit eum spiritus in desertum* <note>the spirit led him down into the wilderness</note>, and *Beza* renders it, *expellit eum spiritus in desertum* <note>the spirit drives him out into the wilderness</note>. And because of the Greek word which is there ἐκβάλλει, he adds this note: <note>A violent expulsion is not signified, but a divine power, which clothed Christ (who until that time had lived as a private person) with a new persona, and prepared him for the coming struggle and ministry.</note> <margin>Catena Aurea, Thomas Aquinas on Luke 4.</margin> Therefore *Origen* says: *Sequebatur plane quasi athleta ad tentationem sponte proficiscens, & quodammodo loquebatur: Duc quo vis, & invenies me in omnibus fortiorem.* <note>He followed clearly as an athlete going of his own accord to the contest, and in a way said: Lead where you will, and you will find me stronger in all things.</note> So it is most plain that he was no otherwise led or carried by Satan than as he was led by the Holy Ghost; thus he went wherever Satan would desire him of his own mind and accord, and did not need to be carried by the Devil. For *St. Luke* uses the same Greek word both for the Holy Spirit’s leading of him and Satan’s leading of him, so that *Satan* did not carry his body in the air, as men vainly conceive. 2. Although *St. Matthew* uses the word παραλαμβάνει, which may signify *assumpsit* <note>he took up</note>, that he took him and set him upon a pinnacle of the Temple, and took him to a high mountain; yet it cannot be understood by that that he took him and carried his body, but that he went before and led Christ to those places that he thought most fit for him to prevail in his temptations. Christ went to those places not by an unwilling constraint or by being hurried and carried in the air, but by a ready willingness, as one who certainly knew and was assured that he would win the *victory* wherever, or how great soever, the combat and temptations were. And therefore *St. Luke* uses the same word from ἄγω, *duco* <note>I lead</note>, for both the Spirit’s and Satan’s leading, as signifying no more than to go before and lead the way, or to draw one to such or such a place by persuasion and desire, and not to be carried in the air; which appears to be a vain and forged interpretation, and not the true meaning of the passages.

The strange feats he had done to astonish and stupefy the *Samaritans* were only juggling tricks, or deceits by conspiracy, and no supernatural things. So here we will say no more, but only add: That though our *English* translation says that he bewitched the people of *Samaria* with sorceries, and that he himself, when he beheld the miracles and signs that were done, wondered; yet the words that they translate in the one place as "bewitching" and in the other as "wondered" are both from one root, which is <term>’Εξίστημι</term> <note>*de statu mentis dejicio, facio ut aliquis mente non constet, perterrefacio, obstupefacio*—to throw out of a state of mind, to cause someone not to be of sound mind, to terrify, to astonish</note>. And therefore, it either ought to be that the *Samaritans* were astonished at the feats that *Simon* performed, and that he himself was astonished at the miracles of *Philip*, or that they were both bewitched; for they were both under the same amazement, and there is no reason at all to give it one sense in one place and a different one in the other.

<margin>Acts 13:10.</margin>
We need not say anything here of *Elymas*, who is styled a Magician, because it is manifest that he was a false prophet, full of all subtlety and all mischief, a child of the Devil, and an enemy of all righteousness. This character, truly given to him by the unerring judgment of St. *Paul*, may be really ascribed to the whole tribe and profession of such kind of seducers and deceivers. <margin>Acts 19:13, 16.</margin> Like him were those seven sons of *Sceva*, a *Jew*, who are called exorcists, who took it upon themselves to call the name of the Lord *Jesus* over those who had evil spirits, saying, *We adjure you by Jesus, whom Paul preaches*, but were soundly beaten for their pains—a fit reward for such vagabonds. And if all who profess or practice such wicked, vain, and lying things were duly punished, the poor ignorant people would not be so much abused as they are.

The other places in the New Testament we have handled and answered, and we have also touched upon that text in *Galatians* where we spoke of Fascination; but lest that be not sufficient, we shall handle it fully here. The words are, *O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you, that you should not obey the truth?* From which they are accustomed to argue: If witchcraft in the Apostle's time had not been known and practiced, he would not have made use of that phrase then. Concerning which, we return these responses:

1. If we consider natural fascination, it was taken by the philosophers and poets only to be contagious vapors flowing from the eyes or breaths of malevolent and envious persons who had some infectious diseases—as we see in the plague, smallpox, *lues venerea* <note>syphilis</note>, soreness of eyes, *tineas* <note>fungal skin infections</note>, and the like, which are contagious to others who lie with them or converse near them. The infected atoms or vapors issuing within a certain sphere of activity are received by the pores or mouths of healthy persons, by which they also come to be infected. And this the poet witnessed: *Nescio quis teneros oculus mihi fascinat agnos* <note>I know not what eye bewitches my tender lambs</note>. Now, this being the common opinion, the Apostle takes the metaphor from there, as if to say: who, with their virulent and poisonous opinions, has infected you,

He identifies figures like Simon Magus and Elymas as frauds and explains Paul's address to the Galatians as a medical metaphor for the spread of bad ideas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of St. Paul's use of the word "bewitched" in Galatians 3:1, arguing that the term is used metaphorically to describe the deception of the mind rather than literal diabolical witchcraft.</meta>

# CHAP. VIII. Supposed Witchcraft.

you, that you should not obey the truth. And this is the genuine meaning of that metaphorical phrase, and no other sense can rationally and consistently be put upon the passage; and this contributes nothing to that opinion of witchcraft that we oppose. 
<margin>Delrio. l. 3. q. 4. sect. 1. concl. 2.</margin> 
For *Philosophica seu Physica fascinatio non nisi impropriè dici potest fascinatio, propriè verò est contagio, seu infectio.* <note>Philosophical or physical fascination can only be called fascination improperly; strictly speaking, it is contagion or infection.</note> And therefore, the learned *Vallesius* spoke to the same purpose: *Sed neq; si quis pestilenti affectus febri, aut etiam sine febre deferens secum seminaria pestis alium intuens intuentem inficiat, dicetur fascinasse, sed peste affecisse.* <note>But neither if someone affected with a pestilential fever, or even without a fever, carrying with him the seeds of the plague, should infect another by looking at him as he is looking back, would he be said to have fascinated him, but to have infected him with the plague.</note>

2. Some of the fathers (which may be offered as an objection) do seem to hold that St. Paul here meant diabolical fascination; for instance, *Tertullian* in English says: 
<margin>See Jo. Lazar. Guttier. regarding fascination.</margin>
> For there is also something among the Gentiles to be feared, which they call fascination, being a more unfortunate outcome of praise and great glory: this we sometimes interpret as being of the Devil.

And St. *Jerome* says upon this passage:
> Fascination is when certain things are shown to the eyes of men through magical illusions to be other than they are. Also, that which hurts children is commonly called fascination, for the eyes of certain persons are said to burn with their gaze, and this act of theirs is called fascination; and it may be that the Devils are subservient to this sin.

And *Thomas Aquinas* says:
> And this also may be done by Devils, who have the power of moving false imaginations, and bringing them to the principles of the senses, by changing the senses themselves.

From which we may note these things: 1. That *Tertullian* says they sometimes interpret this as the Devil's work, but he does not show how truly or upon what grounds; and it seems that sometimes they interpreted it as something else, for his words must necessarily imply that. 2. Secondly, St. *Jerome* sometimes calls fascination magical illusions, and sometimes that which hurts children by the burning of certain eyes; and then he adds that it "may be" that the Devils are subservient to this sin. So he is not certain in his opinion, nor does he truly know what fascination is, except according to vulgar opinion or blind conjectures. 3. And all that the Angelical Doctor says only amounts to the delusion of the senses by false imaginations, so that here is no proof of either the Devil or his instruments causing any real fascination.

### *Of Divine permission, providence and prescience.*

# The Displaying of CHAP. IX.

That God should be the author of sin is false, as these arguments sufficiently testify.

<margin>
Argum. 1.
James 1:13.
Psalm 5:4.
Deut. 32:3.
</margin>
1. That must of necessity be false which the Scriptures declare to be so in open and plain terms. But the Scriptures deny that God should be the author of sin or evil in open and plain terms, as where the Text says: *God cannot be tempted with evil: where both the act and the possibility of it are absolutely denied.* Again: *For you are not a God who has pleasure in wickedness, nor shall evil dwell with you.* Therefore it is false that God is, or can be, the author of sin; and so by consequence the supposed absurdity is a mere impossibility; and an absurdity urged that is impossible is the most absurd of all.

<margin>Argum. 2.</margin>
2. He is a most perfect being (*ens summè perfectum*), and *whatever is in God, is God (quicquid est in Deo, est Deus)*; but sin, however understood or accepted, is an imperfection, defect, and a departure from a just and perfect rule. Therefore, it is simply impossible that God can be the cause of anything that is imperfect, sinful, or evil, if sin is considered as the *evil of fault (malum culpæ)*.

<margin>
Argum. 3.
Rom. 4:15.
</margin>
3. God is not under any binding law given to him by someone else, for then he would cease to be supreme, independent, and omnipotent. Now, for one to whom no law is given to observe, there can be no transgression, for the Apostle says, *where there is no law, there is no transgression;* and therefore it is simply impossible that God should be the author or cause of sin or evil, because there is no law that he can transgress against.

<margin>Argum. 4.</margin>
4. God prohibits and hates sin, as the Scriptures everywhere testify, but God is the cause of nothing but that which he loves, and therefore cannot be the cause of the evil of sin. And to speak properly, sin has no efficient cause, but a deficient one, such as the will of fallen Angels and wicked men, whose irregularity of will, diverging from the command of God, is the only cause that sin and evil have or can have. An efficient cause belongs only to those things that are good, because every efficient cause, by working, brings something into being. But privations (of which sort are sins) bring nothing into being, but truly signify the absence of being. Therefore, Saint Augustine said well: *There is no efficient cause of evil, but only a deficient one (Mali causa efficiens nulla est, sed tantùm deficiens).*

<margin>
De Civitat. Dei, l. 12. c. 7.
Argum. 5.
Gen. 1:31.
John 8:44.
1 John 3:8.
</margin>
5. That which properly has an efficient cause also has an end properly so called. But sin does not have an end properly so called, because the "end" is a state of being, and therefore good, and the perfection of the thing. But the Scripture declares that *all things that God created were exceedingly good;* and that the cause of sin was Man and the Devil; for the text says, *that the Devil was a murderer from the beginning, and stayed not in the truth:* And again, *He that commits sin is of the Devil, for the Devil sins from the beginning.* Therefore, from this it is clear that God neither is nor can be the author or cause of sin.

This plausible claim of being zealous—not to make God the author of sin—we commend as allowable; but it is only like the zeal of the Scribes and Pharisees, which was without knowledge, because they claim an absurdity for something that is a simple impossibility. And they ought to remember the argument of *Job*, which is this: *will you speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?* For just as we ought not to suppose or imply him to be the author of sin, so we ought not to rob him of his Glory by detracting from his power and providence, nor by ascribing that to Creatures which is only due to the Creator—as those do who hold a bare passive permission in him, separate from his will and decree in his providence. Nor does the denying of this imply in any way that he is the author of sin, for we allow a providential permission as the act of his will and decree, as we shall show hereafter.

Now concerning "permission" in God—being a suspension of his active power regarding some acts permitted to the creatures, and that for just and good ends—the definition of it and its features or properties are so obscurely handled even by those who make the most fuss about it, that it would serve rather to turn Men away from the right path than to guide them in it or toward it. Therefore, here we shall only note these three things and pursue them more fully hereafter:

1. There must be the person or power permitting that has the ability, right, and authority to do so.
2. There must be the person or power permitted that has the ability to perform the thing permitted; otherwise, it would be in vain and for no purpose.
3. There must be the thing or action that is permitted to be done, or brought to pass, by the person permitted to act, and that must not be impossible.

1. Before the Creation, it is merely improper to attribute permission to God, because there was no person nor power besides himself that could act in any way, and therefore could not be permitted; and so, the corresponding party being missing, both the relationship and the connection between them must necessarily fall to the ground as having no existence. Thus, it is impossible that permission should be in God when there was no Creature to be permitted, and so it could not be attributed to him before the Creation.

2. It is just as improper to attribute permission to God in respect of the physical agency of <term>second causes</term>, because he not only works all in all, but also through his <term>Divine concourse</term> and sustaining power...

<margin>See Chrysostome on this location.</margin>
"He carries," he says, "all things; that is, he governs all things. For he holds together those things that are falling and tending toward nothingness. For in the act of creation, the essences of things were produced from nothing; but in the act of preservation, those things which have been made are kept from returning to nothing. Therefore, while these things are governed and harmonized despite being naturally opposed to one another, a great and truly marvelous judgment of supreme power is revealed."

But also because he has set all natural things their bounds, and ordered, decreed, and determined their ends in acting. Now, what he has appointed, ordered, and decreed to be the agency of every creature, and determined its end in acting, cannot properly be called "permission," but his will, ordination, and providence. To say that he suffers and permits the Sun and Moon to run their course is an improper expression and injurious to his wisdom and power in his providential government of his creatures, seeing that it is a certain truth, <term>Deus operatur in omni operante</term> <note>God works in every worker</note>. 2. <header>Chap. IX. Supposed Witchcraft.</header>

*...a propensity to sin before his first sin. Nor was it in the Angels, who fell from their state. Second, although a disposition or habit may be present that inclines one to act, it is not in the nature of every disposition or habit to make a man lean toward any particular act, for the sake of which alone it is called permission.* And though it is granted that God did create the Angels, and *Adam*, in a *fallible state* <note>in statu labili</note>, in which they had a sufficiency of power or grace not to have sinned or fallen; and though that power or grace was not withdrawn from them, and there was no coercion upon their wills to force them to sin—for if it had been so, their falls would have been no sin—so neither did God supply them with more assisting grace to have sustained them, for then their state would not have been fallible, nor would they have been in a position to sin. But it is manifest that in their creation they were set in *equilibrium* <note>æquilibrio</note>, and had equal power of free will either to sin or not to sin, and so had no propensity or disposition at all to commit that sin to which they were left by a free permission. And so, propensity and disposition to the act permitted (if permission is understood generally) had no place in the Angels nor *Adam* before their first sinning, according to the Text:

<margin>Eccles. 7. 29.</margin>
*God made man upright*; that is, like a straight or right line that, falling perpendicularly upon another right line, does incline to neither end of the line upon which it falls; so *Adam* was made upright without any propensity or inclination to sin at all. And if this propensity and disposition is understood and applied to Angels in their condition after their fall, then it is true they have not only an inclination but a most strong will and desire to commit more evil and mischief than God in His goodness permits them to perform; for the Devil goes about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour, and it was Satan who not only had a disposition, but desired to sift Peter as wheat. And it is manifest that wicked men have a strong will and desire to commit mischief, but that God has a hook in their nostrils and a bridle in their jaws with which He curbs and restrains them, so that they cannot carry out all the mischief that they intend, as is manifest in the example of Sennacherib and many others.

7. Permission must be referred and reduced to the will of God, for refusal <note>nolition</note> is an act of His will as well as willing <note>volition</note>. And to speak properly and truly, permission is but an act of the Divine Will not to impede such or such particular actions of the creatures; and therefore the same things will follow from His willing not to impede as from His willing the acts of a free agent, seeing neither puts coercion upon the will of the creature that is to act. And that permission is an act of the Divine Will, and to be reduced to it, *Arminius* confesses in these words:

<margin>Twisse de Permiss. as above.</margin>
> *It is known from the very derivation of the word that permission belongs to the category of action, whether in itself or reductively, as they say in the Schools. For the cessation of an act must also be reduced to an act: it has the will as its proximate and immediate cause—not knowledge, not power, not authority, although,* etc.

<margin>Fran. Jun. on the first sin of Adam. p. 111, 114.</margin>
...and these things are required in the one who permits. And when he defines permission, he says: *God’s permission is an act of the Divine will*; than which nothing can be more clear. And not much different from this is the definition of permission given by the learned *Junius* as follows: *Permission is an act of the will, by which he who has it in his power to inhibit the actions of others, does not inhibit them, but leaves the manner of them to the will of the agent.* And again he says: *But with God the Best and Greatest, there is no permission at all that is not voluntary: since every divine permission is from an internal principle—that is, from his own will—and is moved toward the end that his will has predetermined for it.* But we will conclude this with that of St. *Augustine*, translated into English thus:
<margin>August. Enchir. 75, 76.</margin>
> Nothing comes to pass unless the Omnipotent wills it to be done—either that it may be done by his suffering it, or by his volition. Neither is it to be doubted that God does well, even by suffering those things to be done that are done evilly; for he does not permit except by a just judgment, and truly everything is good that is just. Therefore, although those things that are evil, insofar as they are evil, are not good; nevertheless, [the fact] that they are not only good, but also that they are evil, is good. For unless it were good that there should be evils, they would by no means be permitted by the omnipotent good, to whom without any doubt it is always as easy to do what he would as it is easy not to suffer what he would not have to be.

By all of this, it is plain that his permission is the act of his Divine Will, and if he would not have it done, he would not permit it; and so the same consequences will follow from nolition <note>the act of not willing</note> that follow from volition, in respect that they are both acts of the Divine Will.

8. It is a certain truth that all moral actions are performed by a physical power in respect to the sustaining of the will in its natural being while it acts, and that the creature is conserved even in the act as it is natural, though there be obliquity <note>moral deviation or sinfulness</note> in the will of the creature acting in reference to the law given or made known to it. And *Arminius* acknowledges this in these words:
<margin>Twisse as above. 346.</margin>
*It is necessary, therefore, that when God permits some act of a creature's power, that creature is conserved so that it may exist and live, and its power remains fit to produce the act; that no greater or equal power is opposed; that the object finally is offered; and the power is permitted.* From this, therefore—to use the first sin of the Angels and *Adam* as an instance—besides the equal power and liberty of will that they had to sin or not to sin, it is manifest that God willed and determined not to withdraw his sustaining power from them, but that they might exist and live in the very act of their sinning. Neither did he withdraw the power they had, nor oppose a greater or equal power to impede them; much less did he create or infuse any evil into their natures, or place upon them any compulsion of will to force them to sin, but solely left them to the power and liberty of their own free wills. And though by his foreknowledge he certainly knew that they would sin and fall, yet he determined in his purpose not to hinder them, but by his providential decree did set down

9. Furthermore, it is necessary that a creature performing a moral act (especially in the case of the angels and *Adam* before their fall) has liberty and freedom of will, and that the will, at the instant of the act, is not restrained or under a coercive power; otherwise, <term>*malum culpæ*</term> or sin would cease to be evil, and thus there could be no sin at all. And thus far, and in this peculiar respect only, the angels and *Adam*—before their act of sin and in the very instant of the act itself—were permitted; that is, God willed and determined not to impede them, but for the ordering of that sin and fall, the permission was conjoined with his will and providence, and was not separate from it or a bare permission.

<margin>Rom. 7:8, 11</margin>
10. Now we shall come to consider how the fallen angels are under the rule and restraint of this divine and all-governing providence, wherein we shall make it appear that they do nothing in this elementary and sublunary world in any corporeal manner, except as they are ordered, licensed, and limited by the will and decree of the Almighty. 1. It cannot rationally be supposed that God is less wise in ruling and ordering the Prince of Darkness, the Prince of Devils, and the head of all rebellion and rebels, than he is in ruling his subjects and servants, who are all wicked men; but all these he rules with a rod of iron, and breaks them in pieces like a potter's vessel. And therefore, he much more has a restraint upon and a rule over the fallen angels who did not keep their first estate, and therefore are reserved in chains in darkness until the judgment of the great day.

# CHAP. X.

## *Whether fallen angels are corporeal or simply incorporeal, and the absurdity of their assuming bodies, and similar consequences.*

I am not unaware of what great criticism I may incur for entering upon such a delicate and precise point as the corporeality or incorporeality of angels, seeing it has exercised and tormented the minds of the most learned in all ages—especially being but an obscure person, not elevated by those lofty titles that usually increase men's reputations more by those attributes than by the weight and strength of their arguments. Yet, as it is no necessary article of the Christian faith, but rather a matter where a man may lawfully defend either side, it cannot reasonably be judged by discerning readers as either pride or a just offense for me to handle this subject. For seeing that most of the Christian and learned Fathers, for the space of four hundred years after Christ, were of the opinion that they were corporeal,

1. There is a recent way of arguing adopted by Dr. *Moore* and others, in which they undertake to prove a thing to be so or so, or else force a man to deny his own faculties. And so the said Doctor undertakes to prove the existence of immaterial and incorporeal beings, or else he thinks he forces men to deny their own faculties: and these faculties he claims to be common notions, external sense, and evident and undeniable deductions of reason. He concludes that whatever is not consistent with all or some of these is mere fancy, and is of no importance for proving truth or falsehood, regardless of its vigor or complexity. But this will not accomplish the goal he intends, for these reasons. 1. Because the common notion of a spiritual and immaterial being does not exist in all or any man, nor is it (to use his own words) true at first sight to all men in their right minds upon a clear perception of the terms, without any further discussion or reasoning, but is only a bare supposition without any proof or evidence at all. 2. The existence of an immaterial and spiritual substance can in no way enter the senses or affect them, because it is manifest (as *Descartes* has sufficiently proved) that all sensation is produced by physical contact, and not otherwise. And though we do not deny that there have been, are, and may be apparitions that cannot be rationally supposed to be the ordinary *phenomena* of physical matter, yet if they affect the senses, there must be something in them that produces that effect which is physical, or else the senses could not be acted upon; for *the immaterial does not act upon the material, except eminently as God does.* 3. No correct deductions can possibly be drawn from the highest power of reasoning where the understanding has no knowledge of the things from which reason would draw its conclusions; for as the same Doctor frames his axiom: "Whatever things are in themselves, they are nothing to us, except insofar as they become known to our faculties or cognitive powers." But we assert (which we shall prove shortly) that our faculties or cognitive powers (however much some would vainly magnify and extol them) do not have the power of understanding beings that are simply and absolutely immaterial and incorporeal.

As for instance, when a melancholic person truly imagines himself to be changed into a Wolf or Dog, it is not only an easy notion, but it is also truly a notion, and yet it is a false notion; because there is no true congruity between it and the thing from which it is taken, as the Body of the person so conceiving is not at all changed into a Wolf or Dog, but still retains its human shape and figure. Though they are truly his notions—that is, he did think, conceive, and frame them—yet they are not truly abstracted from the things. And so he may be rather judged to be led by speculative and Philosophic Enthusiasm than by the clear light of a sound understanding.

For when we speak of the extension of body as its characteristic property, we only conceive of its superficial dimensions; its internal nature *quatenus Corpus* <note>as a body</note> being utterly unknown to us. It is a certain truth that *Quidditates rerum, non sunt cognoscibiles* <note>the essences of things are not knowable</note>; and as *Dr. More* grants, the naked essence or substance of a thing is utterly inconceivable to any of our faculties. From this we argue, *a minori ad majus* <note>from the lesser to the greater</note>, that if the substance of a body—whose qualities and modifications fully enter into and work upon our senses—is utterly inconceivable to any of our senses, then of necessity the substance of a created spirit, conceived as immaterial and incorporeal, must be much more inconceivable to any of our faculties, because it has no effects, operations, or modifications that can or do operate upon our senses.

<margin>Argument 2.</margin>
2. And just as we do not know the intrinsic nature of body, so also we are ignorant of the highest degree of the purity and spiritual nature of bodies, nor do we know where they end, and therefore cannot tell where to fix the beginning of a mere spiritual and immaterial being. For there is in the universe so great a diversity of created bodies, and of so many sorts and degrees of purity and fineness, one exceeding another, that we cannot determine which of them comes nearest to incorporeity, or the nature of spirit. And many of these, when compared with other more gross and palpable bodies, may be and are called and accounted spirits, although they are nevertheless all corporeal, differing only by degree. So the vital parts in the bodies of men are called spirits by physicians in relation to the bones, ligaments, muscular flesh, and the like; nay, even in respect to the blood, lymphatic humor, lacteal juice, or the *succus nutritius nervosus* <note>nutritious nervous juice</note>, and yet they are still contained within the limits of the body and are just as really corporeal as any of the rest, as are the air and ether. And those visible species of other bodies that are carried in the air and represented to our eyes—by which we distinguish the shape, color, position, and likeness of one body from another—though passed over by the Schools with that slight title of "qualities," as if they were either simply nothing or incorporeal things, are nevertheless really corporeal; otherwise, they could not enter into or affect the visive sensories <note>visual organs</note>. And these intersect and pass through one another in the air (as may be optically demonstrated) without confusion, mixing, or discerption <note>tearing apart</note>, and may comparatively be accounted spiritual and incorporeal, though really they are not so. But what shall we say to that wonderful body, image, or *Idolum* <note>image or specter</note> of ourselves and other things that we behold in a mirror or looking-glass? Must this be a mere nothing, or an absolutely incorporeal thing? Surely not. For it is as much a body as any in the universe, though of the greatest purity and fineness of any that we know; and how near it

...approaches the nature of spirit, is very difficult (if not impossible) to determine. This is because they vanish when the body or subject is removed, because *nullius entis nulla est operatio* <note>nothing has no operation</note>, and *Incorporeum non incurrit in sensus* <note>what is incorporeal does not strike the senses</note>, and because they would pass through the glass, except for the foil or *Bractea* <note>thin metal plate</note> laid on the other side, by which the image is reflected. <margin>Argum. 3.</margin>
3. Dr. More makes substance the genus, and spirit and body the two species, so that body and spirit are of one generical identity. Therefore, there must of necessity be some certain specific difference between them assigned and proved, or else the division is faulty, and the property of spirit is not proved; thus, their opinion of spirit falls totally to the ground. For we affirm (and shall prove) that though a difference may be imagined and supposed, yet it was never yet sufficiently proved. For *omnia supposita, non sunt vera* <note>not everything supposed is true</note>; otherwise, all the impossible fictions and vain chimeras of melancholy and doting persons might pass for true oracles. But it is one thing truly to understand, and another thing to imagine and fancy what indeed is not, nor ever was. And though the supposition seems ever so probable and likely, it will at best only imply the possibility of such an imagined difference, but not prove it really to be so. Therefore, here we shall retort the Doctor’s Axiom against him, which is this:

<margin>The Immortality of the Soul. Axiom. 2. p. 6.</margin>
> “Whatever is unknown to us, or is known but as merely possible, is not to move us or determine us any way, or make us undecided; but we are to rest in the present light and plain determination of our own faculties.”

Now that a spirit is <term>penetrable</term> and <term>indiscerpible</term> <note>incapable of being torn apart or divided into pieces</note> may be imagined as possible to some, but cannot be clearly intelligible to any sober mind. For to imagine and to understand are faculties that are very different. However, even if such a difference is conceived as possible (which cannot enter the narrow gate of my intellect), the difference of being penetrable and indiscerpible is not to move us to determine that a spirit has those distinct properties from bodies, because they are known to us only as merely possible. If spirits cannot expand themselves into an infinite space, nor contract themselves into an infinite smallness, then where are the bounds and limits of this contraction and expansion, or how is it proved that they can do either? Seeing they are properties and affections of bodies and matter, and never were proved to be peculiar to spirits.

And on the other side, if they are held to be simply and absolutely incorporeal, then these absurdities must of necessity follow:

1. If Angels are simply incorporeal, then they can cause no physical or local motion at all, because nothing can be moved except by contact, and that must be either by immediate or virtual contact. For the maxim is certain: *Whatever acts, acts either by mediation of the substance,* as when one’s hand immediately touches a thing and so moves it; *or by mediation of power,* as when a man with a rod or a line draws a thing out of the water. Both of these require a corporeal contact—that is, the surfaces of the body moving or drawing must either mediately or immediately touch the surfaces of the body to be moved or drawn. But that which is absolutely incorporeal has no surfaces at all, and therefore can make no contact, either mediate or immediate; therefore, if Angels are simply incorporeal, they can cause no physical or local motion at all.

But with the Doctor's permission, we must assert that what he says is not allowable, for these reasons: 1. Because imaginary space has no existence in nature, but only in the imagination of the thinker, and *beings of reason are not natural beings existing in the reality of things*. 2. And so that this position may be determined, we ought to have respect for some other bodies which we may consider as immovable. And as we regard various bodies, we may say that the same thing at the same time both changes place and does not change place. As when a ship is carried across the sea, he who sits in the ship always remains in one place if respect is given to the parts of the ship, between which parts he keeps the same position; and yet the same person continually changes place if respect is given to the shores, because he continually recedes from some shores and comes nearer to others. 3. Neither is this distinction valid, because as the same author tells us: *Space, or internal place, and the corporeal substance contained in it, do not differ in reality, but only in the way we are accustomed to conceive of them.* 4. *Dr.* More grants that spirits are substances and have extension, and we affirm that nothing can be so except that which is corporeal, and consequently must be in a place circumscriptively. Therefore, the notion of a definitive place is merely a fictitious absurdity, without ground or reason.

<margin>Objection 2.</margin>
2. There is only one other argument that the persons of the other opinion have urged, such as *Aquinas* and the rest of the *Scholastic* rabble, namely, the text in the Psalm, which is this: <margin>Psalm 104:4, Hebrews 1:7.</margin>

From which they would positively conclude that they are spirits, and absolutely incorporeal; but they fail in their purpose for these clear reasons. 1. The text there cannot be rationally understood as referring to their creation, or of their creaturely nature, but of their offices and administrations, because the word used there is not from ברא (to create, or form out of nothing), but from עשה *made*, that is, by ordering them in their offices and ministries. And again, the word רוח does not always or of necessity signify an incorporeal thing but that which is a body, such as the winds; and so *Luther* and various others translate it. It is commonly attributed to beasts as well as men, as in that passage of *Solomon*: *Who knows the spirit of man that goes upward, and the spirit of the beast that goes downward to the earth?* Where the word spirit, which is the same in Hebrew, is attributed to beasts as well as to men; but no man (I suppose) will believe that the spirit of a beast is simply incorporeal. Therefore, the word spirit in the Psalm cannot necessarily be understood as a simple incorporeal substance, and therefore the conclusion is not necessary.

But the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews must be taken for the best interpreter of these words of the Psalmist; he quotes them only for this purpose: to prove that Christ in dignity and office is far above the angels, who are all ordered to serve and obey him, and are by their offices all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for those who shall be heirs of salvation. By this it is manifest that this passage is to be understood of their ministry and offices, and not of their nature or substances. 2. The first differential distinction is that their bodies do not suffer, nor are they altered or dissipated, by the most strong and active sublunary agent known to us. Among these, we have none of greater force and activity than our culinary fire; yet it is clear that that element did not work upon nor burn the Angel that appeared to *Manoah* and his wife, *who ascended in the flame of the altar, and was not touched or altered at all*, which plainly shows that his body was not to be acted upon by the fierce flame of sublunary fire; and he is there called the Angel of *Jehovah*. This is also confirmed by what *Nebuchadnezzar* saw and confessed: that although *only three men were cast into the fiery furnace, yet he saw a fourth (who by all the learned is judged to be an Angel) and they were not harmed*, that is, the fire did not work upon their bodies to burn, alter, or consume them. So, in this, the bodies of Angels differ from most other bodies, because they do not suffer from sublunary fire, the most violent agent that we know. And this must rationally be taken as proper to Angels in regard to their created natures, and not as something added by a Divine and Almighty Power, as might be granted in some other cases.

And though they may be divided and separated, they may perhaps close as quickly by reunion, and so suffer nothing at all by that division.

<margin>Saints' Everlasting Rest, chapter 7, part 2, page 255.</margin> Concerning the properties of their bodies, it seems to have been the opinion of *Tertullian* (as I find him quoted by Mr. *Baxter*) that they had thin, pure, and aerial bodies which they could dilate and expand, or condense and contract at their pleasure, and so frame them into various and different shapes; his words are these: *Demons contract and expand these bodies of theirs as they will, just like worms and certain other insects.* <note>Dæmones sua hæc corpora contrahunt, & dilatant, ut volunt: sicut etiam lumbrici, & alia quædam insecta.</note> So we see that some worms and insects will extend themselves to a vast length and thinness, so that they can pass through a very small hole or passage, and again contract themselves into a great bulk, reducing their length and increasing their breadth and thickness. Though it remains the same corporeal substance and generally retains the same dimensions in terms of space regardless of the figure it takes, yet in regard to accidental shape or figure, it may change its dimensions in relation to one another—being at one time more in length and less in breadth and depth, and sometimes more in breadth and depth and less in length. So may the bodies of Angels, by contraction and dilation, alter their dimensions in various ways, and consequently their shapes and figures; and all this occurs according to the motion and act of their own wills. However, there must still be limits to these acts of extension and contraction, such that they can do neither to an infinite degree—either becoming an invisible and indivisible point, or being infinitely expanded or dilated. This opinion has sufficient rationality and intelligibility in it. Of this very point St. *Bernard* speaks thus modestly: <margin>On the Song of Songs, page 504.</margin> *It seems that the Fathers have felt differently about such matters, and it is not clear to me from what source I should teach either view; and I confess my ignorance.* <note>Videntur Patres de hujusmodi diversa sensisse, nec mihi perspicuum est undè alterutrum doceam: & nescire me fateor.</note> And though we cannot precisely list nor assign the certain properties of their bodies, yet we may rationally conclude this much. 1. That since they are creatures ordained for high and noble ends, they must necessarily have their bodies and organs fitted and suitably proportioned to fulfill and accomplish those ends, as most clearly appears in the bodies and organs of all other creatures, which are most wisely and fitly framed by the Almighty according to the several ends and uses for which they were created and ordained. 2. It is most probable that, considering there are creatures that can alter the colors and figures of their own bodies as their wills are moved by their passions and affections—as is manifest in worms, and in the colors of the chameleon, as is asserted by the experience of the learned physician *Dominicus Panarolus*—so, from the lesser to the greater, Angels have bodies of

And it is no small wonder to observe our ordinary *Gallus Turcicus* or *Gallopavus* <note>The common turkey</note>, how quietly and humbly he sometimes walks, and then suddenly, by some emotion of spirit, how his tail will be advanced and extended, his wattles swelled and puffed up, and the snood that comes over the beak or *rostrum* be extended or contracted at the pleasure of the animal. And it is much more remarkable to consider the quick and sudden change of the colors of both those parts—sometimes to a whiteness or an ash-color, sometimes purple, sometimes bluish, and sometimes pure red. That creature can give such a quick motion to the spirits and blood that they can so quickly alter and change not only the colors but also the size. And much more may we rationally believe that Angels can alter and change the figure and color of their bodies according to the ministries they are employed in.

<margin>Mark 12:25.</margin>
3. The Scripture informs us that in or at the resurrection, the bodies of men shall be as the Angels that are in heaven, *sicut Angeli* <note>as the Angels</note>. Now this analogy, comparison, or assimilation would be altogether false if Angels had no bodies at all but were merely incorporeal; then it would follow that the bodies after the resurrection were made mere Spirits and so ceased to be bodies, which is false according to the doctrine of St. Paul. He shows us plainly that after the resurrection they are changed in qualities into σώματα πνευματικὰ, *spiritual bodies*, for there is a *natural* soul or *animal body*, and so likewise there is a *spiritual body*. From this, we necessarily conclude that Angels have bodies and that they are pure spiritual ones.
<margin>1 Cor. 15:44.</margin>

Now we shall come to the other point intended in this Chapter, which is to show that the opinion of Angels assuming bodies of the elements here below is a mere fiction, as must necessarily follow if what we have proved is true—namely, that they have bodies; for then the assuming of other bodies must necessarily be in vain and to no purpose. But we shall also show the weakness and folly of that tenet by these positive reasons following.

1. Those who maintain the assumption of bodies dare not affirm that they are so invested with those bodies as human souls are with their bodies; for then there must be a vital union, which cannot exist except by Divine Ordination. But it does not appear anywhere, either by Scripture or sound rational consequence, that God either appointed or gave power to Angels to assume to themselves bodies of whatever shape they pleased, or that he ordained a vital union between the Angels and those bodies they are supposed to assume either by creation or generation. Therefore, if they did assume any such bodies, it must only be as we put on and take off our garments, or as players put on and take off their perukes <note>wigs</note>, masks, and garments according to the various things or persons they intend to represent and impersonate.

2. But the great question will be: who are the tailors that shape and frame these garments for them? What! Must it be they themselves who shape and figure these bodies, just as snails are supposed to frame and make their shells and houses? Surely not, because if they are simply incorporeal, then they can make no contact with corporeal matter, and without physical contact there can be no alteration or organization of matter; consequently, they cannot frame or shape such garments for themselves. Nor can any other actor or agent be assigned that can frame them, and therefore the tenet is a most ridiculous fiction. And again, if they should have such solid bodies framed of the inferior elements—such as the body of a serpent, which the witch-mongers suppose the Devil assumed when he deceived *Eve*, and such bodies as demons are vainly supposed to assume to carry the heavy bodies of men and women through the air—then those bodies would necessarily be of such solidity and compactness that they could not be suddenly wasted away and dissipated. Then, undoubtedly, we would find them sometimes, just as we do the sloughs, *exuviae* <note>cast-off skins</note>, or skins of snakes, for they could not be consumed in a moment. And it would be horrid to suppose that God should instantaneously create them and just as suddenly dissipate and waste them. So, in truth, there is no certainty here; it may be looked upon as a chimera and a poetical fable.

3. And if the angels did not have such bodily organs with which they could move, walk, speak, and perform other such actions before they assumed or crept into such garments, their being enclosed and invested within them would no more enable them to walk or speak than a hollow image would enable a lame man to walk or a mute man to speak if they were enclosed inside it. Therefore, suppose (as the witch-mongers hold) that the Devil should appear to a witch in the assumed shape of a cat, dog, foal, or the like, and walk and talk with him or her; if the Devil could not walk and speak before assuming such a shape, then having crept into such a garment would no more enable him to speak than a dead cat in an empty hogshead or wind trapped in an empty bladder.

# CHAP. XII.
## *Of the Knowledge and Power of Fallen Angels.*

These evil angels of whom we treat undoubtedly participated in the same knowledge and power as those angels who still retain it and did not fall into that defection and rebellion, before they left their habitation and failed to keep their first estate. So our inquiry must be: what knowledge and power do they have?

The other main point that we undertake to handle in this chapter concerns the power of the fallen angels, and that is to be considered in these three particulars: 1. In general in respect of their power, either in spiritual and moral things, or in things natural. 2. Or in respect of spiritual and moral things in particular. 3. Or in respect of physical and <term>sublunary</term> things.

And for the first, it must of necessity be granted that their power since their fall is much diminished, or at least restrained and chained and fettered up. For they, becoming rebels against the Almighty and not keeping their first estate, but having left their own habitation, it was most agreeable to the wisdom and justice of God to take away from them the greatest part of that power and authority that he formerly had given them, and so to imprison and chain them up, so that they might never be able to attempt or perform a similar rebellion again; otherwise the Almighty would not have used that wisdom that is ordinary with earthly princes, who, having overcome those that rebelled against them, do not only disarm them, but also confine or imprison them. And to this very thing do the Scriptures allude, when they say that *they are delivered into chains of darkness, and that they are reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day.* So that though the devils still retain their cruel, wicked, and devouring will and mind, yet they are but like the lion within the bars of iron, or *Bajazet* in the cage of iron led about by *Tamerlane*, and so though they be ever so cruelly bent to do mischief, yet they are under the chains and cooped up in the grates of darkness, and kept in everlasting chains that they are never able to break or unloose.

They have no power by creation or ordination to work upon, move, or alter things that are angelical, celestial, ethereal, and superior, but are only chained in this caliginous <note>dark or misty</note> atmosphere and impure air. Thus, their power (no matter how great some may suppose it to be) is only restrained to these inferior sublunary things.

This occurs when they are commissioned and sent by God to effect specific actions. Instead, it was performed by that afflicting power granted to him by God to carry out that affliction upon *Job* which God had determined for the trial and manifestation of his faith and patience. This cannot for any reason be said to be done by Devils in their transactions with Witches, and therefore these must necessarily be fables and chimeras.

2. We may observe that however great these signs and wonders may be, yet they are but *lying ones*, both regarding the end for which they are done and in respect of their substance. Therefore, however great the signs and wonders may be that *evil angels* perform, yet they are totally different from true miracles. Those are always wrought for the confirmation of the true *doctrine and worship of God*, but these have their end only to establish false doctrine, lies, and erroneous opinions, or *idolatrous worships*. So they differ in their substance, for those miracles that God shows for the confirmation of his truth are always true and real, being against and above the whole power and course of nature. But those wonders wrought by Satan are but delusions, cheats, jugglings, and impostures, which—though they may seem strange to those who are ignorant of their causes—yet only arise from natural causes, or from artificial cunning, conspiracy, and the like. Therefore we may conclude that whatever miracles are wrought by a *divine power* tend to the overthrow of *Satan’s power* in the world, but all false miracles are wrought to uphold the power of *Satan’s kingdom* in the world, following delusions, lies, and false doctrines.

# CHAP. XI. *Supposed Witchcraft.*

The premise of the syllogism is proved in this way: it is the role of the same power to change the order of nature and to create things that did not exist; thus, the changing of the order of nature is a certain kind of new creation. But Satan does not have the power by which he can create things that as of yet had no existence, as all rational people must necessarily confess. From this, it must follow that Satan does not have the power to change the order of nature, and consequently, he cannot work true and real miracles. 3. <margin>Psalm 72:18; 77:14.</margin>
> *Blessed be the Lord God, the God of Israel, who only does wondrous things.* And again, *You are the God that does wonders.*

<margin>Romans 4:17.</margin>
> *God who gives life to the dead, and calls those things that are not, as though they were.* 

Upon which **Beza** gives this note: 
> *By Him who restores life. With whom those things already exist which otherwise in reality do not, as one who can produce anything from nothing by a single word.*

<margin>See Rollock on 2 Thessalonians.</margin>
But if it is objected that although Satan and his angels do not work true miracles by themselves and by their own proper power, might God not work real miracles through them, as He did through the Prophets, Apostles, and His ministers? It is answered: The wonders that are performed by Satan tend toward the goal of confirming lies against God and His glory. But God does not lend His power to confirm lies that are contrary to His glory and against Himself. Therefore, Satan, acting as God's minister, does not work true miracles; for God uses the fallen angels as executioners of His wrath and judgments for the afflicting and punishing of men, but when God performs anything for the good of mankind, either in soul or body, He does not use devils as His ministers, but rather the good and blessed angels, who are ministering spirits sent forth for the good of those who shall be heirs of salvation.

And if it is asked, what kind of things are those wonders performed by Satan and the Antichrist? ### The Displaying of CHAP. XI.

...seem so to us, who do not know the causes that are in nature as well as that old serpent; neither do we understand the manner by which he works and performs his tricks. From this ignorance, it follows that those wonders—which in themselves are no true miracles, nor performed contrary to the order of nature—are taken by us to be true miracles.

But we will draw toward a conclusion of this point with the definition and corollaries that the learned *Zanchy* gives us in these particulars.
<margin>On the Works of God, book 4, chapter 12, page 191.</margin> 
*A miracle (he says) is therefore an external and visible, true and simply wonderful deed, performed for the best purposes and especially for the salvation of men and to promote the glory of God.* From this, these points are to be observed:

1. That a miracle is external and made visible. For so (he says) are all those things that we read of in Scripture that are taken to be true miracles. Therefore, the pretended invisible miracle of <term>transubstantiation</term> (as they call it) in the ordinance of the Lord's Supper is a mere figment, because no such thing was ever made visible or truly witnessed. But let us press this argument a little further. If it be (as indeed it must be) a certain property of a true miracle that it be external and visible so that there may be witnesses of it—otherwise, that which no one ever saw or knew might be the property of a miracle—then those great wonders that witch-mongers affirm that the Devil works with and for witches (such as having carnal copulation with them, sucking upon their bodies, making a corporeal and oral pact with them, carrying them through the air, or changing them into cats or dogs) must of necessity be a mere figment and an impossibility. This is because they have never yet been seen, witnessed, or proved by anyone of sound judgment, right understanding, or clear reason; they are merely the works of darkness, existing nowhere but in the minds and brains of the witch-mongers, who are ruled by the Prince of Darkness.

2. A miracle ought to be really and truly done; that is, it should indeed be such a thing as it appears. For example, the water that Christ changed into wine was really such; that is, it was truly wine to the sight and taste of all those who drank it. Therefore, those things brought to pass by the deceptive jugglery of devils and magicians are indeed no true miracles. To apply this to our present purpose: it is manifest that those things witch-mongers believe that witches do or suffer—such as flying in the air, being present at dances and banquets and yet remaining empty and hungry, and the like—are nothing but mere delusory dreams and cheating fancies in their brains. And if anything is done <term>ad extra</term> <note>externally or in the physical world</note>, it is merely as jugglers do, by drawing the eyes away from observing the manner of their movements, by substituting one thing in the place of another, and the like. So at best, Satan, in respect to what he performs in these aforesaid actions, is but a chief *Hocus Pocus* fellow or juggler, and one who acts for a worse end than our common jugglers do, who act only to provide sport.

3. A true miracle ought to be purely miraculous and wonderful—that is, to everyone and for everyone. And such are those miracles whose causes are hidden from all, and therefore are those things that are done contrary to the order of nature, by the sole virtue and power of Almighty God. Therefore, those things that are done by natural causes, though hidden to many—as are often done by devils—are no true miracles. From this, therefore, we may conclude that whatever is performed in physical actions by natural causes (and it is the general tenet of all that devils in these cases can work nothing except by natural causes) are no miracles; and as they are agents, they are not evil, but only become so in their use and application.

By this particular standard, therefore, all those signs and wonders that are performed by devils are excluded from the name of true miracles, because they are all performed for evil ends, contrary to the glory of God, and for the deception and ruin of men. And therefore, all wonders performed by devils are called lies.

## CHAPTER XII.

### *If the Devil or witches have power to perform strange things, whether they do not bring them to pass by mere natural means, or otherwise. And of Helmont’s opinion concerning the effects caused by devils or witches.*

Having handled the knowledge and power of the fallen angels as far as anything is manifested in the Scriptures, or as may be deduced from them by sound reason, and finding their knowledge and power to be much less in these inferior bodies and elements than is commonly supposed, we are now to proceed to examine what they do simply by their own power, and what they perform by natural means. And first, it cannot be denied that they can, of themselves, dart evil thoughts, suggestions, and temptations into the minds of men immediately by their own power, as well as allure men to sin by the irritation of external objects presented to the senses, and also by means of the fantasy, and especially by the melancholy humor which is *Balneum Diaboli* <note>The devil’s bath</note>. But secondly, the great question is: what do they work in elemental and corporeal things, and whether it is not only by natural means—such as the applying of fit active agents to agreeable passive subjects, whereby the acts ascribed to them are performed—or not? We affirm this based on these grounds:

<margin>See Guttierez on *Fascination*, Doubt 5, page 125.</margin>
1. Because it is the common and unanimous opinion of philosophers, theologians, and physicians that what devils operate in sublunary <note>earthly</note> bodies, or in causing diseases in human bodies, is by the application of fit active agents to convenient passive subjects, by which the effects are brought to pass. And this is an argument sufficiently pressing and convincing, if there be any force in arguments brought from human authority, especially considering that no other causes besides what are natural could ever yet be assigned, much less proved.

2. And this is more plain if we consider what the author quoted last in the margin says to the same purpose: *A demon by his own power cannot transmute corporeal matter, unless he applies to it active agents proportioned to the effects he intends.* As for example, the devil may cause burning because there is a combustible subject, as well as a fiery and burning agent in nature; and this agent, being fire, when applied to combustible matter, would produce that effect which we call cremation or burning. # The Displaying of CHAP. XII.

Whatever effects Devils, or those called Witches, bring to pass in human bodies are wrought by natural means and proceed from natural causes. Because whatever diseases are cured by natural causes and agents must of necessity be introduced into human bodies by natural means. But many diseases attributed to the Devil, or Witches as instruments, have been cured by natural means and applications, as we shall prove both by authorities and matters of fact. And therefore those diseases must of necessity grow and arise from natural causes. And for authority we find *Helmont* affirming this much:

<margin>Injaculat. mod. intrand. p. 603, 604.</margin>
> "And also partly the curing of these diseases is to be had by certain <term>Simples</term> <note>medicinal herbs consisting of a single ingredient</note>, to which the omnipotent goodness has given a gift from the beginning of the Creation: of resisting, preventing, and correcting *Veneficia* <note>witchcrafts or poisonings</note>, and of bringing forth things injected. For (he says) certain Simples do drive away evil spirits (a miserable company of Men, who give worship to Gods that are not able to resist the natural efficacy of Simples) and lists some that take away the penetration of the formal light tied to the excrements. Some do hinder the touch, entrance, or application. And there are many such things that correct the poisons and kill them. And chiefly he commends the *Electrum minerale immaturum* of *Paracelsus*, the *Phu* of *Dioscorides*, being a kind of *Valerian* with purple flowers, and likewise mentions various others."

2. It would seem a point of strange skepticism or disbelief to distrust and reject these reports as lies and fictions, seeing that the authors who recount them mostly attest to them from their own observation or knowledge—or at least from unquestionable eyewitnesses—and that they were men of great reputation and credit who lived in several countries and in different times, and therefore could not have conspired in a lie.

<margin>*Observation 3.*</margin>
3. But notwithstanding all this, we find persons of great learning and sober judgment who use much hesitation about these things, and either suspend their belief in them (having never seen any such things themselves, and therefore may well conclude, as many wise men do, that he who has seen a thing may better believe it than he who has not), or else are utterly skeptical and believe no such matters of fact at all. And indeed, there is no greater folly than to be very inquisitive and industrious in finding out the causes of a phenomenon that never actually existed; therefore, men ought to be cautious and fully assured of the truth of the effect before they venture to explain the cause. And I find that both my Lord *Bacon* and that honorable and learned person Mr. *Boyle*, when they have occasion to mention these things, do so with extreme caution, and always with an "if" or some other sign of notable doubt; also the Lord *Montaigne* in his essays, and our countryman Mr. *Osborne* (no insignificant persons), in their writings seem utterly skeptical of any such matter.

5. If to this we add the consideration of how rare and seldom these things happen, and how long (though it argues only negatively) many physicians have practiced and yet have never met with any such strange accidents; and also that many of these vomitings of strange items and the like have been mere counterfeit jugglery and impostures, as was manifest in the Boy of *Bilson*, *Sommers* of *Nottingham*, and various others; besides, I who have practiced medicine for over forty years could never find any such thing in truth and reality, but have known many who have counterfeited these strange vomitings and the like, which we and others have plainly exposed and detected. So, though we shall not simply deny the truth of these accounts, we cannot but believe that some of them have been cheats and delusions, and others mere mistakes of ignorance and vain credulity; and in the belief of any of them, we ought to proceed with much caution and careful foresight.

3. The next thing that *Helmont* lays down (after he thinks that he has proved the facts sufficiently) is the assigning of the true cause (as he thinks) for bringing about these wondrous effects. And these he makes twofold: first, the Devil, by reason of his league with the witch, brings and conveys the things to be injected to the place, or near the object, and makes them invisible by his spiritual power; secondly, the witch, by the strength of her imagination and the motion of her free will (which he holds to be the only peculiar prerogative of mankind, remaining with both men and women after the fall—namely, a power by their free wills and force of imagination to create or frame seminal and efficacious Ideas to work as if <term>ad nutum</term> <note>at a command or whim</note>), conveys or injects these strange things into the bodies of those they would hurt or torment; and that in this case, as the ultimate attempt of nature, there is and may be a <term>penetration of dimensions</term>, and these things he attempts to prove in the following manner, which we shall first amply lay down and relate, and afterward we shall provide some notes and observations upon them, as matters of great weight and consideration.

This is because the spirit then encloses the body within itself, and therefore, as it were, removes its physical dimensions.
