Having thus traced his footsteps at length in these abstruse and mysterious matters, we shall now come to examine them and make some observations upon them. And although we may be sharply censured for taking it upon ourselves to question the things that he has asserted—having been, <term>suo gradu</term> (in his own rank), an Adept, a person of profound judgment, great experience, general learning, and high reputation, and now generally followed as the chief standard-bearer for Philosophy, Medicine, and Chemistry, so that many esteem it no small glory to be called and accounted a Helmontian—yet, notwithstanding this, we shall note some observations in this order.

<margin>Observ. 1.</margin>
1. He holds that the Devil only makes things invisible, or hides them by his spirit, and brings them near to the object into which they are to be injected, and that the Witch—by the seminal Idea of her imagination and the strength of her desire as the agent or efficient cause—does inject or thrust them into the body of the person intended to be hurt or tormented. By this, he necessarily supposes a league or contract between the Devil and the Witch, and therefore he calls them the Devil's clients and those who are bound to him. But what kind of contract this might be—explicit or implicit, internal and mental, or corporeal and visible—he does not tell us. We utterly deny the latter: that it is in the power of the Devil to practice it whenever he pleases, as we have before demonstrated at length with sufficient arguments. And as for an implicit or mental league, we grant that all thieves, murderers, these kinds of malicious and poisoning Witches, and all other wicked persons are bound in a spiritual contract to him; for he is the spirit that *works in the children of disobedience*. And whatever wickedness he has tempted and drawn them to be willing to commit, he prompts and pushes them on with all his skill and power to perform and execute the same. But still, this is to be understood only of his spiritual and invisible assistance, and not of any visible or corporeal aid; for otherwise (as this Author confesses), he might just as well kill with a knife or a mallet. And therefore, we cannot here pass by the bold and groundless (if not impious) assertion of <margin>*On Incantations, p. 677.*</margin> *Sennertus*, who, though a very learned person in various parts of human literature, yet drawn by the sway of popular opinion, did most miserably err by affirming that although Witches do purpose to hurt men, yet "they neither do nor can effect those things; but that while the Witches are cast into a profound sleep, the Devil in the meantime performs those things by himself." Now from this it is plain that this urinating constantly upon this pin of old black oak-wood caused his bloody strangury, and that the pulling of it up and burning it, with the help of the Birch-Ale, was the cure; but it can in no way be judged necessary that the Devil should fix the oak pin there, but that the witch might do it himself. Neither can it be thought to be any power given by the Devil to the oak pin that it did not have by nature, for in probability it will constantly produce the same effect by a natural power; only so far the Devil had a hand in the action: to draw some wicked person to fix the pin there where the man was accustomed to urinate, thereby to hurt and torture him, and so it was only evil in respect to the end result.

They are performed either by mere natural causes, or the strength of the witch's imagination and her most vehement desire to do mischief to those she hates, or by both joined together. In this, Satan is no further an author or actor than as he leads and draws the minds of the witches to perform such mischievous actions, and pushes them on to seek out and learn from others such secret poisons, charms, images, and other hidden things. When used in certain ways, these may produce the destructive ends to which their wicked and diabolical purposes are led; and in this sense, they are his clients and bounden vassals, and not otherwise.

<margin>Observation 4.</margin>
4. The stories that he relates are either all to be taken as true, or none of them; and if they are all alike equally to be credited, then it will undeniably follow that they were all alike produced by natural causes. Thus, there is no need at all for the Devil’s assistance in performing them, any more than by his working upon the minds of those who used those natural means for a wicked and mischievous end. For first, he gives these instances of very strange things that were voided either by vomit or stool through the ordinary power of nature, without suspicion of diabolical cooperation: such as the voiding of a piece of a brass cannon with its letters, along with an eel wrapped in its <term>secundines</term> <note>The fetal membranes or afterbirth.</note>; the "dragon" that the ox voided after taking three herbs, which had a tail like an eel, a body like or made of leather, a serpentine head, and was no smaller than a partridge; the knife that thieves forced a man to swallow, which he later voided through an <term>apostume</term> <note>An abscess or localized collection of pus; a tumor or swelling.</note> in his side and was afterward found; also the arrowhead three fingers broad struck into a back and later voided by stool, along with various others which we recited before.

And that these solid bodies should have penetrated and passed through parts that cannot tolerate wounds—and in which a wound is mortal—must of necessity be very wonderful. They might as easily and upon as rational grounds be taken to be diabolical as those he lists as being so. For from these examples, it is manifest that either nature, when pushed to her limit, makes a <term>penetration of dimensions</term> <note>A philosophical term for the movement of one solid body through another without displacing it or leaving a wound.</note>, or else so enlarges the pores that those solid bodies may pass without a wound; which (if seriously considered) is a stupendous operation and effect. And just as there is no need for the cooperation of a diabolical power to perform these, no more is there any need for the concurrence of Devils in the others that he relates for that purpose.

Only here is the entire difference: these are wrought by the ultimate endeavor of the <term>Archaeus</term> <note>A term from Paracelsian and Helmontian medicine referring to the vital force or internal "chemist" that governs the body's functions.</note> to save life, without the concurrence of external causes; the others (which are therefore called diabolical) are commonly wrought for a bad end—namely, to hurt or to take away life—and have an external cause: specifically, the force of the witch's imagination and strong desire to do mischief, which is stirred up to that end by Satan. Therefore, in regard to their purpose, they are devilish, though they are both wrought by the agency of nature—the one in the body of the person imagining, the other in the body that the witch intends to hurt by the force of her

<margin>Observation 5.</margin>
5. The arguments that he brings to prove that the "penetration of dimensions" exists in nature, or something equivalent to it, seem to be strong and convincing. For in the generation of things, whoever shall seriously and strictly observe will find (as he alleges) that the spirit of the <term>Archeus</term> <note>A vital principle or internal life force in Paracelsian medicine.</note> (though not altogether incorporeal) penetrates itself in the seeds of things, and their parts penetrate one another. He further supports this with the example of gold generated from water; for it must necessarily be that more than fifteen parts of water must fall into or penetrate one another so that one part of gold may be made from them. For weight does not come from nothing, but indicates that the matter is heavy in the balance. Therefore, water must naturally penetrate its own body as many times as the gold outweighs the water. And even if it is granted that water has pores, it still cannot contain as much as fourteen times its own volume. And therefore he undeniably concludes: *It is therefore common in nature for some parts of water to penetrate into a single place.* And he backs this with an undeniable story of a woman who, longing for mussels, greedily ate some of them with the shells broken two or three times by her teeth, and she gave birth to a child with those same half-eaten shells and a wound in its belly. Therefore, those shells had penetrated the stomach, womb, and <term>fecundines</term> <note>The fetal membranes or afterbirth.</note>, or otherwise the force of the *Archeus* had opened the pores and let them pass in an inconceivable manner. So, if these things are granted to be true (and we confess we do not know how they can be answered), then there is no need to introduce diabolical power to explain the injecting of strange things into men's bodies, since nature is sufficient in itself. Therefore, we can allow no power at all to devils in performing these things (if they are truly done and are not delusions), except in drawing the minds of the witches to these wicked and mischievous courses. Therefore, the Lord *Bacon* said profoundly

<margin>Sylva Sylvarum, Century 10, page 556.</margin>
and wisely these words: *Just as error must be avoided in those operations and their causes, so also the greatest care must be taken that the effects do not deceive us, by judging too hastily those things to be such as have not yet proceeded so far. Thus wise judges, as by a prescribed rule, do not want to believe the confessions of witches rashly, nor even the proof of facts against them. For a vertigo of the imagination disturbs witches, so that they think they do that which they do not do; and here credulity plays with the people, so that they attribute the works of nature to sorcery.*

# CHAP. XII. supposed Witchcraft.

Also, another woman going to see the decapitation of thirteen men did soon after give birth to a full-term child with a bloody neck, the head appearing nowhere. I confess it would stretch the judgment even of the most credulous to the highest pitch to believe these unparalleled stories; but the author relating them as being of his own knowledge, and being a person of unquestionable truthfulness, I cannot conceive how they can rationally be denied, especially finding Mr. *Boyle* to affirm that in those experiments (and even more so in accounts of matters of fact) that *Helmont* vouched for upon his own knowledge, he dared to be his <term>compurgator</term> <note>A character witness or someone who swears to the truthfulness of another's testimony.</note>. Who would not believe that these things could never have been done except by a supernatural and diabolical power? But this author (to whom all judicious persons may reasonably adhere) utterly denies that the arm was either pulled away or conveyed to an unknown place by Satan. Therefore, in such a strange paradox, trivial reasons are not to be allowed; and it would be too much laziness to ascribe all effects to Satan of which we are ignorant. 

And therefore, if a hand, an arm, or even a whole head could be separated from the rest of the body and carried out of the womb by the <term>Archeus</term> <note>Written as "Archent" in the original text; refers to the vital principle or natural spirit in Paracelsian medicine.</note> or natural spirit, excited by the impression of horror and terror in the women: in the same way, by the same power of the natural spirit of man or woman, excited by a vehement and fierce imagination for revenge and to do mischief, strange things may be injected (if there can be any solid proof of such a matter of fact) into the bodies of such men or women as the witches intend to hurt. And yet Satan has no more hand in it, but only as a spiritual agent to move the wills of those wicked and malicious people to do mischief to those that they hate, even without cause. 

And the great secret of that which may be called *witchcraft* is the learning from others, who likewise have received it by tradition, the great force of imagination and the natural spirit, along with the ways and means of how to excite it and elevate it; herein stands the mystery of all *magic*, and it becomes evil only in its use and application. They are to be condemned who use it for such devilish ends, just as those are who use the good creatures that nature produces for poisonous, wicked, and destructive purposes. <margin>Observ. 7.</margin>
7. The other matters of fact that he relates are extraordinary, and are brought to prove that Satan is an actor who conveys these strange things into the bodies of men; they are as follows: A piece of an ox hide taken out of a man's arm; likewise an *Equuleum* <note>Latin for "little horse"; here referring to a wooden frame or rack-like object.</note>, a wood-horse, or a four-footed board with a wheel and ropes twice as broad as the gullet. Another person vomited up perhaps two thousand pins clumped together with filth and hair; another—while he was present—vomited up wooden chips that had been cut off with a hatchet in the smoothing of wood, along with much slime to the size of two fists. Regarding these, we shall note these conclusions: 1. It does not appear in any way (if these things are granted to be true, both in matter and manner), nor does he offer to prove it, that these are any more diabolical than the former cases, except ultimately because they result in the harm and destruction of mankind and not otherwise. Since there is no proof of the Devil’s cooperation further than working upon the minds of those who are agents and instruments to bring these things to pass, we may very well reject those things that are supposed but not proven. 2. The ejecting or expelling of such strange things as he has related here does not necessarily imply their "injection" or thrusting in, because they may be developed there by natural causes. Thus, worms of many sorts and strange shapes, as well as frogs, <term>Dracunculi</term> <note>Small parasitic worms, often guinea worms.</note> and <term>Askers</term> <note>A regional term for newts or small lizards.</note> have been expelled, and undoubtedly developed there through natural causes, and were not injected or thrust in. For proof of this, I refer the reader to the accounts of the learned *Schenchius* (book 3, page 363) regarding those strange sorts of worms and other creatures that he shows, from various authors, have been vomited up, which without any doubt were not injected but developed there. It does not appear that *Helmont* was present at the very instant when the children vomited up the wooden horse or four-footed board, but rather that it was the bystanders who drew it forth, who might have been parties to the cheat or were themselves deluded and so persistently asserted it to others.

For I have in my practice known a young girl about nine or ten years old who—so that she might be pitied and have a life of idleness—had made her father and mother believe that live worms came out of her ear. However, by diligent watching, she was found to get them privately from under stones or wood and so cunningly conveyed them into her hair; but once discovered, she was reformed by due correction, and so the wonder ceased. 8. ### CHAP. XIII.

*That the ignorance of the power of Art and Nature and such like things, has much advanced these foolish and impious opinions.*

THE opinions that we reject as foolish and impious are those we have often named before, namely, that those who are commonly accounted Witches make a visible and physical contract with the Devil, that he sucks upon their bodies, that he has carnal copulation with them, that they are transformed into Cats, Dogs, Squirrels, and the like, or that they raise tempests and fly in the air. Other powers we grant to them: to operate and effect whatever the force of natural imagination—joined with envy, malice, and a vehement desire for revenge—can perform or commit, or whatever harm may be done by secret poisons and similar ways that work by purely natural means.

And here we are to show the chief causes that do and have advanced these opinions, and this we principally attribute to men's ignorance of the power of Nature and Art, as we shall demonstrate in the following particulars.

1. There is nothing more certain than that, however great the knowledge of Men is taken to be, the ultimate sphere of nature's activity or ability is not perfectly known. This is made most manifest in the fact that every day new discoveries of her secrets are made, which prove plainly that her store is not yet totally exhausted, nor her utmost efficiency known. And therefore those Men must necessarily be hasty, and build upon a sandy foundation, who would attribute physical effects to Devils while not yet knowing the extent of nature; for no Man can rationally assign a beginning for supernatural agents and actions who does not certainly know where the power and operation of nature ends.

2. And as it is thus in general, so it is in many particulars—especially in being ignorant of many natural agents that work at a great distance and very hiddenly, both to help and to hurt, as in <term>the weapon salve</term>, <term>the Sympathetic powder</term>, the curing of diseases by <term>mumial applications</term>, by <term>Amulets</term>, <term>Appensions</term> <note>items hung upon the body for medicinal or magical purposes</note> and <term>Transplantations</term> <note>the practice of attempting to transfer a disease from a person to a plant or animal</note>, which all have been, and commonly are, attributed to Satan, when they are truly wrought by natural operations. And so (as we have sufficiently shown before) by many strange and secret poisons, both natural and artificial, which have no bewitching power in them at all, but work naturally; they may only be harmful in their use through the wickedness of some persons who use them for various evil ends.

3. There is nothing that does more clearly demonstrate our limited

They ascribe the performance of it by *Paracelsus*, *Lullius*, *Sendivogius*, and others to the Devil; so malevolent do men become when they are led by lack of knowledge and ignorance.

5. The ignorance of the strange and wonderful things that Art can bring to pass has been no less a cause why the most admirable things that Art brings to pass are, through blind ignorance, ascribed to Devils. For in this way, many brave, learned artists and mechanics have been accused of being conjurers, as happened to *Roger Bacon*, *Dr. Dee*, *Trithemius*, *Cornelius Agrippa*, and many others, when what they performed was by lawful and commendable art. The strange things that Mathematics and Mechanics can perform are hardly to be enumerated. Johannes Ernestus Burgravius, in his work called *Biolychnium, or concerning the Lamp of Life and Death*, as cited by Marcellus Vranckheim, Doctor of both laws, as also in reading that profound and mysterious piece written by *Roger Bacon*, *On the Admirable Power of Art and Nature, and the Nullity of Magic*, with the learned notes of *Dr. Dee* upon it, says this: *So that it may be seen that all magical power is inferior to these works and unworthy.* And therefore there can be nothing more unworthy than for any man, who claims any portion of reason, to be so foolish or to allow himself to be led by ignorance and rashness as to attribute those strange things that Nature and Art, or both joined together, produce to Devils. And yet nothing is more common, not only among the uneducated masses, but even among those who would otherwise be considered learned and wise enough; pride and folly attend most of the sons of men.

6. There is another gross mistake in assuming that those strange things performed by vaulters, tumblers, rope dancers, and the like, are not possible to be done except by the assistance of the Devil, when they are entirely brought to pass and achieved through use, custom, exercise, and the nimbleness and agility of the body. And yet we have known some, not only of the common sort, but many who thought themselves wise, learned, and religious, who have been so blind as to attribute these things to Devils, and to seriously seem to believe that the performers of these things had made a league and compact with the Devil, by whose help they performed them. And I remember that a quite active young man, within these last few years, traveled around this Northern Country with a fine Bay Mare, showing tricks for money. These were very odd and strange; for if she had been blindfolded, and several pieces of money were taken from different persons and wrapped in a cloth, the mare would give everyone back their own piece of money. This and many other feats she performed were judged—not only by the common people, but by others who should have been wiser—to be performed by no other means but by the Devil. Some were even so stark mad as to believe and claim that the mare was not a natural one, but that it was the Devil performing those strange tricks in the shape of a mare, when more sober judgments knew that they were performed by the master’s eye and rod directing the mare.

<margin>Error and credulity have great power over men.</margin>

8. The ignorance or misunderstanding of these things, joined with the notions men have imbibed from their infancy, together with irreligious education, are the true and proper causes that make so many ascribe that power to Devils and Witches which they neither have, nor ever had, nor can ever bring into action. And therefore it behooves all who would judge rightly of these abstruse matters to labor to understand the secret operations of nature and the strange works of art, to divest themselves of their false, imbibed notions, and truly and rightly to understand the Articles of the Christian Faith, and to be daily conversant in reading the Scriptures; they will then be more fit to judge of these things, and not to call light darkness, nor darkness light.

## CHAPTER XIV.

*Of various <term>impostures</term> framed and invented to prove false and lying miracles by, and to accuse persons of <term>witchcraft</term>, from late and undeniable authorities.*

In the preceding treatise we have often made mention of delusions and <term>impostures</term>, which we shall handle at length in this place: and though Mr. *Glanvil* and others do object that, even if many pretended possessions or <term>witchcrafts</term> have been proved to be mere cozenings and impostures, it does not therefore follow that all are so. To which we shall provide these answers.

1. If it does not necessarily conclude that they are all impostures, yet it gives a very strong cause for <term>dubitation</term> that they may be so. And the objection does not depend upon a necessary connection between the subject and predicate; for some being direct and palpable impostures, it is not by necessity, but by contingency or accident that the others are not so, and they ought first to have been proved, which has never yet been performed.

2. But we affirm that a general conclusion drawn from an inductive argument is good and sound where no instance can be clearly made out to the contrary. But as yet no true instance, really and faithfully attested, has ever been brought to prove that any

# CHAP. XIV. *Supposed Witchcraft.*

None of these things that we deny were ever performed by diabolical power. For who was ever present—being a person of sincerity and sound judgment—who could truly testify and assert that the Devil, in a visible and physical shape, made a contract with a witch? Or that he sucked upon his or her body? Or that he had sexual intercourse with them? Or who saw when a witch was actually changed into a dog or a cat, or saw them fly or be carried through the air? Since no instance can be given to prove any of these to be undoubted truths, it must necessarily follow that they are mere fictions, or at best nothing but absolute impostures. And again, it is merely unsupported, and a *<term>petitio principii</term>* <note>begging of the question</note>, to imagine that any persons who have vomited up or passed strange objects saw or knew that they were put there by devils; for those objects were either naturally produced there, or else were mere impostures and delusive juggling tricks.

And therefore we shall propose some histories of strange and extraordinary frauds and impostures from recent and unquestionable authorities, by which all the rest may be judged and discerned; of which, take this for one.

Her false and feigned miracles, and the subtle and clever schemes that were brought to pass by the help of her fellow accomplices, and her and the others' public confession of them, may be found at length in *Holinshed*, *Stow*, and the writings of <margin>See the Chronicles of Holinshed; Stow, Year 25 of Henry VIII, page 1013.</margin> Mr. *Lambarde*, to which I refer my reader for brevity's sake; I shall only provide the account here in the words of Speed, which are these: The Romanists (he says), fearing greatly that *Babel* would fall <margin>The Pope.</margin> if Queen *Anne* might be heard against wicked Haman, sought to shore up its foundations with certain devices of their own. <margin>Observation 1.</margin>
1. We may from here note how subject human nature is both to deceive and to be deceived, and that not only the common people, but also the wiser and more learned minds may most easily be imposed upon. And, therefore, in things of this nature and the like, we cannot use too much circumspection, nor use too much diligence to discover them.

<margin>Observation 2.</margin>
2. We may note that when such strange impostures or false miracles are pretended, there is commonly some sinister and corrupt end aimed at under the guise of religion; and those who are most ready to publish such things as true miracles and divine revelations are generally those who plotted and devised them. Therefore, the greater the number of those who praise them, and the higher the reputation of the people who spread such things, the greater suspicion we ought to have of their falsehood and forgery. We should always remember that the greater the fame and number of the people who conspire and confederate together, the greater the things they may accomplish and the more they may be able to deceive, as was manifest by the priests attending the oracles; who, though they labored to attribute their predictions to some deity, yet it was manifest that it was nothing else but their own conspiracy, impostures, and trickery.

Upon this, I went to the house where he was to stay for the night, where I found him and two very suspicious-looking persons who conducted him and managed the business. I desired to have some conversation with the boy in private, but they utterly refused. Then, in the presence of a great many people, I took the boy near me and said, "Good boy, tell me truly and in earnest: did you see and hear such strange things of the meeting of witches as is reported by many and as you relate, or did someone teach you to say such things yourself?" 

But the two men, not giving the boy leave to answer, pulled him away from me and said he had been examined by two capable Justices of the Peace, and they had never asked him such a question; to whom I replied that the accused persons had therefore suffered all the more wrong. 

But at the following Assizes at *Lancaster*, seventeen were found guilty by the jury; yet, by the prudent discretion of the judge, who was not satisfied with the evidence, they were reprieved. His Majesty and his Council being informed by the judge of the matter, the Bishop of *Chester* was appointed to examine them and to certify what he thought of them, which he did. Thereupon four of them—namely *Margaret Johnson*, *Francis Dicconson*, *Mary Spenser*, and *Hargrave's Wife*—were sent for to *London* and were viewed and examined by His Majesty’s physicians and surgeons <note>originally "Chirurgeons"</note>, and afterward by His Majesty and the Council. No cause of guilt appeared, but there were great suspicions that the boy had been suborned <note>bribed or unlawfully persuaded to commit perjury</note> to accuse them falsely. Therefore, it was resolved to separate the boy from his father; since they had both followed the women up to *London*, they were both taken and put into separate prisons. Shortly thereafter, the boy confessed that he was taught and suborned to devise and feign those things against them, and had persevered in that wickedness by the advice of his father and some others, whom envy, revenge, and hope of gain had prompted toward that devilish design.

Thus, having brought these unquestionable histories to demonstrate the horrid cheats and impostures practiced for base, wicked, and devilish ends, we must conclude by opposing that objection proposed at the beginning of this chapter, which is this: That though some cases are discovered to be counterfeits and impostures, not all are so. To this we further answer:

<margin>Reason 1.</margin>
1. That all those things nowadays supposed to be done by demoniacs or those who pretend to be possessed, as well as all those strange feats claimed to be brought about by witches or witchcraft, are all performed either by purely natural causes (for it is granted on all sides that devils in physical matter can perform nothing except by applying suitable active agents to compatible passive subjects). And since miracles ceased long ago, it must follow that devils do nothing but draw the minds of men and women toward sin and wickedness, and thereby they become deceivers, cheats, and notorious impostors. So, we may rationally conclude that all other strange feats and delusions must necessarily be no better, or of any other kind, than those we have recited, unless they can show that they are brought about by natural means. Must not all persons of sound understanding judge and believe that all those strange tricks related by Mr. *Glanvil* regarding his drummer at Mr. *Mompesson’s* house—whom he calls the Demon of *Tedworth*—were abominable cheats and impostures (as I am informed by persons of high standing they were discovered to be)? For I am sure Mr. *Glanvil* can show no agents in nature that the demon, applying them to suitable subjects, could produce any such effects by; and therefore, we must conclude all such cases to be impostures.

<margin>Reason 2.</margin>
2. It is not a sound way of reasoning to use the principles of knowing either to prove the existence of things or the modes of such existence, because the principle of being is the cause of the principle of knowing, and not the other way around. Therefore, our failure to discover all impostures that are or have been acted does not at all prove that the rest which pass undiscovered are diabolical or wrought by a supernatural power. For it ought first to be demonstrated that there are nowadays things wrought by the power of devils that are supernatural, in elementary and physical matter—which never was nor can be the case, as we have shown before from the testimonies of all the learned. And therefore, a man might as well argue that there are no more thieves in a nation than those who are known and brought to deserved

### CHAP. XV.

->*Of various creatures that have a real existence in Nature, and yet by reason of their wondrous properties, or seldom being seen, have been taken for spirits and devils.*<-

Before we come to speak of apparitions in general, we shall premise a few things by way of caution, because there is not one subject (that we know of) in the world that is liable to so many mistakes, due to the preconceived fancies of men in adhering to those fictions of spirits, fairies, hobgoblins, and many such like, which are continually heightened by ignorant education and vain melancholy fears. We shall not mention those many apparitions that are frequently practiced through forgery and conspiracy for base ends and interests, as were commonly used in the time of Popery, and attempted in our days, though with little success. Also by other persons for base profit or worse intentions, of which we have known some notorious ones that have been discovered. <margin>History 1.</margin> Neither shall we speak of those feigned ones that have been practiced to hide thievery and roguery, as we once knew that certain persons who stole men's sheep in the night carried them away upon a thing made like a bier covered with a white sheet. By this means, those who saw them took it to be an apparition, and so dared not come near them, and thus the majority of the people of three or four villages were terrified, and the report was far spread that it was a walking spirit; and yet it was at last discovered to be a cunning piece of knavery to hide their theft withal. Neither shall we say anything of those ludicrous apparitions that are often practiced to terrify, abuse, and affright others. But we shall here give the account of some strange creatures that, being seldom seen or found, have induced more ignorant persons to take them for demons, and these we shall list in this order.

<margin>History 2.</margin> 1. It has been, and still is, a strong opinion among the common people and witch-mongers also, that witches, transforming themselves into various shapes, entered into people's houses in the night time and then and there sucked the breasts or navels of infants in their beds or cradles, so that they were weakened or consumed away. This inveterate opinion was the more firmly believed because children who were very well at night were in the morning...

Rather, these idols were made in the figure or shape of satyrs or hairy creatures, as the text says: *And he ordained for himself priests for the high places, and for the hairy idols (or satyrs), and for the calves that he had made.* It is the same Hebrew word here that our English translators render as "devils" that in the two former places of *Isaiah* they translate as "satyrs"; and as the calves are not rendered as "devils," why should the images that were like satyrs be translated so? Surely the devil was as much in the calves, and as much worshipped in those dumb idols, as he was in the dumb and dead idols or images of the satyrs, and so there is no more reason to call one "devils" than the other. But that which totally overthrows the idea that they were real devils in physical shapes and figures is this: both the calves and the images of these satyrs were made by *Jeroboam*. Now, it is manifest that he could not make a real devil, but only images of calves and satyrs, in which and by which the devils might be worshipped in those idolatrous ways.

### CHAP. XV. Supposed Witchcraft.

4. There has been no less a mistake regarding those fishes that are called *Tritons*, *Sirens*, mermaids, or mermen and merwomen, which have been supposed and taken by many to be spirits or demons, and commonly nymphs, when in deed and truth they are real creatures, as these examples make manifest.

It is little more than a fable that they believed they imitated the voices of men and women. But that there are beasts found in the sea with human faces (he says), I shall not deny. However, I will not (he says) list the accounts of the ancients, for they are full of stories about mermaids. Among more recent authors, these have handled this topic here and there: *Scaliger* (*in book 2, History of Animals, t. 108*), *Rondoletius*, *Licetus* (*on spontaneous life*), *Marcus Marci* (*on Ideas*), and *P. Boistuan* (*History of France, Vol. 1, ch. 18*). “At *Enkhuizen* in *Holland* (he says) the image of a certain mermaid is to be seen painted, which had formerly been cast upon the shore by the force of the waters. It is (he says) commonly said among our common folk that a mermaid was caught in Denmark that spoke, foretold things to come, and could spin. A Father of the Society of *Jesus*, returning back from *India* to *Rome*, had seen a merman there wearing a bishop’s miter, who seemed to have barely endured his captivity in his corner; but being set loose and returned to the sea, he seemed to give thanks for his liberty by bowing his body before he went under water. This (he says) the Jesuit used to tell to *Corvinus* the elder, as his son (he says) told me at *Rome*.” But this being only a story told to Bartholinus second-hand, and originally from the mouth of a Jesuit (who doubtless had some motive for it), I leave it to the judgment of the wise and prudent. But he proceeds thus: “It is (he says) most certain that fishes are to be found in the ocean that resemble land animals in shape: such as the Sea-Fox, the Wolf, the Sea-Calf <note>A seal.</note>, the Dog, the Horse, etc. Therefore, why should we deny a human shape to sea monsters? Certainly, on the earth there are apes which, though lacking reason, display the external shape and gestures of man. “All sea monsters of this sort we classify (he says) as types of *phocae* or seals. The head and the breast as far as the navel were of human shape, but from the navel even to the lower limbs, it was deformed flesh, without any sign of a tail. But so that I may not (he

The hand does consist of five fingers, as ours do, with as many articulations as ours, but only this is unique: all the bones of the fingers are broader and compressed, and a membrane joins them together in sequence, as in birds like geese, ducks, etc., which help to stretch forth the foot in the water. The extremities of the two middle fingers are broader, the extremities of the other two sharp. The *radius* and *cubit* <note>The ulna.</note> are very short, for the convenience of swimming, scarcely the length of four fingers' breadth. Neither is the shape of the shoulder any larger. The ribs are long and thick, almost exceeding common human ribs by a third.

And that their breasts being pressed do send forth very white milk."

We have (he says) the hands to be seen with eyes, and we show the mermaids to be such as in truth they are seen to be. Neither do the hands and ribs deceive, whose pictures we have provided, drawn according to the truth of nature."

### CHAPTER XVI.

->*Of Apparitions in general, and of some unquestionable stories*<-
->*that seem to prove such things. Of those apparitions*<-
->*claimed to be made in Beryls and Crystals, and of the*<-
->*Astral or Sidereal Spirit.*<-

IN this treatise we have before sufficiently proved that the denying of the existence of such a witch as does make a visible contract with the Devil, or upon whose body he sucks, or that has carnal copulation with a demon, and that is transubstantiated into a cat or a dog, or that flies in the air, does not infer the denial of spirits, either good or bad, nor utterly overthrow the truth of apparitions, or of such things as seem to manifest some supernatural operations. And therefore here we shall fully handle the question of Apparitions, and things that seem to be of that nature, and that in this order:

1. We shall not deal with Apparitions in the large extent of the word, for so it may comprehend the appearing of new stars, comets, meteors and other portents and prodigies, which (though unusual and wondrous) have yet their production from natural causes. But only here we shall treat of such apparitions as are taken to be performed by supernatural creatures, or in such a way and by such creatures as we commonly account to be different from (if not above) the power of ordinary and visible nature—as of angels good or bad, the souls of men departed, or their <term>Astral Spirits</term>, or of some other creatures that are, or may be, of a middle nature.

2. As for the apparitions of good angels sent by God in times past, both in sleep and otherwise, the Scriptures do give us most full and ample assurance, as these few instances may undeniably demonstrate.

<margin>Judg. 13.</margin>
1. That an *Angel of the Lord* (that is, a good angel) did appear visibly unto *Manoah* and his wife, and did vocally and audibly talk and discourse with them both, and did after in both their sights openly and visibly ascend in the *flame that did arise from the altar.* Now a more plain and indubitable apparition visibly seen and audibly heard than this cannot be found nor read of, having the unquestionable authority of Sacred Writ to vouch for it.

<margin>Luke 2. 26. to 39.</margin>
2. Another parallel unto it, and of equal authority, truth, and clarity, is the sending of the Angel *Gabriel* unto the Virgin *Mary*; her seeing of him, hearing of his salutation, having discourse with him, and seeing his departure—both of which are undoubted testimonies of the true and real appearance of good angels even to sight and hearing.

3. That sometimes the good angels have been sent to the servants of God, and have appeared and spoken unto them in dreams; as when the *Angel of the Lord appeared unto Joseph*

3. Of the visible apparition of evil angels, we have almost no evidence at all in the Scriptures, unless we take suppositions for proofs, or disputable passages to be certain demonstrations, or twist and pull the Word of God to make it serve our preconceived opinions. For I do not find any single place in all the Scriptures where any apparition of evil spirits is plainly and positively recorded, or where such a visible appearance can be proved or deduced by any rational and necessary consequence. For we have clearly proved that the tempting of *Eve* by the Serpent does not necessarily imply that it was by a visible apparition, but rather by a mental delusion; and that the case of *Saul* and the Woman of *Endor* (or the Mistress of the bottle <note>A literal translation of the Hebrew 'ob', referring to a medium with a familiar spirit</note>) was neither *Samuel* in soul and body, nor his soul alone, nor the Devil in his shape—which we believe we have proved beyond doubt. We have also shown that the tempting of our blessed *Saviour* by *Satan* was internal, or at least the greatest part of it; so that there remains very little certain proof of the apparition of devils in that gross manner, and so common and frequent as many too stubbornly affirm. Yet, for all this, we think it rational to grant that, just as God has in times past often sent messages by good Angels for the teaching, counseling, and comforting of his servants, to be perceived both audibly and visibly; so also God might sometimes not only send evil spirits internally and mentally to deceive and seduce the wicked (as in the case of the lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab's prophets), but also to appear visibly to terrify, punish, and destroy the wicked, or to make way for the manifestation of his glory. And the Scriptures that mention *demoniacs*, and those who are commonly said to be possessed (though that was not by an essential indwelling, but by an effective operation upon both the souls and bodies of the persons so affected and afflicted), plainly show that the operative effects of the Devil's power were both heard and seen through their words and actions.

For we are only inquiring here after such appearances of Devils that necessarily imply their presence by operating in and upon creatures or physical matter, so that by sight, hearing, or other senses, it may be certainly manifest that they work above the ordinary power of nature. 4. But though it is granted ever so freely and fully that in the ages and times mentioned in the Old and New Testament (and perhaps for a century or more after) there were persons who were possessed and afflicted by Devils, and also that many miracles were performed during that time; yet now it will be said that miracles have totally ceased, as they are not in any way necessary to confirm the Gospel, which is now established and settled. We confess that this is so strongly and convincingly proved by the Divines of the reformed Churches that we consider anyone who opposes it to be willfully blind. Yet, despite the fact that miracles have totally ceased, I grant that some strange things have happened in recent ages, and some in our own time, that cannot be solved in any way by mere ordinary natural causes, and appearances made by some kind of creatures that must be derived from such causes as those of good or bad Spirits, or from creatures of a similar nature. And although miracles have ceased, it does not therefore follow that everything that has a cause above or differing from the usual and ordinary course of nature must also have ceased; for *quanquam nunc non sint miracula, possint tamen esse miranda* <note>Although there are no miracles now, there may still be wonders</note>; and though miracles have ceased, it does not follow that apparitions have as well, because apparitions are not miracles. For a good Angel to be sent and to appear cannot be said to be a miracle, because it is the purpose for which he was created; they (that is the Angels) *are all ministering spirits sent forth for the good of those who shall be heirs of Salvation.* And the same can be said of evil Angels or any other creatures that may make these apparitions; for as they are and must be creatures, so there are and must be certain purposes for which they were created and are employed.

5. But to prove the truth of apparitions, or other strange phenomena equivalent to them, as having been truly performed as matters of fact, is extremely difficult and almost impossible. This is because the histories and accounts of things of this nature are strangely fabulous, and therefore are by no means to be relied upon, as will most

<header>CHAP. XV. *supposed Witchcraft.*</header>

<meta>catchword: 6. But; pencil mark "10" at bottom left</meta>

...manifestly appear through undeniable reasons, if we examine them in distinct parts in this order:

1. The histories and accounts that are given either by the poets or most of the ancient philosophers regarding these things are so seemingly impossible, and so extremely fictitious, that a person must necessarily have almost totally abandoned his own reason to give any credit at all to them. And especially they are so filled with the horrible fables of the numerousness of their feigned gods, demigods, spirits, hobgoblins, *Lares*, *Lemures*, men's shadows and the like, that they would make a man believe that the world was full of nothing else; and this was chiefly done to uphold their idolatrous and superstitious religion. And all these kinds of authors that have written from the time of *Homer* until the end of the ages in which the two *Plinies* and *Plutarch* lived, have followed the same course, all their accounts tainted with the influence of impossibilities, superstition, and fabulousness.

2. And if we look into the Papal writers, especially those who have recorded stories of this nature since the sixth century, we shall find such a collection and heap of boastful lies and invented fables of both apparitions and witches, that no rational man can well give assent to one in a thousand of them; they seem so incredible that they would rather make a wise man distrustful of all such matters of fact than to yield credit to any. And a man might as reasonably believe the forged and lying miracles of *Mahomet*, as those monkish fables. For the extreme desire that those authors had to advance their false and feigned doctrine of Purgatory—and thereby to uphold the gain and benefit that was gotten by imposing such penances and charitable deeds to redeem souls from there—drove them to invent thousands of false stories of the apparitions of souls after death, which had not one bit of truth in them at all.

3. Those who are called the Reformed Divines (because they returned to that pure and true doctrine and worship that had been settled and practiced in those previous ages that were truly Catholic and Apostolic), being altogether intent upon the main and principal points of the Faith, and those that concerned the true worship of God, took little heed of matters of this nature, as they were more circumstantial and therefore not accounted by them to be so essential and necessary. From this it came to pass that *Lambertus Danaeus*, *Hemmingius*, *Erastus* and others, did without due examination and caution receive the opinions and stories of the Papists indiscriminately. From this (I conceive) it came to pass that *Ludovicus Lavaterus*, a learned Divine of the reformed religion at *Zurich*, wrote a book of apparitions and such matters, but brought no other proofs of the truth of these things *in fact*, but the often-repeated stories of heathen authors, and some few from ecclesiastical authors who are of dubious credit, but not any from his own knowledge.

He notes that early Protestant reformers often accepted these stories without enough scrutiny because they were focused on more central theological issues.</summary>

6. But if we come to consider the recent histories that are reported concerning apparitions and similar things—which must necessarily contain something that resembles a supernatural cause—we may in part receive more ample satisfaction, which will be manifest in these few following particulars.

1. *Meric Casaubon*, Doctor of Divinity, in his treatise of *Credulity and Incredulity* (which we have quoted previously), has strongly endeavored to justify all those impossible and absurd things that are ascribed to witches. Though he has pitifully failed to do so, he has said enough to prove that there are many strange things that seem to prove the existence of demons or spirits, even though he has not brought forward any story from his own knowledge or that occurred in his own time. We have shown before that apparitions are no certain ground for Christians to believe in the existence of demons; only the word of God is. But in his preface to the account concerning Dr. *Dee*, he relates two stories told by that venerable and learned prelate, Bishop *Andrewes*, to his father, *Isaac Casaubon*.

> The one (he says) concerned a noted—or at least by many suspected—witch or sorceress, whom the Devil in a strange shape waited upon (or rather waited for) at her death. The other concerned a man who, after his death, was restored to life to make a confession of a horrible murder committed upon his own wife, for which he had never been suspected. And both of these (he says) that learned Bishop believed to be true; indeed, for one of them—the apparition—it seems he spoke from his own knowledge, and the other he had from an eyewitness.

And considering the status of Bishop *Andrewes* for both learning and piety, these accounts carry much weight, and they may be seen at length in the previously cited preface.

2. I cannot help but wonder that Dr. *Henry Moore*, a grave person and one who for many years has resided in a most learned and flourishing Academy, whose name is well-known both at home and abroad, having published so many books, should make such a bad choice of authors from whom he takes his stories, or that he should settle upon those that seem so fabulous, impossible, <margin>*Antidote against Atheism, ch. 8, 9, p. 209.*</margin> and incredible. So that I may not seem to accuse him without cause, I desire the reader to perusal his two accounts: the one of the shoemaker of *Breslaw* in *Silesia* in the year 1591, and the other of *Johannes Cuntius*, a citizen of *Pentsh* in *Silesia*, and to say whether he can rationally believe those things either to have been true or possible. As for the author, *Martinus Weinrichius*, a *Silesian* physician, I cannot find anything regarding his reputation or writings, and it is most strange that he should be omitted by that diligent and impartial author *Melchior Adam*. There were far better authors of more credit to have chosen for such stories than either *Bodin* or *Remigius*; neither can much credit be given to any of the stories he relates, except for the one

“ knew where he was. Thereupon, a public search was made for him in all the pits around the area, lest he should have accidentally fallen into any of them. One *Thomas Haworth* of the said town, a yeoman, was for many nights together much troubled with broken sleep and dreams of the murder; he revealed his dreams to his wife, but she worked to conceal them for a long time. One day he went into the house to ask for him, and there was a neighbor who said to *Thomas Haworth*, 'It is said that *Waters* lies under this stone,' (pointing to the hearthstone) to which *Thomas Haworth* replied, 'And I have dreamed that he is under a stone not far away.' The constable of the town, whose name was *Myles Aspinall*, happened to be in the house and urged *Thomas Haworth* to make known in more detail what he had dreamed, which he related thus: 'I have,' said he, 'many a time within these eight weeks (for that was how long it had been since the murder) dreamed very restlessly that *Waters* was murdered and buried under a broad stone in the cow-house; I have told my troubled dreams to my wife alone, but she refuses to let me make it known. But I am not able to conceal my dreams any longer; my sleep departs from me, and I am pressed and troubled with fearful dreams which I cannot bear any longer, and they increase upon me.' The constable, hearing this, made a search immediately and found, just as he had dreamed, the murdered body buried for eight weeks under a flat stone in the cow-house. *Ribchester* and *Gyles Haworth* fled and never returned. *Anne Waters* (for that was the name of *Waters’s* wife), being apprehended, confessed to the murder and was burned. From this, we may observe the following:

<margin>Observation</margin>
1. That this is the full and precise account of this bloody and detestable murder from *Haworth’s* wife (who was then a very old woman) and the son, and it does not differ at all from what Sir *Richard Baker* writes, except they say his brains were dashed out with an axe, while he says he was strangled. This is only a detail of the manner of it, but in the substance they both agree: that it was a certain truth that *Waters* was murdered, and Sir *Richard Baker’s* information might have failed in that particular detail of the method. And if it is thought strange that the two little children knew nothing of it, it is certain that they were much too young; it was said that they were twins, not more than half a year old. But the only reason we have brought this up is for the extraordinary way of its discovery through *Thomas Haworth’s* dreaming, a point in which both accounts closely agree, and which was the chief and only reason why Sir *Richard Baker* included it in his Chronicle. And *Stow* has also recorded the same in more detail in his Chronicle. Now, what should the cause be that *Thomas Haworth* should be hindered from sleep and have restless dreams, and that his dream should hit so precisely upon the place where he was buried, more than any other person in the same town?

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and theological analysis of the discovery of Mr. Waters' body through Thomas Haworth's dreams, rejecting naturalistic or demonic explanations in favor of divine intervention, before beginning a new account of a murder in Yorkshire.</meta>

<header>C H A P. XVI. *supposed Witchcraft.*</header>

Certainly, it cannot be attributed to fortune or chance, for they have no causality at all and are only names that we impose upon certain effects and accidents: *Te facimus fortuna Deum, cæloq; locamus* <note>We make you, Fortune, a goddess and place you in heaven</note>, as the Poet said. Neither can it rationally be thought to be melancholy because, although it is a subtle humor and renders those who are affected by it very imaginative and thoughtful, yet even if we suppose *Thomas Haworth* were of that temperament and disposition, it might make him think and meditate more deeply upon the rumor of *Waters* being missing or upon the suspicion of his murder, but it could not inform him in dreams to know precisely the place where he was buried. And if some should imagine it to be the soul of the murdered person *Waters*, as a Papist <note>Catholic</note> would doubtless be ready to affirm, yet that opinion is directly contrary to the Scriptures and is sufficiently refuted by the reformed theologians. And if it should be attributed to the operation of the astral or sidereal spirit, that is an opinion embraced by only a few and is hard to prove as a certain truth, of which we shall speak at length shortly. Neither can it by any sound reason be thought to be the Devil, because it is manifest that God does not use the ministry of evil angels for any good end, such as for the discovery of murder and the bringing of the guilty persons to deserved punishment; but on the contrary, he uses their service to tempt, seduce, deceive, punish, and torment. Therefore, we conceive that it was brought to pass by the finger of God, who, either immediately by himself or by the ministry of a good angel, represented those dreams to *Thomas Haworth* and revealed the precise place of *Waters'* burial.

And his own sister, overhearing his confession and account of it to another person, immediately revealed it to Sir *William Sheffield*—who lived in *Rascall* <note>Likely Raskelf, North Yorkshire</note> and was a Justice of the Peace—through fear of losing her own life. The two men were hung up in irons, and the woman was buried under the gallows. I have recited this story punctually as a thing that has been very much fixed in my memory, being then but young, and as a certain truth; I was (with many more) an ear-witness to their confessions and an eye-witness of their executions, and likewise saw *Fletcher* when he was taken up, where they had buried him in his clothes—which were a green fustian doublet pinked <note>Ornamentally slashed or perforated</note> over white, gray breeches, and his walking boots and brass spurs without rowels."

<margin>Observation.</margin>
Some will say there was no extrinsic apparition to *Raynard* at all, but that all this only arose from the guilt of his own conscience, which represented the shape of *Fletcher* in his imagination. But then why was it done precisely at that time, and not at any others? It being far from the place of the murder, or the place where they had buried *Fletcher*, and there was nothing there that might bring it to his remembrance more than at any other time. If it had only arisen from within and appeared so in his imagination, it would have been more likely to have been moved when he was in or near his backside <note>A yard or field behind a house</note> where the murdered body of *Fletcher* lay. But it is certain that he affirmed it was the shape and voice of *Fletcher*, as surely to his eyes and ears as he had ever seen or heard him in his life. And even if it were granted that it was only intrinsic, yet that will not exclude the Divine Power, which doubtless at that time labored to make him sensible of the cruel murder and to remind him of the approaching revenge. And it could not be brought to pass either by the Devil or *Fletcher’s* soul, as we have proved before; and therefore, in reason, we conclude that either it was wrought by the Divine Power to show His detestation of murder, or that it was the astral or sidereal spirit of *Fletcher* seeking revenge for the murder, of which we shall say more shortly.

<margin>*Observation*</margin>
And this I confess to be one of the most convincing stories (being
of undoubted truth) that I ever read, heard, or knew of, and it
carries with it the most evident force to satisfy the most incredulous
spirit that there are really sometimes such things as apparitions.
And though it is not easy to assign the true and proper cause of
such a strange effect, yet we must not judge all things to be, or
not to be, to be true or false, according to the extent of our
understandings; for if there are many of the *great works of nature*
<note>*magnalia naturae*</note> that yet lie hidden from the wisest of men, then much more
<margin>*Romans* 11:33.</margin>
may the *great works of God* <note>*magnalia Dei*</note> be unknown unto us, *whose judgments are
unsearchable, and his ways past finding out*. And as in the rest we
cannot attribute this strange apparition to any diabolical operation,
nor to the soul of the murdered woman, so we must conclude
that either it was merely wrought by the Divine Power, or by the
astral spirit of the murdered woman, which last seems most
rational, as we shall show hereafter.

<margin>Observation 1.</margin>
1. Although Mr. *Hotham* seems to judge that this accused person had the white powder from some spirit, and specifically one of the evil sort, and upon a contract by the engaging of his soul, we have before sufficiently proved the nullity of a visible and corporeal contract with the Devil. Neither was it ever yet proved that the Devil did any good, either real or apparent, but is the sworn enemy of all mankind, both in their souls and in their bodies; yet this powder performed that which was really good—namely, the curing of diseases—and therefore rationally cannot be thought to be given by an evil spirit.

<margin>Observation 2.</margin>
2. There were some who thought that the simple man told a plain and true story, and that he had the powder from those people we call Fairies. There are many who believe and affirm that there are such people, of whom *Paracelsus* wrote a treatise for that purpose, holding that they are not of the seed of Adam, and therefore he calls them <term>non-Adamicks</term>; he claims that they have flesh and bones, and so differ from spirits, and yet that they can glide through walls and rocks (which he calls their <term>Chaos</term>) as easily as we go through the air, and that they have children and are mortal like those whom *Hieronymus Cardanus* relates appeared to his father *Facius Cardanus*. These he calls <term>Pygmæi</term>, <term>Silvestres</term>, <term>Gnomi</term>, and <term>Umbratiles</term>. But his proof of their existence does not seem satisfactory to me; what others may think of it I leave to their own demonstrations, if they have any.

<margin>Observation 3.</margin>
3. There were some (and those not of the merely ignorant sort) who judged that, although the man was simple, the story he told was only framed and taught to him the better to conceal the person from whom he received the white powder. For they thought that some notable chemist, or rather an <term>Adeptist</term>, had in charity bestowed that powder upon him for the relief of himself and his family, as we know it has often happened to other persons at other times and places. And this last opinion seems most consonant with reason, and I believe it all the more because, not many years after, it was certainly known that there was an <term>Adeptist</term> in that country; and we ought not to bring in supernatural causes to explain effects when natural causes may serve the purpose.

Gregorius *Horstius*, a physician of great experience, learning, and no less integrity, records this story, translated into English as follows:

<margin>Append. de Cruent. cada- ver. p. 143.</margin>
> “In the year of our Lord 1604, on the twenty-sixth day of *December*, a young nobleman, twenty-five years old, was shot with a gun in the night time around nine o'clock from a high window of a house in the town of *Blindmarck* in lower *Austria*. The bullet, entering his left breast, went out through his right side, and he died immediately on the spot. The dead body being viewed again and the wound considered, the same size for both the entrance and exit was found, with a great deal of blood issuing forth. The following day, being the twenty-seventh of *December* in the morning, the body of the murdered young man had other clothes put upon it, and so was kept still for the space of two days. Furthermore, on the thirtieth of *December*, he was laid upon the bier and kept in the church without any further movement; nevertheless, from the upper wound, fresh blood flowed daily until the eighth of *January* 1605, at which time the *hemorrhage* ceased. But again on the thirteenth of *February*, about noon, the flow of blood from the lower wound was observed to issue for an hour or two, as though the killing had been newly done. In the meantime, the condition of the entire body was such as most easily matched what it was when living; the color of his face remained ruddy and healthy even until his burial, and the vein appearing in his forehead was filled with good blood. No sign of beginning putrefaction appeared for so many weeks; no stench or unpleasant odor, which otherwise accompanies dead bodies within a few days, was found here at all. The fingers of the hands remained soft, movable, or flexible, without any wasting away, the natural color being not very much changed, except that in the course of time, during the last week before burial, they began in a certain manner to turn blue at the extremities.

Some may think that I have been too long-winded and tedious in piling
up so many stories concerning the bleeding of the bodies of those
that have been murdered; but I did it for this reason: because there
are many who think it to be but a fable of the gullible public,
and others think that it is but an ordinary matter that happens to
any bodies that are dead, with no extraordinary or supernatural thing
in it at all. But whosoever shall use even so much patience as seri-
ously to read and consider these select histories that we have recited,
may easily be satisfied, both that such bleeding is absolutely true *in*
*fact*, and also that there is something more than ordinary in it;
and therefore we shall expand upon these observations.

<margin>Observ. 1.</margin>
1. It will not be found to hold true upon diligent observation
and strict inquiry that all dead bodies bleed fresh and rosy
blood, especially after the third or fourth day, or after some weeks,
as various of the instances given above manifestly prove; and
therefore it is an occurrence incident to some dead bodies and not to all.
And it will just as certainly fail that wounded bodies, which have been slain in the
wars, after the natural heat is gone, will bleed any
fresh or crimson blood at all upon being moved; for we ourselves in the recent times of
Rebellion have seen some thousands of dead bodies that have had
various wounds, and lying naked and being turned over and over, and
thrown ten or twelve into one pit, and yet not one of them has
issued any fresh and pure blood. Only from some of their wounds,
some <term>sanious matter</term> would have flowed, putrefaction beginning by
reason of the moisture and acidity in the air, but no pure blood;
and therefore it is not a common occurrence to all human bodies that
die naturally or violently, but only is peculiar to some, and espe-
cially to those that are murdered by premeditated malice, as ap-
pears in the histories recited above.

<margin>Observ. 2.</margin>
2. We shall acknowledge with *Gregorius Horstius*, *Sperlingius*,
and *Gothofredus Voigtius* that sometimes the bodies of those that
have been murdered do bleed when the murderer is not present, as
is manifest from the sixth history recited from *Horstius* of the young
man of twenty-five years old, who bled so long and so often,
though the murderer was not present; from which they conclude
that the presence of the murderer is not a necessary cause of the
bleeding of the murdered body, and therefore that the bleeding
of the body is not always a certain and infallible sign of discov-
ering the murderer. To which we reply, that the issuing of fresh
and crimson blood from the wound or the nostrils of the person's
body that has been murdered is always a certain sign that the

Again, if the murderer is certainly known, or has confessed the crime, in regard to the final cause—which is discovery—there is no reason why the corpse should bleed. And though the presence of the murderer may not be the efficient cause why the corpse does bleed, yet it is the occasional cause, as is manifest undeniably by several of the histories that we have related, where the murderers would not have been certainly known except for the bleeding of the murdered body.

<margin>Observ. 3.</margin>
3. Whereas the three authors named above, thinking they have sufficiently refuted those who ascribed this effect of the bleeding of the dead body to sympathy or antipathy, or to the movement of the bodies, or heat in the air, have assigned the cause to be the beginning of putrefaction in the murdered bodies, by which a new motion is caused in the humors, and so in the blood, by which means it flows afresh; against this, these two reasons oppose themselves. 1. Must putrefaction necessarily begin at that very moment when the murderer touches the body? For in several of them there was no bleeding until the murderers were present or did touch the bodies, and their touching could not cause the beginning of putrefaction; and soon after their removal the bleeding has ceased, so that putrescence *in fieri* <note>putrefaction in progress</note> cannot be the cause of the fresh bleeding. 2. Putrefaction beginning could not be the cause of why the murdered shepherd's body in the ninth history should point with its hands to the wound and to the murderers, nor that the hands of the girl murdered by the Jews, in the tenth history, should be stretched forth to the Prince of Baden, or that the lips and nostrils of the body of *Gawkley* should work and open at the touch of the murderer *How*; this must of necessity proceed from some higher cause than putrefaction, or any other they have laid down.

<margin>Observ. 6.</margin>
6. There are some who ascribe these strange bleedings of murdered
bodies, and their strange motions—along with the sweating of blood,
as upon the peddler's curved dagger or knife mentioned in the
eleventh history—unto the Astral or Sidereal spirit (and that not
improbably). They suggest that this is a middle substance between the soul and
the body which, when separated from the body, wanders or hovers near
about it, bearing with it the irascible and concupiscible faculties <note>the faculties of anger and desire</note>.
Being stirred up to hatred and revenge, it causes that
ebullition <note>bubbling or boiling</note> and motion in the blood, that oozing of blood upon
the weapon, and those other wonderful motions of the body, hands,
nostrils, and lips, thereby to discover the murderer and bring
him to deserved punishment. Nor is any tenet yet brought forward by
anyone that is more rationally probable to solve these and many other
wonderful phenomena than this of the Astral Spirit, if it can
but be fully proved that there is such a part of man that does
separately exist, which we shall endeavor to prove before we end this
chapter.

<margin>Observ. 7.</margin>
7. But it is granted on all sides that if the murderer is brought
into the presence, or the touch, of the murdered person who is not
quite dead, then the wounds—though closed and stopped from bleeding—
or the nostrils, will freshly break forth and bleed plentifully. The
reason is obvious: because the soul being yet in the body, retaining
its power of sensation, imagination, and understanding, will easily
have a presension <note>foreknowledge or intuitive feeling</note> of the murderer. Then it is no wonder that through
the vehement desire for revenge, the irascible and concupiscible
faculties strongly move the blood (which before was beginning to
become stagnant) to motion and ebullition, and may exert so much force
upon the organs as to move the whole body,
the hands, or the lips and nostrils for some small time. So all that is to be done
is to prove that the murdered person is not absolutely dead,
and that the soul is not totally separated or departed out of the
body; and this we shall do by such undeniable proofs as follow in this order.

# CHAP. XVI. Supposed Witchcraft.

1. Although we generally consider death to be a perfect separation of the soul from the body—which is most certainly a great truth—exactly when this is certainly brought to pass is a most difficult point to determine. Because when the soul ceases to operate in the body in a way that can be perceived by our senses, it does not follow that the soul is therefore absolutely departed and separated.

<margin>Observ. Medic. p. 617, 618.</margin>
2. It is manifest that many persons, through this mistake, have been buried alive in times of the Plague; likewise, some women have been treated this way who lay only in fits of the "suffocation of the womb" <note>an old medical term for hysterical or respiratory fits</note>, and yet were taken to be dead. So, from the judgment of our senses, no certain conclusion can be made that the soul is totally departed, because it goes away invisibly. For many who were accounted dead—not only in the judgment of the common people, but even in the opinion of learned physicians—have nonetheless revived, as the learned *Schenckius* has furnished us with this story from *Georgius Pictorius*:

> "that a certain woman lay in the strangulation of the womb for six continuous days without sense or motion, her arteries having grown hard, and was ready to be buried; yet she revived again. He also cites *Paraeus* regarding some who have lain for three days in hysterical suffocations and yet have recovered, and various others that may be seen in the place quoted in the margin.

3. So, although the organs of the body may be rendered so unfit by various means—either natural or violent—that the soul cannot perform its accustomed functions in them or by them in a way perceptible to our senses or judgments, that does not at all prove that the soul is separated and departed entirely from the body. Much less can we be able to define or establish the precise time of the soul's stay in the body, nor the final period when it must depart; for the union may be (and undoubtedly is) stronger in some than in others, and the lamp of life is much sooner and more easily extinguished in some than in others. And the soul may have a much greater love <note>amorosity</note> to stay in a body that is lively, sweet, and young, than in others that are already decaying and beginning to rot. It may, in all probability, have both the power and the desire to stay longer in that lovely habitation from which it is driven by force—especially so that it may satisfy itself by discovering the murderer (the most cruel and inhuman separator of that loving pair which God had divinely coupled together) and to see itself, before its final departure, in a hopeful way to be revenged.

4. If we physically consider the union of the soul with the body through the mediation of the spirit, then we cannot rationally conceive that the soul utterly forsakes that union until, by putrefaction leading to an absolute change, it is forced to bid farewell to its beloved tabernacle. For its not operating externally <note>ad extra</note> to our senses does not necessarily infer its total absence. And it may be that there is more in that passage of Abel's blood crying to the Lord from the ground, in a physical sense, than is commonly understood,

There is another kind of supposed apparitions that are believed to be performed in beryls and clear crystals, and are therefore called by *Paracelsus* <term>Ars Beryllistica</term>, which he also calls nigromancy <term>nigromancy</term> because it is practiced in the dark by the inspection of a boy or a maid who are virgins. What truth there may be in this assertion of his, I have yet met with no reasons or experiments that can satisfy me, and therefore I leave it to every man to judge as he pleases.

I admit I have heard strange stories of things that have been revealed by these supposed apparitions from persons of both great worth and learning; but seeking more narrowly into the matter, I found them all to be superstitious delusions, fancies, mistakes, cheats, and impostures. For the most part, the child says anything that comes into his imagination, or deliberately frames and invents things that he never sees at all, and the inquirers immediately adapt them to their own thoughts and suspicions. Some who pretended to show and foretell strange things in order to get money have been discovered to have had accomplices who carried away men's goods into secret places and informed the <term>cunning man</term> where they were hidden; then the child was taught a prepared story to describe what kind of man took them away and where they were. When these were found, it brought enough credit to the swindlers, and I know this was practiced by individuals named *Brooke* and *Bolton*. Some have had artificial glasses into which they would project little pictures, as Dr. *Lambe* had.

2. However, it requires a longer time than the body because it consists of purer elements than the other, and some of these Astral Spirits or bodies decay sooner than others, depending on whether they are more or less pure. And this Astral Spirit is nothing more than that part of man that is commonly called the sensitive soul, and by the Schools is commonly defined thus: <margin>*On the Soul of Brutes, Ch. 1, 2.*</margin> *The sensing soul is the power that apprehends and perceives those things which are outside of itself.* And this is corporeal, and (as Dr. *Willis* holds) mortal and coextended with the body; it has the power of imagination, appetite, desire, aversion, and the like, and in a manner, a sensitive way of reasoning, yet it is distinct from the rational soul or *mens* that is incorporeal, immortal, and far more excellent. And the insightful *Helmont*, holding this sensitive soul to be distinct from the *mens* or immortal and rational soul, says this: *Therefore the sensitive soul is perishable, mortal, a mere vital light given by the Father of Lights, and not explainable in any other way or word.* But of the rational soul he says: *But the immortal mind itself is a luminous, incorporeal substance, immediately reflecting the image of its God, because it received that same image inscribed upon itself at the moment of creation, or in the very instant of ensoulment (Empsychois).* So both these recent and learned authors hold that in every man there are two distinct souls: the sensitive that is mortal, corporeal, and coextended with the body; and the rational that is immortal and absolutely incorporeal. Thus, though they seem to differ in words and terms, they agree in substance. For the Hermetic School, the Platonists, *Paracelsus*, *Jacob Behemen*, and others hold that there are three parts in man which they call Soul, Spirit, and Body. These last two authors hold the body to be one part in man, and two souls besides—the sensitive and rational—which are two distinct parts, the one corporeal and mortal, and the other incorporeal and immortal, and so they only differ in name. And now our task must be to prove, first, that there are such three parts in man, and that after death they separately exist, which we shall attempt in the following order.
