8. Lastly as to this point, it is a certain truth that two extremes cannot be joined or coupled together, but by some middle thing that participates in or comes near to the nature of both. So the Soul which (by the unanimous consent of all men) is a spiritual and pure, immaterial and incorporeal substance cannot be united to the body, which is a most gross, thick, and corporeal substance, without the intervention of some middle nature, fit to conjoin and unite those extremes together, which is this sensitive and corporeal Soul or Astral Spirit, which in respect of the one extreme is corporeal, yet of the most pure sort of bodies that are in nature, and that which approaches most near to a spiritual and immaterial substance, and therefore most fit to be the immediate receptacle of the incorporeal Soul: And also it being truly body does easily join with the gross body, as indeed being congenerate with it, and so becomes *vinculum & nexus* <note>a bond and connection</note> of the immaterial Soul and the more gross body, that without it it could not be united.

# CHAP. XVII.

## Of the power and efficacy of Words or Charms: whether they effect anything at all, and if they do, whether it be by Natural or Diabolical power and force.

There is almost nothing so common, not only among the poets (who have been the primary disseminators of many such things) but in most other authors, as the mention of the power of charms and incantations. And yet, if we search narrowly into the bottom of the matter, there is nothing more difficult than to find any truth regarding their effects in matters of fact. Therefore, so that we may more clearly explain what we have proposed in this chapter, we shall first set forth these few points:

1. Those who believe their effects to be great—as many theologians, philosophers, and physicians do—suppose no efficacy to be in the charms alone, holding that *quantitates rerum nullius sunt efficaciæ* <note>the quantities of things have no efficacy</note>. Instead, they believe charms are only signs from the Devil to delude the minds of those who use them, while in the meantime the Devil produces the effects. But it would have been well if those who hold this opinion had shown us the ways and means by which the Devil operates such things, seeing as he can do nothing in physical matter except by natural means. So, we must either confess that there is no power at all in charms, or that the effects produced are by natural means.

2. Nor can we fully agree with those who hold that the force of imagination can work strange things upon other bodies, distinct and separate from the body of the person imagining—though it is not denied that imagination has the power to operate very wonderful things upon one's own body. This is for the reason given by the most learned Lord Verulam, which is this: <margin>Sylva Sylvarum, Century 10, page 583.</margin> *Experimenta quæ vim imaginationis in corpora aliena solidè probent, pauca aut nulla prorsus sunt; cum fascini exempla huc non faciant, quod Dæmonum interventu fortasse non careant.* <note>Experiments that solidly prove the power of imagination upon the bodies of others are few or none at all; since examples of fascination do not apply here, as they perhaps may involve the intervention of demons.</note>

3. I said I did not agree "fully," because there are some reasons that incline me to believe in the possibility of it, even though there are hardly any experiments found that solidly prove it. For as the said Lord Verulam says again: <margin>Ibid., page 594.</margin> *Movendi sunt homines, ne fidem detrahant operationibus ex transmissione spirituum, & vi imaginationis, quia eventus quandoque fallit.* <note>People are to be urged not to deny faith to operations resulting from the transmission of spirits and the power of imagination, simply because the outcome occasionally fails.</note> And there are so many learned authors of all sorts (though Dr. Casaubon, in his scurrilous manner, styles them <term>Enthusiastical Arabs</term>) who so stubbornly maintain the power of the imagination upon external bodies with such strength of argument, that I hesitate greatly concerning the point, and therefore dare not say I fully agree with either side. For the learned Dr. Willis, having (as we conceive) unanswerably proved that there

How far the force of imagination, which is its instrument, may reach, or what it may work at a distance, is not easy to determine. And if the Soul—as *Helmont* labors to prove by the prerogative of its creation—can, when excited by strong desire and exalted fantasy, operate *per nutum* <note>by a mere command or nod of the will</note>, then it must necessarily follow that it may work upon other bodies than its own. But if these three conclusions be certain and true, written by the pen of a most learned, though less commonly known Author, namely: “1. The Soul is not only in its proper visible body, but also outside it; neither is it circumscribed within an organical body. 2. The Soul works outside, or beyond its proper body commonly so called. 3. From every body flow corporeal beams, by which the Soul works by its presence, and gives them energy and power of working; and these beams are not only corporeal, but consist of diverse parts also.” If these (I say) be certain, then the imagination does work at a distance by means of those beams. Consequently, Words and Charms, and such like, may be the means and instruments by which the imagination (being the principal power of the sensitive Soul) may operate strange things at a distance, and so what the learned *Agrippa* tells us would not be in vain:

<note>“It is not Hell, nor the stars of Heaven, that dwell in us; the Spirit that flourishes within us does those things.”</note>

And we must in all reason acknowledge that the sensitive Soul must necessarily be of as much purity and energy as those that we call the sensible or visible species of things; then it must necessarily follow that it, by means of the imagination, may operate at a great distance, and so words and charms may from there have power and operation. For the learned *Agrippa*, that great Philosopher and master of lawful and natural Magic—and not of that which is accounted diabolical (as the wretched pen of *Paulus Jovius* has depicted him)—holds this: *Quod unicuique homini impressus est Character Divinus, cujus vigore potest pertingere ad operandum mirabilia.* <note>That a Divine Character is impressed upon every man, by the vigor of which he can attain to working wonders.</note> If this is so, then many words, charms, and the like have a natural efficacy to work wonderful things, and that at a great distance also.

Augerius Ferrerius, whom *Thuanus* calls a *Most Learned Physician*, in his treatment of Homeric medication, after he has quoted *Galen's* recantation from *Trallianus*, and various arguments and examples to prove the efficacy of words, charms, and characters from him, from *Aetius*, and others, he concludes thus: "When you see their experience placed before your eyes and confirmed by the authority of so many illustrious men, what will you do? For to go against those things which are exposed to the senses is not the mark of a sane man; and to invalidate the experiments of the learned is rash." <note>Quorum experientiam cum ob oculos positam, & tot illustrium virorum authoritate confirmata videris, quid facies? Lastly, for the sake of authority, we shall add the opinion of the wise *Helmont*, who wrote a book he titled, *In words, herbs, and stones there is great power* <note>In verbis, herbis, & lapidibus est magna virtus</note>; and concerning the efficacy of words he says only this: "I have spoken frankly of certain things regarding the great power of words, which I admire more than I apply." <note>De magna virtute verborum quædam ingenue dixi, quæ magis admiror quam applico.</note> By which it is manifest that though *Helmont* did not make use of words or charms, yet knowing their efficacy, he could not help but admire them.

These authorities joined with the examples may suffice to convince any rational man that at certain times and places, and by some persons, the use of charms has produced strange effects. Therefore, taking the matter of fact to be true, we should come to examine the cause of these effects; but first it will be necessary to present some cautions and necessary considerations, which we shall pursue in this order.

<margin>*Natural History, book 28, chapter 2, page 397.* Consideration 1.</margin>
1. We are to consider the intricacy and difficulty of this point, which has exercised the wits of the learned in all ages and forced *Pliny* to say: "It is a very great question, and always uncertain, whether words and the incantations of songs have any power." <note>Maxima quæstionis, & semper incertæ est, valeantne aliquid verba & incantamenta carminum.</note> And again more particularly: "Opinions vary regarding these things, according to each person's character or chance, as to whether wild animals are soothed by speech; indeed, whether it is true or false that even serpents are drawn out by chanting and forced into punishment, life has not decided." <note>Varia circa hæc opinio, ex ingenio cujusque; vel casu, mulce-ri alloquio feras: quippe ubi etiam Serpentes extrahi cantu cogiq; in pœnas, verum falsumne sit, vita non decreverit.</note> It seems by *Pliny* that learned men of old were very much divided in their opinions about this matter, so much so that he does not dare to take it upon himself to decide it, but leaves it free for every man to believe as they see cause. And therefore we ought not to be condemned if we do not absolutely decide it either; it is enough if we bring so much light to the matter that it may be better understood, even if not absolutely determined, *In great things, it is enough to have willed them* <note>In magnis voluisse sat est</note>.

About three weeks later, when the stump was nearly healed and I was away from home, his mother was lying in the same room with him. Having had too much to drink, she did not hear him when he called upon her to help him to the commode <note>close-stool</note>. He scrambled up himself as well as he could, but hit the end of the stump that was not quite closed, whereby the arteries were opened and a great hemorrhage followed. And there being an honest, simple man who owned the house where he lay, who had a vain confidence that with a charm he said he possessed, he could undoubtedly stop the bleeding, he therefore would not allow them to call my assistant to stop the flow <note>flux</note> until daybreak. Because it continued so long, and the vain and fruitless charm accomplished nothing, though my assistant did stop it when he arrived, he had lost so much blood that he died the next day. This may serve as a sufficient caution against vain confidence in charms."

<margin>Consideration 4.</margin>
4. Furthermore, we are to consider that there are many notorious impostures, frauds, and cheats committed upon the poor, ignorant, credulous, and simple common people. Some make the people believe that their diseases are inflicted by certain saints, and therefore they must use various strange purifications <note>lustrations</note>, ritual burnings <note>suffumigations</note>, and other vain, superstitious rites and ceremonies. Others pretend to drive away evil spirits by exorcisms and conjurations, and others pretend to cure almost all diseases with words, charms, characters [written symbols], amulets, and the like. Most of these pretenders are mere ignorant knaves and impostors who do nothing but cheat the overly credulous people of their money and defame and dishonor the most noble art of medicine, of which we have known various sorts, some of which we have mentioned before in this treatise.

<margin>*On the Sacred Disease, book, section 3, page 301.*</margin>
To such as these, that ancient author (supposed by some to be *Hippocrates*) in *On the Sacred Disease*, gives sufficient reproof, saying of them: *“And to me, certainly, those who first attributed this disease to the gods seem to be such as are magi, purifiers, charlatans, and arrogant pretenders, who feign themselves to be very pious and to know a great deal.”* A very large catalog of these kinds of pestiferous impostors, and many others, you have fully and vividly portrayed by *Paracelsus* in his preface to his *Lesser Surgery*, where he has sufficiently stigmatized them with all those wicked marks and brands that justly belong to them. The same is also fully performed by the learned *Langius* in his epistles, to whom I refer the readers.

### CHAP. XVII. Supposed Witchcraft.

There are chiefly three opinions, among those that grant the truth of the matter of fact, concerning the proper cause of these effects produced by words. 1. Of which the first sort are those that hold there is no efficiency at all in the words themselves, which are nothing but the sign of the league and compact between the Charmer and the Devil, and that whatever is brought to pass is only effected by the Devil's power; and of this opinion are the greatest part of the learned. 2. Are those that hold that the words or charms are but means to heighten the imagination, and that it is the strength of the exalted imagination only that produces those things that seem to be effected by those words or charms; and of this opinion was *Avicen* and many of the Arabians, *Ferrerius*, *Montanus* and many others. 3. There are those that hold that there is a natural efficiency in words and characters rightly fitted and joined together in proper and agreeable constellations; and of this opinion were *Johannes Ludovicus de la Cerda*, *Johannes Branus Camisius Lusitanus*, *Paracelsus*, *Galeottus Martius*, *Henricus Cornelius Agrippa*, and many others; and of these we shall speak in order.

<margin>Reason 1. against this opinion.</margin>
1. The first opinion takes up a false supposition for its ground, namely that the Devil makes a visible and corporeal league with the Charmer, by virtue of which compact the effects are produced; and if this compact be not explicit, yet it may be implicit, and so the Devil operates the effects, thereby to draw the Charmer into his league and service. But we have before sufficiently proved the invalidity <note>nullity</note> of any such Covenant, and shown plainly that it is a false, impious, and diabolical tenet, and that there is not, nor can be, any other league between the Devil and wicked men but what is spiritual, internal, and mental; and therefore that the Devil does not bring those effects to pass by pretense of a league that has no being or existence.

<margin>Reason 2. against this opinion.</margin>
2. We have proved by the unanimous consent of the entire army of the learned that the Devil can work no alteration or change in natural bodies except by the applying of fit agents to agreeable patients; but what agent could the Devil have applied to make the iron that stuck in the soldier's shoulder bone, related by *Benevenius*, to come forth without pain? Surely none at all. For where an agent in nature is wanting to produce an effect, there the Devil must necessarily also be ineffectual <note>lame</note> and can effect nothing; and if either the words had a sufficient natural power to cause the iron to come forth, or the soldier's imagination was exalted by confidence in the Charm and Charmer, then the Devil's help is in vain implored,

3. It cannot for any reason be imagined that the Devil, who for the space of over five thousand years has been the bitter and inveterate enemy to the health of man, both in soul and body, should now have become a physician and a healer. We read that God sent forth evil angels among the people, but he sent forth his word and they were healed. But it is manifest that the evil angels, since their fall, are ordained by God to be the instruments and organs for the executing of his wrath, and the good angels are his ministering spirits for the good of his people, both in souls and bodies. Therefore, that the Devil should be the author or instrument of curing any disease at all would be to make him act contrary to that end for which God has ordained him; for he is the destroyer, who is ordained to destroy, but not to heal.

4. *Avicenna*, *Algazel*, *Alkindus*, *Marsilius Ficinus*, *Jacobus de Forlivio*, *Pomponatius*, *Paracelsus*, and others, sometimes hold

Sometimes they hold that the whole soul (meaning the sensitive) goes completely out of the body and wanders into far distant places, and there not only sees what things are done, but also acts upon something itself."

And with this opinion (meaning only the immortal and immaterial soul), Dr. *Moore* and Mr. *Glanvil* seem to agree: namely, that the soul may for a time depart from its body and return again. And to prove this, the argument of *Avicenna* is this: superior things (he says) have dominion over the inferior, and the Intelligences rule and change corporeal things. And as the soul is a spiritual and separable substance, it may therefore act upon corporeal things in the same manner and change them, as may be seen at length, with the responses, in the book of *Fienus*.

Now we come to the third and last opinion of those who positively hold that there is a force in words and characters (if rightly framed) to effect strange things, and this is strongly denied by many. Therefore we shall only offer the most convincing arguments that we meet with and leave it to the judgment of others, in this order.

But before we enter upon the positive arguments, we think it fit—lest we be mistaken (though we may have touched on some of them before)—to lay down a few cautions and considerations, which we shall do in this manner.

And so many secrets of both nature and art are esteemed to be magical by the unlearned. And magicians do foolishly trust in charms and characters, judging virtue to be in them, and because of their vain confidence in them, they forsake the work of nature and art by reason of the error of charms and characters. By the same reason, there are certain celestial virtues and actions in existence which, being sown into gems (which were called *Peantides* and *Gamahii*—otherwise *gemma huya*—by the ancient magicians), later spring up no differently than a seed which falls from a tree and regerminates. So (he says) we have seen *Gemmas Huyas*, that is *Peantides*, in which the sign of Sagittarius was engraved for protection against weapons, and these were effective against wounds made with swords. We have also known (he says) that magicians have made stones effective for curing fevers—and not only have they made them strong enough to cure diseases, but also wounds and their symptoms, namely hemorrhage, <term>synovia</term> (or joint-water), convulsions, and epilepsy. But as the use of these was frequent and their authority great in that age, so by degrees, as the false arguments of fake philosophers increased, they fell into disuse and contempt, and other childish things have been substituted in their place. But these stones (because now the position and influence of the heavens are clearly different than they were in times past) are no longer as effective as they were then; therefore, it is necessary that they be prepared anew.

> “The Magical Art—because it was more secret and not known to common philosophers, and because it produced wonderful virtues not only in stones but also in similar words—began to be called the 'prestigious' [deceitful] art, an offensive term. For men who were unskilled in these things, yet who nonetheless claimed the title of the Art for themselves, devoted themselves to artificial operations, crosses, and exorcisms. From that, the common people, being unskilled in the Magical Art, began to attribute this virtue to exorcisms, characters, short prayers, seals, crosses, and other frivolous things. But the matter (he says) is quite different: for the astrological alignment under which the stones and words are prepared brings about the virtues, not the exorcisms.

<margin>Argument 7.</margin>
7. There is also an experiment that has been sufficiently tried and attested, which does much induce me to believe that there is efficacy in words and charms above their significance by imposition and institution, and that is this. They take two lutes rightly stringed and laid upon a long table, and then they lay a light straw, chaff, or feather upon the unison string of the one, and then they strike, or move the unison string of the other lute that lies at the other end of the table. By this motion of the unison string at the one end of the table, the straw, chaff, or feather upon the unison string of the lute at the other end of the table (though it be of the longest sort) will by the vibration of the air be moved, or struck off; and yet it will not do it if the straw be laid upon any other string and then the unison of the other lute moved. By which it is manifest that the striking or moving the unison string of the one lute does so shape <note>figurate</note> and dispose the atoms of the air that they are fit and apt to move the unison string of the other lute, and so to make the straw fall off, as being of an agreeable mood and temper for the reception <note>susception</note> of the motion, which the rest of the other strings (being of different degrees and nature) are not: for the maxim is true, *Whatever is received, is received according to the manner of the recipient* <note>*Quicquid recipitur, recipitur ad modum recipientis.*</note>. And this being so, it must also be granted that words and rhythms fitly joined and composed, being pronounced, do put the atoms of the air into such a position <note>site</note>, motion, figure, and composition <note>contexture</note> that may at a distance operate upon the subject for which they are so fitted, and produce such effects as they were composed and intended for: especially being framed under powerful and suitable constellations, from which they receive their greatest force.

<margin>Argument 8.</margin>
8. The chief objection that is usually brought against the natural agency of fitly composed words or rhythms is a maxim of the Schools, ill understood and worse applied, which is this: *The quantities of things are of no efficacy* <note>*Quantitates rerum, nullius sunt efficaciæ*</note>: unto which we shall provide these responses.

1. If quantity be taken mathematically and abstractly, then it is true that it is of no efficacy or operation, because it is then only a thing of reason <note>*ens rationis*</note> and exists only in the intellect, and so can operate nothing externally <note>*ad extra*</note>. But if it be taken concretely, physically, and as material <note>materiate</note>, then it is of force and very operative, as two pounds of lead will weigh down one pound of the same lead, and two ounces of the same gunpowder will carry a bullet of the same size <note>quantity</note> further and more forcibly than one ounce of the same will do. And one scruple of white hellebore may be taken when a dram <note>drachm</note> will kill, and a fire of a yard in diameter will warm a man at a greater distance than a fire but of one foot in diameter.

no quantities: For figures and characters are only delineations and circumscriptions of some kind of matter, and are all, whether natural or artificial, properly contained under quality, and denote what figure or Form the thing is of. Figure therefore is properly attributed to artificial things, such as a circle, a square, a triangle, and the like; and form to animate things, such as a man, a horse, an ox, and the like: And so characters, whether engraved in metals, gems, stones, clay, plaster or wood, or written upon parchment, paper, or the like, of what figure or form soever they be, are but qualities, and do qualify the matter according to the form and figure impressed in the subject matter; which being artificially done, the matter is the patient <note>the thing acted upon</note>, the figure or character is the exemplar cause <note>the model or pattern</note>, and the force that makes the impression is the efficient cause; and that these as qualities have some efficacy, no rational man can deny.

<margin>Ramus, *Geometria*, book 19, p. 144.</margin>
3. But to make it more clearly manifest, let us suppose three various figures that are isoperimetral <note>having equal perimeters</note>, such as a circle, a plain square, and an equilateral triangle: Though they be all of equal circumference, yet the circle shall contain more than either the square or the triangle; and therefore the learned *Ramus* does lay down this rule: *Circulus è planis Isoperimetris inæqualibus est maximus* <note>The circle is the greatest of unequal isoperimetrical planes</note>. But when the question is asked, what is the cause why a circle, among figures of equal circumference, contains the most? The answer is commonly made, *Quia omnium figurarum perfectissimus, & capacissimus est circulus* <note>Because the circle is the most perfect and capacious of all figures</note>; but if it be again urged, what is the cause that a circle of an equal circumference to a plain square should be more capacious than the square? Here (the thing being found true by ocular experience) the capaciousness of the circle, more than the square (they being both of equal circumference), can be ascribed to nothing else at all but only to the figure, and therefore of necessity, figures have in them some efficiency.

<margin>See *Logica Systematis Harmonici* by Alsted, p. 249.</margin>
4. That which we call speech, or oration, is considered in three ways. 1. That which is mental and only conceived in the mind, and not expressed. 2. That which is expressed or uttered by the vocal organs. 3. And that which is written. And these are called mental, vocal, and written. The two—that is, the mental and that which is written—are referred to the predicament <note>category</note> of quality. And whereas vocal oration is by some referred to the predicament of quantity, as it is the measure of sounds and syllables as it is pronounced, whereof some are made long and some short; and so while distinct sounds and syllables are uttered in a certain mode, they are said to be measured, and to belong to quantity: But if we will understand aright, one thing in different respects may belong both to the predicament of quantity and quality. So the utterance of sounds or syllables in respect of their modification, and comparing one to another, some may be long and some may be short, and have a different part of time in their pronunciation, and so may analogically, and by way of similitude, be said to be measured, and consequently referred to the predicament of quantity. Because of this, such a great diversity of impulses or sounds is made upon the eardrum that we are naturally able to distinguish one from another. Now, human convention discovered ways to make these various sounds or tones appropriate to specific things, or to signify the diversity of creatures and objects, according to the various pacts and agreements men made among themselves. Thus, what one sound signifies in one language may signify something else in another. So, setting aside the convention or invention of this or that meaning for various sounds in different languages, every sound or articulate utterance naturally creates a distinct and separate impulse upon the ear and thereby the senses; consequently, the mind is variously affected by them.
